source.title: 19th Batch CVP 112 Booklet · corrected edition
source.availability: Every source question is logged with its original PDF page. Large original retained outside the publisher package.

questions.question: Influx of which of the following ions contributes most to maintaining the plateau in a ventricular myocyte action potential?
questions.explanation: A — Calcium. Inward L-type Ca²⁺ current sustains the plateau. B drives the rapid upstroke, C mainly flows out during the plateau, and D provides no major plateau current.
reasons: Calcium entry is the relevant inward plateau current.
Fast sodium current chiefly drives the ventricular phase-0 upstroke.
Potassium currents are primarily outward in this plateau/repolarization context, not the inward current asked for.
Chloride is not the principal inward current sustaining the plateau.
questions.sourceQuestion: Influx of which of the following ions contributes most to maintaining the plateau in a ventricular myocyte action potential?

questions.question: In this SA node action potential, which channel is responsible for the phase marked by the Arrow?
options: Decrease in conductance of T-type calcium channels
Decrease in conductance of L-type calcium channel
Increase in conductance through fast Na+ channels
Increase in conductance through funny current Na+ channels
questions.explanation: D — Funny current. The arrow points to early phase 4. HCN channels carry a mixed Na⁺/K⁺ current with net inward flow. A would reduce a later depolarizing current, B helps end the upstroke, C is typical of fast-response tissue, and E favors repolarization. Physiological Reviews (https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00043.2021)
questions.sourceQuestion: In this SA node action potential, which channel is responsible for the phase marked by the Arrow?

questions.question: During phase 4 of the ventricular action potential which ion is the plasma membrane most permeable to?
questions.explanation: A — K⁺. Inward-rectifier K⁺ channels dominate ventricular resting conductance. B, C and D have lower resting conductance.
questions.sourceQuestion: During phase 4 of the ventricular action potential which ion is the plasma membrane most permeable to?

questions.question: Which of the following movements of ions across the surface membrane of the ventricular muscle cell is responsible for the plateau phase (phase 2) of the ventricular muscle? (Use the diagram in question 3)
questions.explanation: B — Ca²⁺ in, K⁺ out. These currents nearly balance in phase 2. A and C reverse K⁺ flow, C and D reverse Ca²⁺ flow, and E substitutes Na⁺ extrusion for the main outward K⁺ current.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following movements of ions across the surface membrane of the ventricular muscle cell is responsible for the plateau phase (phase 2) of the ventricular muscle? (Use the diagram in question 3)

questions.question: What is the effect of the sympathetic nervous system on the action potential of SA node?
questions.explanation: C — Steeper phase 4. β₁ stimulation increases cAMP and accelerates diastolic depolarization. A would slow firing. B describes repolarization and misses the main rate effect.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the effect of the sympathetic nervous system on the action potential of SA node?

questions.question: What ion channels are responsible for the part of the graph with the arrow?
options: Opening of L-type Ca2+ channel and closing of delayed K+ channel.
Closing of L type Ca2+ channel and opening of delayed rectifier K+ channel.
Opening of T-type Ca2+ channel and closing of delayed K+ channel.
Opening of a funny current channel and closing of a delayed K+ channel.
questions.explanation: B — L-type Ca²⁺ current wanes and delayed-rectifier K⁺ current repolarizes. The arrow marks the peak and transition into phase 3. A favors the upstroke. C and D favor phase 4 depolarization.
questions.sourceQuestion: What ion channels are responsible for the part of the graph with the arrow?

questions.question: Which of the following currents initiates the slow depolarization (phase 4) of sinoatrial node cells?
questions.explanation: A — Funny current. HCN channels activate at negative voltage after repolarization. B drives the nodal upstroke, C assists later phase 4, and D drives the upstroke in fast-response cells.
reasons: The funny current initiates the gradual pacemaker depolarization described.
L-type calcium current is especially important for the nodal upstroke.
T-type calcium can contribute near threshold but is not the initiating current specified here.
Fast sodium channels do not generate the usual SA nodal phase-0 upstroke.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following currents initiates the slow depolarization (phase 4) of sinoatrial node cells?

questions.question: Early repolarization (phase 1) of the ventricular action potential is caused by which of the following membrane currents?
questions.explanation: B — Rapid transient outward K⁺ current. It creates the phase 1 notch after fast Na⁺ channels inactivate. A causes phase 0, C drives later repolarization, D sustains phase 2, and E chiefly stabilizes the resting voltage.
questions.sourceQuestion: Early repolarization (phase 1) of the ventricular action potential is caused by which of the following membrane currents?

questions.question: A person had a surgery where he got a pacemaker. Which of the following has been most likely substituted?
questions.explanation: B — SA node is the intended answer. It is the normal dominant pacemaker. A and C are lower-order pacemakers. Underspecified: an implanted device can also bypass AV block by pacing the ventricle despite an intact SA node.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person had a surgery where he got a pacemaker. Which of the following has been most likely substituted?

questions.question: Prolonged phase 4 of the Slow response of the SA nodal Pathway will cause which of the following?
questions.explanation: D — Slower atrial rate. A longer phase 4 delays the next SA discharge. A and B predict acceleration, and C ignores the longer cycle. Ventricular rate usually slows too if AV conduction is intact.
questions.sourceQuestion: Prolonged phase 4 of the Slow response of the SA nodal Pathway will cause which of the following?

questions.question: What will happen if purkinje fibers are not functional?
options: Prominent QRS complexes on an ECG
questions.explanation: C — Delayed ventricular activation. Purkinje fibres distribute excitation rapidly through the ventricles. A involves atrial tissue, B says the rate speeds up, and D misses the expected widening or distortion of QRS. Wording: ventricular activation is slower. The effect on beats per minute depends on the rhythm and lesion.
questions.sourceQuestion: What will happen if purkinje fibers are not functional?

questions.question: Which of the following channels is present in Nodal cells , ventricular and purkinje.
questions.explanation: B — Delayed rectifier. Delayed-rectifier K⁺ currents participate in repolarization across these tissues. A dominates stable resting voltage in fast-response cells, C is especially relevant to pacemaking, and D produces early repolarization mainly in fast-response tissue.
reasons: The strong inward-rectifier conductance that stabilizes ventricular resting potential is not the characteristic resting conductance of SA nodal cells.
Delayed-rectifier potassium currents support repolarization in both slow-response nodal and fast-response ventricular/Purkinje tissue.
T-type calcium current contributes to pacemaking and is not the common dominant repolarizing current in all these cells.
Transient outward Ito is especially associated with the early ventricular repolarization notch, not a universal nodal-current description.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following channels is present in Nodal cells , ventricular and purkinje.

questions.question: What is the effect of ACh on the heart?
questions.explanation: B — Heart rate falls. Vagal ACh increases nodal K⁺ conductance and reduces cAMP. A is the sympathetic direction, C ignores the vagal effect, and D is unrelated.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the effect of ACh on the heart?

questions.question: If the sinus node stops discharging, what is the expected heart rate (in beats/minute) if the A-V node takes over as the cardiac pacemaker?
questions.printedAnswer: D (keep in mind that AV node rate is 40–60/min, so any number within this range should be
questions.explanation: D — 50 bpm. The junctional escape range is about 40–60. A/B/C are below that typical range, while E is more consistent with a sinus rate.
questions.sourceQuestion: If the sinus node stops discharging, what is the expected heart rate (in beats/minute) if the A-V node takes over as the cardiac pacemaker? (repeated)

questions.question: What ion is responsible for phase 0?
questions.explanation: C — Calcium. The figure shows a nodal pacemaker, whose phase 0 is L-type Ca²⁺ entry. A drives phase 0 in working myocardium, B mediates repolarization, and D is no major upstroke current.
questions.sourceQuestion: What ion is responsible for phase 0?

questions.question: What happens in phase 1 of the cardiomyocyte AP?
options: Sodium channels open, causing a rapid influx of sodium ions
Calcium channels open, creating a prolonged plateau phase
Sodium channels close, and voltage-gated potassium channels open
Potassium channels close, allowing the cell to return to its resting potential
questions.explanation: C — Na⁺ channels inactivate and transient outward K⁺ channels open. A is phase 0, B is phase 2, and D reverses the role of outward K⁺ in repolarization.
questions.sourceQuestion: What happens in phase 1 of the cardiomyocyte AP?

questions.question: Which phase of the ventricular action potential coincides with diastole? (see attached figure)
questions.explanation: E — Phase 4. Stable electrical rest broadly coincides with ventricular diastole. A is the upstroke, B early repolarization, C the plateau, and D final repolarization around the end of systole.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which phase of the ventricular action potential coincides with diastole? (see attached figure)

questions.question: The conduction pathway through the heart is the fastest in which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: A — Purkinje fibres. They have the highest typical conduction velocity. B and D conduct rapidly but more slowly. C is pacemaker tissue and E is specialized to delay conduction.
reasons: Purkinje fibers conduct fastest among these listed structures and distribute excitation through the ventricles.
Bundle branches conduct rapidly, but terminal Purkinje tissue is the standard fastest-conduction answer.
The SA node is the normal pacemaker, but pacemaker dominance does not mean the fastest conduction velocity.
The His bundle carries the impulse into the ventricular conduction network but is not the fastest listed tissue.
The AV node is the slowest major conducting region and introduces a physiological delay.
questions.sourceQuestion: The conduction pathway through the heart is the fastest in which of the following structures? (repeated)

questions.question: If someone has a complete AV block on ECG, what is the heart rate?
questions.explanation: B — 40 bpm is the intended estimate. A distal escape often runs at 20–40 bpm. A/D are above typical escape ranges. Underspecified: C can occur with a junctional escape (about 40–60 bpm), so the rate requires the tracing or escape focus. AHA ACLS supplementary material (https://studylib.net/doc/25928760/acls-supplementary-material)
questions.sourceQuestion: If someone has a complete AV block on ECG, what is the heart rate? (Repeated)

questions.question: A patient presents to the emergency department and is found to have a sinoatrial (SA) block. Which of the following is the most likely heart rate for this patient?
questions.explanation: A — 45 bpm. Persistent SA exit block can produce a junctional escape at 40–60. B/D/E are in the usual sinus range and C is tachycardic. Intermittent block can present with pauses and a different average rate.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient presents to the emergency department and is found to have a sinoatrial (SA) block. Which of the following is the most likely heart rate for this patient?

questions.question: What occurs at the SA node to decrease heart rate?
questions.explanation: D — More ACh. A/B promote inward depolarizing current, C removes a hyperpolarizing influence, and E steepens phase 4 via β₁ stimulation.
reasons: Greater inward sodium permeability during pacemaker depolarization would generally favor faster threshold attainment.
Greater calcium entry generally favors nodal excitation rather than the parasympathetic slowing described.
Reducing outward potassium conductance removes a hyperpolarizing influence and does not explain vagal slowing.
Acetylcholine activates M2 signaling, which slows SA nodal firing through potassium and cAMP-dependent mechanisms.
Norepinephrine activates beta-1 signaling and normally increases SA nodal rate.
questions.sourceQuestion: What occurs at the SA node to decrease heart rate?

questions.question: How long does it take for the impulse to travel from the SA node to the beginning of the purkinje fiber? (the P-R interval)
questions.explanation: C — 0.16 s. This is a typical PR interval. A/B greatly exceed the normal 0.12–0.20 s range and D is far too short. The PR interval is measured from onset of P to onset of QRS.
questions.sourceQuestion: How long does it take for the impulse to travel from the SA node to the beginning of the purkinje fiber? (the P-R interval)

questions.question: Which of the following inhibits the SA node?
questions.explanation: B — ACh inhibits the SA node. A accelerates firing through β₁ receptors and C favors depolarization.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following inhibits the SA node?

questions.question: If the AV node is the pacemaker of the heart, what would be the heart rate?
questions.printedAnswer: A (keep in mind that AV node rate is 40–60/min, so any number within this range should be
questions.explanation: A — 55 bpm. It fits the 40–60 bpm junctional range. B/C are faster than the expected escape and D is more consistent with a distal escape.
questions.sourceQuestion: If the AV node is the pacemaker of the heart, what would be the heart rate? (repeated)

questions.question: The rate of AV node discharge/excitation is decreased by:
questions.explanation: A — ACh. Vagal M₂ activation suppresses nodal automaticity and slows AV conduction. B is stimulatory, C/D favor depolarization, and E reduces outward K⁺ current.
questions.sourceQuestion: The rate of AV node discharge/excitation is decreased by: (repeated)

questions.question: If the S-A node discharges at 0.00 seconds, when will the action potential normally arrive at the septum?
questions.explanation: C — About 0.16 s. Septal ventricular activation starts around QRS onset after atrial and AV conduction. A/B are delayed relative to the textbook estimate, D is its lower normal PR boundary, and E is too early for the intended estimate.
questions.sourceQuestion: If the S-A node discharges at 0.00 seconds, when will the action potential normally arrive at the septum?

questions.question: Which of the following increases the firing of action potentials at the SA node?
questions.explanation: A — Norepinephrine. β₁ activation increases pacemaker slope. B is vagal, C favors hyperpolarization, and D/E diminish inward depolarizing current.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following increases the firing of action potentials at the SA node?

questions.question: During phase 4 of the ventricular action potential, which ion is the plasma membrane most permeable to?
questions.explanation: A — Potassium. Resting ventricular conductance is dominated by K⁺. B/C/D/E lack a comparable resting conductance.
questions.sourceQuestion: During phase 4 of the ventricular action potential, which ion is the plasma membrane most permeable to?

questions.question: Which of the following does calcium bind to when cardiac muscles contract?
questions.explanation: A — Troponin C. Ca²⁺ binding moves the troponin–tropomyosin complex away from actin’s myosin-binding sites. B moves indirectly. C activates D in smooth muscle.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following does calcium bind to when cardiac muscles contract?

questions.question: During relaxation of cardiac muscle (diastole) which of the following proteins contributes the most to the decline of cytosolic calcium?
questions.explanation: A — SERCA. It pumps most cytosolic Ca²⁺ back into the SR in typical human ventricular cells. B extrudes a substantial smaller share through NCX. C makes a small contribution and D is a Ca²⁺-binding regulator.
reasons: SERCA actively resequesters calcium into the SR and is the major process asked for.
Sodium–calcium exchange contributes extrusion but is not the largest pathway in this comparison.
Sarcolemmal calcium ATPase contributes a smaller extrusion pathway.
Calmodulin is a calcium-binding regulator rather than the major calcium-removal pump.
questions.sourceQuestion: During relaxation of cardiac muscle (diastole) which of the following proteins contributes the most to the decline of cytosolic calcium?

questions.question: During dilated cardiomyopathy, the intercalated discs will be dysfunctional. Which of the following will happen?
options: Gap junctions will stop spreading action potential
questions.explanation: E — Impaired propagation through gap junctions. Intercalated-disc dysfunction weakens electrical coupling. A/B are changes in nodal rate, C assumes structural degeneration of an unrelated system, and D goes against impaired coordination and pumping. The degree of propagation failure can vary.
questions.sourceQuestion: During dilated cardiomyopathy, the intercalated discs will be dysfunctional. Which of the following will happen?

questions.question: Which of the following hydrolyses the most ATP in ventricular cells ?
questions.explanation: A — Myosin ATPase. Actomyosin cycling dominates ATP use in a contracting ventricular cell. B pumps Ca²⁺ into SR, C denotes membrane ATPases, and D restores Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients. These pumps use a smaller share under typical contraction.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following hydrolyses the most ATP in ventricular cells ?

questions.question: Frank–Starling law states the:
options: Relation between cardiac output and end-diastolic volume
Relation between venous return and end-systolic volume
questions.explanation: A — Filling and output. Higher EDV increases fibre stretch and stroke volume at a fixed contractile state. CO rises if rate is fixed. B substitutes end-systolic volume for the preload variable.
questions.sourceIssue: The source recalls only 2 choices; preserved verbatim.
questions.sourceQuestion: Frank–Starling law states the:

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of intercalated discs in a cardiac myocyte?
options: Hold muscle cells together more tightly
questions.sourceIssue: The corrected booklet accepts multiple answers: B/C. Self-check; excluded from single-answer grading.
questions.explanation: B and C — Electrical coupling and adhesion. Gap junctions enable rapid current spread and adherens junctions/desmosomes keep cells attached. Ambiguous: A also describes the structural contribution in broad terms. A single key requires specifying electrical or mechanical function.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following best describes the function of intercalated discs in a cardiac myocyte?

questions.question: What is the most characteristic feature of the ventricular conduction system?
options: Striation is visible in all sarcoplasm
questions.explanation: B — Intercalated discs, among the available choices. A is wrong because Purkinje cells are large. C is wrong because myofibrils tend to be sparse and peripheral. Intercalated discs are shared with working myocytes. Large, pale, glycogen-rich cells distinguish Purkinje fibres more reliably.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the most characteristic feature of the ventricular conduction system?

questions.question: If the Ca level decreased in cytoplasm right before relaxation, what has caused the decrease in the level of Ca?
questions.explanation: D — Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange. Forward NCX removes cytosolic Ca²⁺. A releases Ca²⁺ from the SR. B and C describe influx pathways. SERCA also lowers cytosolic Ca²⁺ and is absent from the choices.
questions.sourceQuestion: If the Ca level decreased in cytoplasm right before relaxation, what has caused the decrease in the level of Ca?

questions.question: What part of the intercalated disc transmits low electrical resistance through which excitation passes from one cell to the other?
questions.explanation: C — Gap junctions. Connexon channels let ions pass from cell to cell. A resists separation, B anchors actin, and D seals intercellular spaces.
questions.sourceQuestion: What part of the intercalated disc transmits low electrical resistance through which excitation passes from one cell to the other?

questions.question: What is the length of the PR segment in the following ECG?
questions.explanation: B — 0.04 s is the printed key and is plausible for the PR segment. The PR segment is only the short isoelectric gap from the end of P to QRS onset (about one small box = 0.04 s). Figure annotation is inconsistent: the blue bracket appears to span the P wave, not just that gap, so it does not demonstrate the keyed measurement; the stem/key distinction between PR segment and PR interval should be retained. A/C/D/E would require 3/4/5/6 small boxes at 25 mm/s.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the length of the PR segment in the following ECG?

questions.question: The negative electrode of lead II is placed on the:
questions.explanation: A — Right arm. Lead II measures LL minus RA. B is its positive electrode and C is the negative electrode for lead III.
questions.sourceQuestion: The negative electrode of lead II is placed on the:

questions.question: When recording lead III on an ECG, the negative electrode is the:
questions.explanation: A — Left arm. Lead III measures LL minus LA. B is positive, C is the reference/ground, and D/E list pairs rather than the negative electrode.
questions.sourceQuestion: When recording lead III on an ECG, the negative electrode is the:

questions.question: By using the einthoven law, the lead I voltage was 0.4 and lead II voltage was 0.9, which of the following would be the voltage of lead III?
questions.explanation: A — 0.5 mV. III = II − I = 0.9 − 0.4. B/C/D/E overestimate this difference.
questions.sourceQuestion: By using the einthoven law, the lead I voltage was 0.4 and lead II voltage was 0.9, which of the following would be the voltage of lead III?

questions.question: If in an ECG, the voltage at lead I is 0.8 mV and the voltage at lead II is 1.2 mV, what is the voltage at lead III?
questions.explanation: C — 0.40 mV. III = 1.2 − 0.8. A gives a larger difference and B adds the leads.
questions.sourceQuestion: If in an ECG, the voltage at lead I is 0.8 mV and the voltage at lead II is 1.2 mV, what is the voltage at lead III?

questions.question: What stage in the ECG corresponds to total ventricular depolarization?
questions.explanation: D — Label 4, ST segment. The ventricles are fully depolarized in region 4. Ambiguous wording: C (region 3, QRS) is correct if the question means the event of ventricular depolarization. A is P, B is the PR segment, E is T, and F is U.
questions.sourceQuestion: What stage in the ECG corresponds to total ventricular depolarization?

questions.question: In a normal ECG, Which of the following is correct?
options: ST segment represents the duration of ventricular action potential
Duration of the QRS complex is 1 sec
questions.explanation: C — T wave is ventricular repolarization. A exceeds the usual PR range. B confuses ST with the longer period of ventricular electrical activity. D is far too long for QRS and E measures the time between successive ventricular beats.
questions.sourceQuestion: In a normal ECG, Which of the following is correct?

questions.question: Which of the following leads will have a strong negative QRS complex for the following depolarizing signal?
questions.explanation: A — aVL and V6. The illustrated vector points toward the patient’s right and inferiorly, away from left-facing aVL and V6. B includes inferior aVF, C includes two inferior-facing leads, and D includes inferior/rightward lead III and anterior V2.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following leads will have a strong negative QRS complex for the following depolarizing signal?

questions.question: During which wave or segment on the ECG trace below marks ventricular depolarization?
questions.explanation: C — Mark C spans QRS. A is the P wave, B the PR segment, and the diagram’s E the T wave.
questions.sourceQuestion: During which wave or segment on the ECG trace below marks ventricular depolarization?

questions.question: Which component of the ECG is the result of a conduction of a wave of depolarization through the atrial muscle?
questions.explanation: B — P wave. A includes atrial depolarization plus conduction delay, C is ventricular depolarization, D is the fully depolarized ventricular period, and E is ventricular repolarization.
reasons: The PR interval includes the P wave and atrioventricular conduction, so it is broader than atrial depolarization alone.
The P wave is the direct surface representation of atrial depolarization.
The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization.
The ST segment is associated with the ventricular plateau after activation.
The T wave represents ventricular repolarization.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which component of the ECG is the result of a conduction of a wave of depolarization through the atrial muscle?

questions.question: Which of the following will be a result of the direct consequences of slowing the action potential conduction to the AV node?
questions.explanation: D — Longer PR interval. Slower AV transmission delays QRS onset after P. A does not follow, B requires slower intraventricular conduction, and C relates to ventricular electrical duration.
reasons: Increased cardiac output is not a direct necessary consequence of delaying AV nodal conduction.
A widened QRS points to slower ventricular conduction, not simply an isolated AV nodal delay.
QT duration concerns ventricular depolarization and repolarization, rather than the isolated atrioventricular delay.
The PR interval includes AV nodal transit, so slowing that transit prolongs PR.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following will be a result of the direct consequences of slowing the action potential conduction to the AV node?

questions.question: You are looking at an ECG of a patient whose MEA is +60°, which lead would have an S wave with the biggest amplitude? (Not included in 19th batch curriculum)
questions.explanation: D — aVR is the intended lead. Its −150° axis gives the most negative projection of a +60° mean QRS vector. I, III and aVF project positively, while aVL is approximately perpendicular. Wording: mean axis predicts net QRS polarity. The precise S-wave amplitude also depends on terminal depolarization vectors.
questions.sourceQuestion: You are looking at an ECG of a patient whose MEA is +60°, which lead would have an S wave with the biggest amplitude? (Not included in 19th batch curriculum)

questions.question: General impulse travels towards apex which leads to the tallest positive QRS?
questions.explanation: B — Lead II. Its +60° orientation aligns with the usual net apex-directed vector. I (0°), aVF (+90°), aVL (−30°) and III (+120°) are less aligned with that assumed direction.
questions.sourceQuestion: General impulse travels towards apex which leads to the tallest positive QRS?

questions.question: The ECG tracing shown below was taken from a patient during a routine examination. What is the best estimate of heart rate taken from this ECG record in beats per minute (bpm)?
questions.explanation: B — 50 bpm. About six large boxes separate R peaks. At 25 mm/s, 300 ÷ 6 = 50. A/C/D would require about 10/4.3/3.3 large boxes.
questions.sourceQuestion: The ECG tracing shown below was taken from a patient during a routine examination. What is the best estimate of heart rate taken from this ECG record in beats per minute (bpm)?

questions.question: Which of the following is in the normal time range for the PR segment?
questions.explanation: A — 0.08 s. The PR segment is end of P to start of QRS. B/C are more characteristic of PR interval values that include P. D even exceeds the usual PR interval upper limit.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is in the normal time range for the PR segment?

questions.question: Sympathetic nerve stimulation of AV node increases conduction velocity through the node. Which of the following is likely to decrease because of this intervention?
questions.explanation: B — PR interval falls. Faster AV nodal conduction shortens the delay. A/E generally rise with sympathetic drive, while C/D often rise with increased myocardial workload.
reasons: Sympathetic stimulation usually increases rather than decreases heart rate.
Faster AV nodal conduction reduces the AV-conduction component of the PR interval.
Myocardial metabolic demand generally increases with sympathetic stimulation.
Coronary flow commonly rises to meet increased cardiac metabolic demand.
Sympathetic beta-1 stimulation generally increases cardiac contractility.
questions.sourceQuestion: Sympathetic nerve stimulation of AV node increases conduction velocity through the node. Which of the following is likely to decrease because of this intervention?

questions.question: Where is the negative electrode of Lead I attached?
questions.explanation: B — Right arm. LA is positive in lead I, LL contributes to leads II/III, and RL is the reference.
questions.sourceQuestion: Where is the negative electrode of Lead I attached?

questions.question: If Lead III = 0.4 mV and Lead II = 0.9 mV, what is Lead I?
questions.explanation: A — 0.5 mV. I = II − III = 0.9 − 0.4. B adds the voltages, and C/D are smaller than the difference.
questions.sourceQuestion: If Lead III = 0.4 mV and Lead II = 0.9 mV, what is Lead I?

questions.question: Where do you put the positive electrode of lead 1?
questions.explanation: A — Left arm. RA is negative in lead I, LL is positive in II/III, and the pair in D is not the positive electrode for I.
reasons: The left arm is the positive measuring electrode of lead I.
The right arm is the negative measuring electrode of lead I.
The left leg is the positive electrode for leads II and III.
Lead I has a single positive measuring pole at the left arm, rather than both left-sided limbs.
questions.sourceQuestion: Where do you put the positive electrode of lead 1?

questions.question: If in an ECG, the voltage at lead 1 is 0.8 and the voltage at lead 3 is 0.4, what is the voltage at lead 2?
questions.explanation: B — 1.2 mV. II = I + III = 0.8 + 0.4. A is just III, C multiplies the values, and D is neither the sum nor the difference.
questions.sourceQuestion: If in an ECG, the voltage at lead 1 is 0.8 and the voltage at lead 3 is 0.4, what is the voltage at lead 2?

questions.question: The probability of the random desynchronization of the myocardium is highest when the electrical signal arrives at the myocardium during the vulnerable phase of the cardiac cycle. This phase corresponds with which of the following waves on the electrocardiogram (ECG)?
questions.explanation: E — T wave. During heterogeneous ventricular repolarization a premature impulse can trigger a dangerous rhythm. A is atrial depolarization, and B/C/D are components of ventricular depolarization.
reasons: The P wave is atrial depolarization and does not identify the classic ventricular vulnerable period.
The S wave is part of ventricular depolarization rather than the vulnerable repolarization phase.
The Q wave is part of the ventricular depolarization complex.
The R wave reflects ventricular depolarization, when much of the ventricle is entering refractoriness.
The T wave marks ventricular repolarization, during which heterogeneous recovery can permit dangerous re-entry.
questions.sourceQuestion: The probability of the random desynchronization of the myocardium is highest when the electrical signal arrives at the myocardium during the vulnerable phase of the cardiac cycle. This phase corresponds with which of the following waves on the electrocardiogram (ECG)?

questions.question: Q22.Which of the following is the normal time of the P-R interval?
questions.printedAnswer: E (While the normal range of PR interval is 0.12 – 0.20s , 0.16s is considered the average PR
questions.explanation: D and E — Both 0.12 and 0.16 s are normal. Multiple correct choices. E is a typical midpoint and the printed key. A/B/C exceed the standard adult 0.12–0.20 s range. Brazilian Society of Cardiology ECG guideline (https://abccardiol.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/Revista_ABC_11904_ingles.x65822.pdf)
questions.sourceQuestion: Q22.Which of the following is the normal time of the P-R interval?

questions.question: Which labelled portion [1 to 5] of the ECG diagram in the attachment represents ventricular depolarization?
questions.explanation: C — Label 3 spans the QRS. A is P, B the PR segment, D the ST segment, and E the T wave.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which labelled portion [1 to 5] of the ECG diagram in the attachment represents ventricular depolarization?

questions.question: What does the following ECG indicate?
questions.explanation: E — Sinus bradycardia. The complexes are slow and regularly conducted from sinus P waves. A requires prolonged PR, B has progressive PR lengthening and a drop, C has abrupt dropped beats, and D has independent atrial and ventricular activity.
questions.sourceQuestion: What does the following ECG indicate?

questions.question: From the ECG shown, which is the most likely condition in this patient?
questions.explanation: C — Complete AV block. Multiple P waves march through a slow broad-complex escape with no fixed PR. A requires sinus P-to-QRS conduction, B usually gives a narrow junctional escape, and D/E retain intermittent atrioventricular conduction.
questions.sourceQuestion: From the ECG shown, which is the most likely condition in this patient?

questions.question: What is the heart condition in the following ecg?
questions.explanation: B — First-degree AV block. PR is prolonged and constant with one QRS per P. A and D have dropped QRS complexes, and C has AV dissociation.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the heart condition in the following ecg?

questions.question: From the attached ECG trace, what is the most likely condition affecting this patient?
questions.explanation: C — Sinus tachycardia. The tracing is fast and regular, with a P before each QRS. A requires PR prolongation, B/D produce dropped beats, and E lacks organized sinus P waves and is usually irregularly irregular.
questions.sourceQuestion: From the attached ECG trace, what is the most likely condition affecting this patient?

questions.question: A patient experiences a cardiac arrhythmia and presents with the following ECG, what is the diagnosis of his condition?
options: Third Degree AV Block (Complete AV block)
questions.explanation: D — Complete AV block. P waves and QRS complexes march independently. A would retain 1:1 conduction, B would show a rapid ventricular rhythm, and C would remove some atrial depolarizations.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient experiences a cardiac arrhythmia and presents with the following ECG, what is the diagnosis of his condition?

questions.question: A 42 year old woman complained of palpitations, her ECG is shown here. Which of the following best describes her ECG?
questions.explanation: A — Regularly irregular. Groups of beats and pauses recur in a pattern. B/C imply nearly equal R–R intervals and D implies no repeating pattern.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 42 year old woman complained of palpitations, her ECG is shown here. Which of the following best describes her ECG?

questions.question: From the attached ECG, what is the most likely condition affecting this patient?
questions.explanation: C — Complete AV block is the best fit. Several P waves appear through the long gap between broad escape complexes without an evident fixed PR. A usually gives a faster narrow escape, B retains 1:1 conduction, and D/E would show some conducted P waves. The short strip limits certainty about intermittent conduction.
questions.sourceQuestion: From the attached ECG, what is the most likely condition affecting this patient?

questions.question: Which of the following is most likely to cause ventricular fibrillation?
questions.explanation: A — Severe extracellular hyperkalemia can trigger VF. Sustained depolarization inactivates Na⁺ channels and disrupts conduction. B and E are physiological states. C and D may precipitate arrhythmias in susceptible hearts, but severe hyperkalemia is the clearest direct electrical disturbance listed. UK Kidney Association hyperkalemia guideline (https://guidelines.ukkidney.org/hyperkalaemia/11-1-ii-hyperkalaemia-in-hospital/11-1-2-ii-hyperkalaemia-in-hospital-14-1-14-2/)
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is most likely to cause ventricular fibrillation?

questions.question: What does slow ventricular ejection correspond to on an ECG?
questions.explanation: A — T wave. Slow ejection is late systole and overlaps ventricular repolarization. B QRS is depolarization/onset systole; C P is atrial depolarization; D ST is plateau/early ejection; E PR is AV conduction.
questions.sourceQuestion: What does slow ventricular ejection correspond to on an ECG? (Repeated)

questions.question: During exercise the cardiac cycle is shortened. Shortening of which of the following phases is mostly responsible for this?
questions.explanation: D — slow ventricular filling. Exercise shortens diastole disproportionately; rapid filling and isovolumic intervals are brief and less responsible. B/C are systolic/transition phases.
questions.sourceQuestion: During exercise the cardiac cycle is shortened. Shortening of which of the following phases is mostly responsible for this? (Repeated)

questions.question: You are listening to a patient's heart sounds while simultaneously recalling the cardiac cycle events. Which of the following most likely occurs at the same time as the S2 heart sound?
options: Left ventricular volume reaches its maximum value
Left ventricular pressure reaches its maximum value
The dicrotic notch in the aortic pressure valve
Aortic pressure approaches its minimum value
questions.explanation: C — aortic dicrotic notch. S2 follows semilunar closure, producing the notch. A maximum LV volume is end-diastole; B peak LV pressure is earlier; D minimum aortic pressure is late diastole; E rapid ejection precedes S2.
questions.sourceQuestion: You are listening to a patient's heart sounds while simultaneously recalling the cardiac cycle events. Which of the following most likely occurs at the same time as the S2 heart sound?

questions.question: Ejection fraction is 0.8, ESV is 30 mL, and heart rate is 100 bpm. Calculate the cardiac output in L/min.
questions.explanation: B — 12 L/min. EF=.8 and ESV=30 gives EDV=150, SV=120 mL; CO=120×100=12,000 mL/min. Other choices do not follow the computed product.
questions.sourceQuestion: Ejection fraction is 0.8, ESV is 30 mL, and heart rate is 100 bpm. Calculate the cardiac output in L/min.

questions.question: What is the difference in ejection between the right and left cardiac components of the heart?
options: Right side ejects less amount of blood.
Right side ejects slower than left
Right side ejects against a lower afterload
Left side ejects against lower afterload
questions.explanation: C — right ventricle ejects against lower afterload. Both sides eject equal long-term volumes; the right side's pulmonary resistance/pressure is lower. A is false; B is not a defining difference; D reverses afterload.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the difference in ejection between the right and left cardiac components of the heart?

questions.question: Which of the following represents the ventricular ejection phase?
questions.explanation: A — phase 3. Figure sequence appears to mark ejection as phase 3; other numbers denote other loop phases. Key likely OK; depends on diagram labels.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following represents the ventricular ejection phase?

questions.question: Which correctly pairs an ECG wave with the corresponding cardiac event?
options: P-wave: Depolarization of the AV node
questions.explanation: C — QRS = ventricular depolarization. P is atrial depolarization, not AV-node depolarization; QRS is not ventricular repolarization; T is ventricular repolarization, not atrial.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which correctly pairs an ECG wave with the corresponding cardiac event?

questions.question: Calculate the ejection fraction if the End diastolic volume is 200 and end systolic volume is 150?
questions.explanation: B — 25%. EF=(EDV−ESV)/EDV=(200−150)/200=.25. A/C/D do not match.
questions.sourceQuestion: Calculate the ejection fraction if the End diastolic volume is 200 and end systolic volume is 150?

questions.question: A patient with valve disease undergoes cardiac catheterization to compare vascular and intracardiac pressures for comparison with normal values. Which of the following is found in a normal heart?
options: Aortic diastolic pressure is less than pulmonary artery systole pressure
Right atrial pressure is greater than left atrial pressure
Mean systolic aortic pressure is less than aortic diastolic pressure
Pulmonary artery diastolic pressure is greater than right atrial pressure
questions.explanation: D — pulmonary artery diastolic pressure exceeds right atrial pressure. Normal PA diastolic is around 8–12 vs RA about 2–6 mmHg. A is false (aortic diastolic far exceeds PA systolic); B reverses normal LA>RA; C reverses systolic/diastolic.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient with valve disease undergoes cardiac catheterization to compare vascular and intracardiac pressures for comparison with normal values. Which of the following is found in a normal heart?

questions.question: What causes the “a” wave in the jugular waveform?
questions.explanation: C — atrial contraction. The JVP a-wave is right atrial systole; A relaxation relates to x descent, B tricuspid closure to c wave, D filling is not the a wave.
questions.sourceQuestion: What causes the “a” wave in the jugular waveform?

questions.question: What is mostly correlated after the QRS complex on an ECG?
questions.explanation: C — isovolumetric contraction. QRS precedes ventricular systole and the initial pressure rise before ejection. A follows valve opening; B is later diastole; D follows ejection.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is mostly correlated after the QRS complex on an ECG?

questions.question: During which phase of the cardiac cycle does the mitral valve open?
questions.explanation: D — end of isovolumetric relaxation. Mitral valve opens when LV pressure falls below LA pressure. A is late filling; B is end contraction; C/E occur with aortic valve open.
questions.sourceQuestion: During which phase of the cardiac cycle does the mitral valve open?

questions.question: At what point does rapid ventricular ejection start?
questions.explanation: C — point C. Rapid ejection starts when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure and the aortic valve opens; the figure labels this upper-right transition C. Other points mark distinct loop transitions.
questions.sourceQuestion: At what point does rapid ventricular ejection start?

questions.question: Calculate the Ejection fraction for the following PV loop.
questions.explanation: B — EF 0.65. The loop is EDV 120 mL, ESV about 42 mL; EF=(120−42)/120≈0.65. A/C/D are inconsistent.
questions.sourceQuestion: Calculate the Ejection fraction for the following PV loop.

questions.question: In the attached PV loop, isovolumic relaxation begins at which of the following points?
questions.explanation: D — point D. Isovolumetric relaxation begins at aortic valve closure, the upper-left transition labeled D. A/B/C are other loop corners/phases.
questions.sourceQuestion: In the attached PV loop, isovolumic relaxation begins at which of the following points?

questions.question: How does the sympathetic nervous system affect the heart?
questions.explanation: A — decreased ESV. Sympathetic inotropy increases ejection and lowers ESV; it generally raises SV, HR and pressure, so B–D are wrong.
questions.sourceQuestion: How does the sympathetic nervous system affect the heart?

questions.question: If the contractility increases, which of the following parameters will decrease in the PV loop?
options: Pressure difference from point D to A
End systolic pressure volume relationship slope
questions.explanation: D — ESV decreases. Increased contractility steepens ESPVR and reduces ESV; SV/work generally rise and pressure difference/slope do not decrease.
questions.sourceQuestion: If the contractility increases, which of the following parameters will decrease in the PV loop?

questions.question: What change occurred to move the solid PV loop to the dashed one?
questions.explanation: E — decreased ESV. The dashed loop’s left edge moves left, indicating lower ESV/increased contractility; A/D imply weaker ejection, B/C alter filling.
questions.sourceQuestion: What change occurred to move the solid PV loop to the dashed one?

questions.question: What happens at point D on the cardiac output curve?
questions.explanation: A — aortic valve closes. The figure labels point D at the top-left corner (end ejection). B says aortic opening (top-right), C AV opening (bottom-left), D AV closure (bottom-right).
questions.sourceQuestion: What happens at point D on the cardiac output curve?

questions.question: Which of the following increases Stroke Volume?
questions.explanation: C — increased EDV. Greater preload raises SV by Frank–Starling; increased afterload or reduced preload/contractility lowers SV.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following increases Stroke Volume?

questions.question: A 50-year-old man has a body weight of 110 kg, resting heart rate is 90 beats/min, arterial pressure 120/70 and normal body temperature. His pressure volume diagram of the left ventricle is shown in the figure. What event occurs at point A?
questions.explanation: D — AV valves open. Point A is the lower-left corner after isovolumic relaxation, when the mitral valve opens; B/E duplicate aortic opening and C is a third heart sound, not a valve event.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 50-year-old man has a body weight of 110 kg, resting heart rate is 90 beats/min, arterial pressure 120/70 and normal body temperature. His pressure volume diagram of the left ventricle is shown in the figure. What event occurs at point A?

questions.question: What happens at the beginning of the isovolumetric relaxation?
questions.explanation: D — aortic valve closes. It closes at the start of isovolumetric relaxation. A opens at end contraction; B mitral closes at contraction onset; C mitral opens after relaxation.
questions.sourceQuestion: What happens at the beginning of the isovolumetric relaxation?

questions.question: Between which interval does the ventricle fills?
questions.explanation: A — A to B. The diagram’s filling limb runs from the lower-left (ESV, mitral opening) to lower-right (EDV, mitral closure). Other intervals are contraction/ejection/relaxation.
questions.sourceQuestion: Between which interval does the ventricle fills?

questions.question: What change occurred to move the solid PV loop to the dashed one?
questions.explanation: D — increased afterload (printed key). This should raise end-systolic pressure/ESV and narrow the loop; A/E alter preload, B lowers afterload and C raises contractility. A black block obscures part of the comparison, limiting direct verification. Key plausible; figure partly obscured.
questions.sourceQuestion: What change occurred to move the solid PV loop to the dashed one?

questions.question: What change occurred to move the solid PV loop to the dashed one?
questions.explanation: B — increased contractility. A steeper ESPVR moves the end-systolic point up/left and increases SV; other listed changes move the loop differently. Key plausible; figure partly obscured by a black block.
questions.sourceQuestion: What change occurred to move the solid PV loop to the dashed one?

questions.question: Use the pressure-volume loop to calculate the cardiac output of the ventricle if the heart rate is 70 beats/min? (see the attached figured)
questions.explanation: C — 5.25 L/min. Loop width is 75 mL; 75×70=5,250 mL/min. Other choices imply different SVs.
questions.sourceQuestion: Use the pressure-volume loop to calculate the cardiac output of the ventricle if the heart rate is 70 beats/min? (see the attached figured)

questions.question: 15a. A sixty-year-old woman has a body weight of 110 kg, resting cardiac output is 5,000 ml/minute. Her pressure-volume diagram of the left ventricle is shown below. What is her resting heart rate in beats/minute?
questions.explanation: C — 50 beats/min. The loop gives SV≈100 mL, so HR=5,000/100=50. Other rates imply another SV.
questions.sourceQuestion: 15a. A sixty-year-old woman has a body weight of 110 kg, resting cardiac output is 5,000 ml/minute. Her pressure-volume diagram of the left ventricle is shown below. What is her resting heart rate in beats/minute?

questions.question: 15b. What is the ventricular ejection fraction?
questions.sourceQuestion: 15b. What is the ventricular ejection fraction? (Repeated)
questions.caseText: 15a. A sixty-year-old woman has a body weight of 110 kg, resting cardiac output is 5,000 ml/minute. Her pressure-volume diagram of the left ventricle is shown below. What is her resting heart rate in beats/minute?

questions.question: 15c. What is the ESV (End Systolic Volume)?
questions.explanation: B — 50 mL. ESV is the loop’s left boundary, 50 mL; A/C/D do not match.
questions.sourceQuestion: 15c. What is the ESV (End Systolic Volume)?
questions.caseText: 15a. A sixty-year-old woman has a body weight of 110 kg, resting cardiac output is 5,000 ml/minute. Her pressure-volume diagram of the left ventricle is shown below. What is her resting heart rate in beats/minute?

questions.question: 16a. What is the cardiac output in millilitres per minute? Considering the heart rate is 90bpm.
questions.explanation: E — 9,000 mL/min. The loop gives SV≈100 mL; 100×90=9,000. A–D are smaller products.
questions.sourceQuestion: 16a. What is the cardiac output in millilitres per minute? Considering the heart rate is 90bpm.

questions.question: 16b. What is the ventricular ejection fraction?
questions.explanation: D — 67%. The loop’s SV/EDV is about 2/3. A/B/C/E are not supported.
questions.sourceQuestion: 16b. What is the ventricular ejection fraction? (Repeated)
questions.caseText: 16a. What is the cardiac output in millilitres per minute? Considering the heart rate is 90bpm.

questions.question: In the volume pressure loop what happens at point C?
questions.explanation: A — aortic valve opens. Point C is the upper-right corner after isovolumetric contraction. B is closure at upper-left; C option says AV valve open (lower-left); D AV closure (lower-right).
questions.sourceQuestion: In the volume pressure loop what happens at point C?

questions.question: A 60-year old-woman has a resting cardiac output of 9000 ml/min, arterial pressure of 90/50 mmHg and normal body temperature. Her pressure-volume diagram of the left ventricle is shown below. What is her resting heart rate in beats per minute?
questions.explanation: C — 90 beats/min. CO 9,000 divided by the depicted SV≈100 mL gives 90/min. Other rates imply another SV.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 60-year old-woman has a resting cardiac output of 9000 ml/min, arterial pressure of 90/50 mmHg and normal body temperature. Her pressure-volume diagram of the left ventricle is shown below. What is her resting heart rate in beats per minute?

questions.question: A 33-year-old man is roller skating. What happens to his preload?
options: Increased left and right ventricular preload
questions.explanation: A — increased left and right preload. Aerobic activity increases venous return to both ventricles; B is incomplete and C opposite.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 33-year-old man is roller skating. What happens to his preload?

questions.question: At the onset of normal aerobic exercise, which of the following parameters decreases?
questions.explanation: E — ESV decreases. Exercise raises sympathetic contractility, lowering ESV; HR, SV and often EDV rise, and stroke work rises.
questions.sourceQuestion: At the onset of normal aerobic exercise, which of the following parameters decreases? (Repeated)

questions.question: What is the stroke volume of the given PV loop?
questions.explanation: D — 100 mL. Stroke volume is loop width EDV−ESV=150−50. Other choices mismatch the plotted width.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the stroke volume of the given PV loop?

questions.question: What phase corresponds to the curve between C and E?
questions.explanation: C — ventricular ejection. C–E is the ejection arc in the supplied diagram. A/B describe other cycle phases; D/E are not phases of the PV loop.
questions.sourceQuestion: What phase corresponds to the curve between C and E?

questions.question: In increased ventricular afterload, which one of the following parameters happen?
questions.explanation: A — decreased SV. Increased afterload impedes ejection and raises ESV. B/C are opposite or unrelated.
questions.sourceQuestion: In increased ventricular afterload, which one of the following parameters happen? (Repeated)

questions.question: An increase in which of the following would cause a decrease in the stroke volume?
questions.explanation: C — increased afterload. Increased afterload reduces SV; increased inotropy/preload/prolonged filling tends to increase it.
questions.sourceQuestion: An increase in which of the following would cause a decrease in the stroke volume?

questions.question: Exercise would lead to which of the following ?
questions.sourceIssue: The corrected booklet accepts multiple answers: B/C. Self-check; excluded from single-answer grading.
questions.explanation: B and C both describe exercise; key is ambiguous. Exercise generally increases EDV and decreases ESV through increased venous return and contractility. A/D are opposite. The printed “B/C” is valid as two answers, not a single-best key. Key ambiguous by design.
questions.sourceQuestion: Exercise would lead to which of the following ? (Repeated)

questions.question: Which of the following has the highest total cross-sectional area?
questions.explanation: A — capillaries. Their parallel networks provide the greatest summed cross-sectional area; individual capillaries are tiny, but the total area is largest. B–D have less aggregate area.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following has the highest total cross-sectional area? (Repeated 5X)

questions.question: A marathon runner was suspected to be receiving erythropoietin injections, which increase his RBC count. Which of the following is most likely to decrease?
questions.explanation: D — blood flow. More RBCs raise hematocrit/viscosity and resistance, reducing flow at a given pressure gradient. A/C are not the direct expected change; B rises, not falls.
questions.sourceQuestion: A marathon runner was suspected to be receiving erythropoietin injections, which increase his RBC count. Which of the following is most likely to decrease?

questions.question: An arteriole branches into two smaller arterioles. If the resistance of the parent vessel is 2 peripheral resistance units and the resistance if each daughter vessel is 4 peripheral resistance units, which of the following is the combined resistance of all of the blood vessels?
questions.explanation: D — 4 units. Daughter vessels are parallel: 4‖4=2; in series with parent 2 gives total 4. A/B/C/E are wrong. The original printed key D is correct.
questions.sourceQuestion: An arteriole branches into two smaller arterioles. If the resistance of the parent vessel is 2 peripheral resistance units and the resistance if each daughter vessel is 4 peripheral resistance units, which of the following is the combined resistance of all of the blood vessels?

questions.question: If the lumen of one blood vessel decreases from 9 mm to 3 mm, what is the change of resistance?
questions.explanation: C — resistance ×81. Radius falls from 4.5 to 1.5 mm, so Poiseuille resistance scales as (3)^4=81. A/B/D wrong.
questions.sourceQuestion: If the lumen of one blood vessel decreases from 9 mm to 3 mm, what is the change of resistance?

questions.question: What vessel controls blood flow in the capillary bed?
questions.explanation: B — arterioles. Their smooth muscle sets resistance and capillary-bed inflow; arteries/veins/venules are less direct controllers.
questions.sourceQuestion: What vessel controls blood flow in the capillary bed?

questions.question: Change in which of the following parameters has the greatest impact on resistance?
questions.explanation: D — radius. Resistance varies with inverse radius to the fourth power; viscosity and length are linear, flow is not a resistance determinant.
questions.sourceQuestion: Change in which of the following parameters has the greatest impact on resistance?

questions.question: What causes increased blood flow, if an increase of pressure will lead to increased flow?
questions.explanation: D — decreased length/viscosity. Both lower resistance and raise flow at fixed ΔP. Sympathetic vasoconstriction and decreased diameter raise resistance; parasympathetic effect is not the general systemic explanation.
questions.sourceQuestion: What causes increased blood flow, if an increase of pressure will lead to increased flow?

questions.question: Fastest velocity of blood flow occurs in which vessel?
questions.explanation: B — arteriole (among offered choices). Of these, its area is less than the venous/capillary beds and hence velocity higher. A/C/D have lower velocity. Key OK, though aorta is omitted and normally has the highest velocity.
questions.sourceQuestion: Fastest velocity of blood flow occurs in which vessel?

questions.question: An inflow vessel branches into 4 vessels in parallel, each with a resistance of 2, and merges to form an outflow vessel. What is the total peripheral resistance in this system? Inflow pressure: 140 units Outflow pressure: 60 units
questions.explanation: A — 0.5 resistance units. Four parallel resistors of 2 each give 2/4=0.5. B–D are not the parallel equivalent. The listed inflow/outflow pressures are irrelevant without flow.
questions.sourceQuestion: An inflow vessel branches into 4 vessels in parallel, each with a resistance of 2, and merges to form an outflow vessel. What is the total peripheral resistance in this system? Inflow pressure: 140 units Outflow pressure: 60 units (Repeated)

questions.question: A 53-year-old woman is found by arteriography to have 50% narrowing of her left renal artery. What is the expected change of blood flow through the stenotic artery?
questions.explanation: D — flow falls to 1/16. If diameter/radius is halved, R rises 16-fold under Poiseuille assumptions; at fixed ΔP flow becomes 1/16. A–C understate the effect. Key OK; wording “50% narrowing” should mean diameter.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 53-year-old woman is found by arteriography to have 50% narrowing of her left renal artery. What is the expected change of blood flow through the stenotic artery? (Repeated 3X)

questions.question: Which of the following increases turbulent flow?
questions.explanation: D — partial occlusion. Abrupt narrowing raises velocity and promotes turbulence; complete occlusion stops flow, while high viscosity/hematocrit lower Reynolds number.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following increases turbulent flow? (Repeated)

questions.question: What is the right formula for pressure resistance and flow?
options: Flow = Change in pressure x Resistance
Change in pressure = Flow x Resistance
questions.sourceIssue: The corrected booklet accepts multiple answers: B/C. Self-check; excluded from single-answer grading.
questions.explanation: B and C are equivalent correct forms. ΔP=F·R and R=ΔP/F are both Ohm/Poiseuille relations; A/D invert the relation. Printed two-answer key correctly recognizes both. Key OK, duplicate correct choices.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the right formula for pressure resistance and flow?

questions.question: Based on the law of Laplace, what would increase the wall tension?
questions.explanation: A — increased pressure. Laplace wall tension rises with transmural pressure (and radius); reducing radius or pressure lowers tension, and greater thickness lowers circumferential stress.
questions.sourceQuestion: Based on the law of Laplace, what would increase the wall tension?

questions.question: What will decrease the blood flow?
options: Decrease the length of the vessel
questions.explanation: A — decreased diameter. Smaller radius greatly raises resistance and reduces flow. Shorter length, lower viscosity, or higher pressure gradient would raise flow.
questions.sourceQuestion: What will decrease the blood flow?

questions.question: Which of the following increases turbulent blood flow?
questions.explanation: B — sudden narrowing. It accelerates flow and causes separation/turbulence; complete occlusion leaves no flow, lower velocity and higher viscosity reduce turbulence.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following increases turbulent blood flow? (Repeated 2X)

questions.question: Which of the following vessels has the most Distensibility?
questions.explanation: A — veins. Veins distend substantially with small pressure changes; arteries/aorta are less compliant and capillaries are not capacitance vessels.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following vessels has the most Distensibility? (Repeated)

questions.question: During a routine angiography of a patient, it is noted that a stenosis has reduced the lumen by 50%. A stent is inserted into the affected area and the lumen of the stenotic segment is returned to normal. What would be the expected improvement (increase) in blood flow through the repaired segment?
questions.explanation: C — 16-fold. Restoring a lumen whose diameter was halved cuts resistance by 16× and raises flow 16× at fixed gradient. A/B/D/E mismatch fourth-power law. Key OK; “lumen” should specify diameter.
questions.sourceQuestion: During a routine angiography of a patient, it is noted that a stenosis has reduced the lumen by 50%. A stent is inserted into the affected area and the lumen of the stenotic segment is returned to normal. What would be the expected improvement (increase) in blood flow through the repaired segment? (Repeated)

questions.question: What increases blood flow?
questions.explanation: B — dilation. Larger radius lowers resistance; elongation/viscosity lower flow and a smaller ΔP lowers flow.
questions.sourceQuestion: What increases blood flow?

questions.question: Calculate the total resistance to the nearest number (units are depicted in the diagram):
questions.explanation: C — 5 units. The figure shows 1 unit in series before three 6-unit branches in parallel (equivalent 2), then 2 units in series: 1+2+2=5. A/B/D/E do not match.
questions.sourceQuestion: Calculate the total resistance to the nearest number (units are depicted in the diagram):

questions.question: Which of the following explains the law of laplace ?
options: An increase of diameter would lead to a decrease of tension
An increase of diameter would lead to an increase of tension
A decrease of transmural pressure would lead to an increase of tension
An increase of wall thickness directly increases the total wall tension
questions.explanation: B — larger diameter increases tension. For a thin-walled vessel at fixed pressure, T≈P·r; A/C reverse this relation, while wall thickness affects wall stress rather than total tension in the asserted way.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following explains the law of laplace ?

questions.question: A 52-year-old male has developed a stenosis in his femoral artery which has reduced the cross-sectional area in this region by half. If the velocity of flow in the un-stenosed proximal segment is 5.0cm/sec. What would the average velocity of flow be in the stenosed segment?
questions.explanation: D — 10 cm/s. Continuity: halving cross-sectional area doubles velocity from 5 to 10. A/B/C/E violate Q=A·v.
questions.sourceQuestion: 0cm/sec. What would the average velocity of flow be in the stenosed segment?

questions.question: The tendency for the blood flow to be turbulent is increased by which of the following?
options: Complete occlusion of a blood vessel
questions.explanation: B — increased velocity. Reynolds number rises with velocity; greater viscosity or hematocrit lowers it, as does reduced output. Complete occlusion abolishes flow.
questions.sourceQuestion: The tendency for the blood flow to be turbulent is increased by which of the following? (Repeated)

questions.question: Vascular resistance increased when?
questions.explanation: A — decreased radius. Poiseuille resistance varies inversely with r⁴; lowering viscosity, hematocrit, sympathetic tone, or length tends to lower resistance.
questions.sourceQuestion: Vascular resistance increased when? (Repeated 2X)

questions.question: Which is the correct expression? F= flow, ΔP = pressure gradient, R= resistance.
questions.explanation: A — F=ΔP/R. Rearrangement gives ΔP=F·R and R=ΔP/F; B/C invert those relations and D multiplies instead of divides.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which is the correct expression? F= flow, ΔP = pressure gradient, R= resistance. (Repeated)

questions.question: The diameter of the aorta was decreased by half, which of the following states by how many times does the flow decrease?
questions.explanation: E — flow decreases 16-fold. Halving diameter raises resistance 16-fold and cuts flow to one-sixteenth at fixed ΔP. A–D understate.
questions.sourceQuestion: The diameter of the aorta was decreased by half, which of the following states by how many times does the flow decrease?

questions.question: Which of the following segments of the cardiovascular system has the highest resistance to blood flow?
questions.explanation: B — arterioles. Small arteries/arterioles create the largest adjustable pressure drop; the other listed segments have lower resistance.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following segments of the cardiovascular system has the highest resistance to blood flow?

questions.question: What effect should the stenosis have on the following? Blood flow: Blood velocity: Laminar blood flow:
questions.explanation: B — flow down, velocity up, laminarity down. A stenosis raises local velocity, resistance reduces total flow, and disturbed flow becomes more likely. Other sequences reverse one or more effects.
questions.sourceQuestion: What effect should the stenosis have on the following? Blood flow: Blood velocity: Laminar blood flow:

questions.question: During extreme exercise, which of the following is correct?
questions.printedAnswer: B (C can also be correct but the intended answer is B since diastole decreases significantly more
questions.explanation: B — TPR decreases. Exercising muscle vasodilation lowers systemic resistance; A/D/E reverse exercise responses. C can also be true in extreme exercise (systolic duration shortens modestly), so the item is not strictly single-best. Key acknowledges an additional true option; ambiguous.
questions.sourceQuestion: During extreme exercise, which of the following is correct? (Repeated )

questions.question: Which one of the following blood vessels exhibits the highest blood velocity?
questions.explanation: C — aorta. It has the highest velocity because its cross-sectional area is the smallest summed area in the systemic circuit. Capillaries are slowest; B/D are intermediate.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which one of the following blood vessels exhibits the highest blood velocity?

questions.question: What decreases venous resistance?
questions.explanation: A — decreased sympathetic stimulation. Venodilation lowers venous resistance; sympathetic constriction and viscosity increase resistance. External compression tends to propel/alter venous flow but does not reduce intrinsic resistance as the stated answer implies. Key broadly OK; D is underspecified.
questions.sourceQuestion: What decreases venous resistance?

questions.question: What increases vascular resistance?
questions.explanation: C — increased sympathetic tone. Arteriolar constriction increases resistance. A may cause local hypoxic vasodilation; B is not an independent increase in resistance; D/E tend to lower it.
questions.sourceQuestion: What increases vascular resistance? (Repeated)

questions.question: Which of the following increases blood flow?
questions.explanation: B — increasing diameter. Dilation lowers resistance and raises flow; A/C do the opposite. Parasympathetic tone is not a generalized systemic flow determinant.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following increases blood flow?

questions.question: A patient suffered a hemorrhage, which of the following vessels shift blood to compensate for the blood loss?
questions.explanation: D — capacitance veins. Venoconstriction mobilizes stored blood toward the heart after hemorrhage. A–C are not major blood reservoirs.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient suffered a hemorrhage, which of the following vessels shift blood to compensate for the blood loss?

questions.question: Left heart failure causes pulmonary edema due to the increasing net filtration rate. Which of the following pressures will increase?
questions.explanation: B — capillary hydrostatic pressure. Left-heart failure backs pressure into pulmonary veins/capillaries and promotes filtration. A opposes filtration; C/D are not the initiating pressure rise.
questions.sourceQuestion: Left heart failure causes pulmonary edema due to the increasing net filtration rate. Which of the following pressures will increase?

questions.question: Increase in which of the following parameters would increase venous return?
questions.explanation: A — venous constriction. It raises mean systemic filling pressure and venous return; higher RAP reduces the return gradient, and ESV is not the direct determinant.
questions.sourceQuestion: Increase in which of the following parameters would increase venous return?

questions.question: A patient got a lymph injury in the ankle region which led to edema. Which of the following is increased in that region?
questions.explanation: A — interstitial colloid osmotic pressure. Lymphatic obstruction leaves protein in interstitium, raising its oncotic pull and edema. B is plasma oncotic pressure; C/D can vary but are not the defining consequence.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient got a lymph injury in the ankle region which led to edema. Which of the following is increased in that region?

questions.question: A person suddenly stands up from supine position, which of the following represents what will happen to the Central Venous Pressure, Right atrial Pressure, and the Venous return of this person if the compensatory mechanism is not functional?
options: CVP Decreases; RAP Increases; VR Increases
CVP Increases; RAP Increases; VR Increases
CVP Increases; RAP Decreases; VR Increases
CVP Increases; RAP Decreases; VR Increases
CVP Decreases; RAP Decreases; VR Decreases
questions.explanation: E — CVP↓, RAP↓, VR↓. Standing pools blood in dependent veins, reducing central filling and venous return when compensation fails. A–D predict increases and/or inconsistent RAP.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person suddenly stands up from supine position, which of the following represents what will happen to the Central Venous Pressure, Right atrial Pressure, and the Venous return of this person if the compensatory mechanism is not functional?

questions.question: Capillary osmotic pressure causes fluid to move from?
questions.explanation: A — interstitium to capillary. Plasma oncotic pressure pulls water inward; B reverses it, C/D are incorrect.
questions.sourceQuestion: Capillary osmotic pressure causes fluid to move from?

questions.question: What increases lymph flow through lymphatic vessels?
options: Paralysis of smooth muscle of lymphatic vessel
questions.explanation: B — increased interstitial hydrostatic pressure. It drives lymph into lymphatics; lower capillary pressure/filtration coefficient or paralysis reduces lymph flow.
questions.sourceQuestion: What increases lymph flow through lymphatic vessels?

questions.question: Calculate Net Filtration Rate and direction. Capillary hydrostatic pressure: 26; Interstitial hydrostatic pressure: -1; Plasma oncotic pressure: 28; Tissue oncotic pressure: 3.
questions.explanation: E — filtration by 2 mmHg. NFP=(26−(−1))−(28−3)=27−25=+2 outward. A–D conflict with this calculation.
questions.sourceQuestion: Calculate Net Filtration Rate and direction. Capillary hydrostatic pressure: 26; Interstitial hydrostatic pressure: -1; Plasma oncotic pressure: 28; Tissue oncotic pressure: 3.

questions.question: What increases venous compliance?
questions.explanation: B — decreased sympathetic tone. Venodilation increases venous compliance; increased sympathetic tone lowers it. Parasympathetic alternatives are not the principal control.
questions.sourceQuestion: What increases venous compliance?

questions.question: Calculate Net Filtration Rate and direction: Capillary hydrostatic pressure: 25 Interstitial hydrostatic pressure: -1 Plasma oncotic pressure: 22 Tissue oncotic pressure: -5
questions.explanation: C — absorption by 1 mmHg. NFP=(25−(−1))−(22−(−5))=26−27=−1. A/B/D give wrong direction/magnitude.
questions.sourceQuestion: Calculate Net Filtration Rate and direction: Capillary hydrostatic pressure: 25 Interstitial hydrostatic pressure: -1 Plasma oncotic pressure: 22 Tissue oncotic pressure: -5

questions.question: What causes an increase in pulse pressure?
questions.explanation: A — decreased arterial compliance. For a given SV, stiffer arteries produce larger pulse pressure. B lowers it; C is not the governing isolated change.
questions.sourceQuestion: What causes an increase in pulse pressure? (Repeated)

questions.question: Capillary pressure = 17 mmHg; interstitial fluid = –1; plasma colloid = 28; interstitial colloid = 4. What is the net filtration rate and direction?
questions.explanation: A — absorption by 6 mmHg. NFP=(17−(−1))−(28−4)=18−24=−6. B reverses direction; C miscalculates.
questions.sourceQuestion: Capillary pressure = 17 mmHg; interstitial fluid = –1; plasma colloid = 28; interstitial colloid = 4. What is the net filtration rate and direction?

questions.question: Increase in which of the following decreases lymph flow?
questions.explanation: B — increased plasma osmotic pressure. It draws fluid into capillaries, reducing interstitial volume and lymph flow. A/C generally increase filtration/lymph flow.
questions.sourceQuestion: Increase in which of the following decreases lymph flow?

questions.question: Which of the following increases in lymph flow?
options: decreased the size of the capillary pore
questions.explanation: B — increased interstitial fluid pressure. Higher interstitial pressure increases lymph entry/flow. A/C/D/E reduce filtration or interstitial fluid.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following increases in lymph flow?

questions.question: In a capillary the hydrostatic capillary pressure was 17, the plasma colloid pressure was 24, the interstitial pressure was -3 and the interstitial colloid pressure was 4. What is the direction of fluid movement and the net driving force?
questions.explanation: A — no net movement. NFP=(17−(−3))−(24−4)=20−20=0. B/C/D have nonzero driving forces.
questions.sourceQuestion: In a capillary the hydrostatic capillary pressure was 17, the plasma colloid pressure was 24, the interstitial pressure was -3 and the interstitial colloid pressure was 4. What is the direction of fluid movement and the net driving force?

questions.question: In a capillary the hydrostatic capillary pressure was 21, the plasma colloid pressure was 24, the interstitial pressure was -3 and the interstitial colloid pressure was 4. What is the direction of fluid movement and the net driving force?
questions.explanation: C — +4 mmHg filtration. NFP=(21−(−3))−(24−4)=24−20=+4. A/B/D/E mismatch.
questions.sourceQuestion: In a capillary the hydrostatic capillary pressure was 21, the plasma colloid pressure was 24, the interstitial pressure was -3 and the interstitial colloid pressure was 4. What is the direction of fluid movement and the net driving force?

questions.question: Which two statements are correctly paired?
options: decrease cardiac output / increase venous return.
increase cardiac output/ increase total peripheral resistance.
Increase total peripheral resistance/ decrease venous return.
questions.explanation: C — higher TPR lowers venous return. Increased resistance to flow lowers VR; A/B and D have incorrect direction, and afterload does not increase SV as D states.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which two statements are correctly paired?

questions.question: Which of the following will result in a decrease in pulse pressure?
questions.explanation: B — increased arterial compliance. A more compliant arterial tree buffers systolic pressure and narrows pulse pressure. A/C usually widen it; D is not the direct relation.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following will result in a decrease in pulse pressure?

questions.question: Which of the following would most likely increase the tendency for edema to develop in the lower extremities?
questions.explanation: D — decreased plasma protein concentration. Lower oncotic pressure favors outward filtration and edema. Walking promotes muscle pump; decreased venous pressure reduces filtration; increased CO is not the most direct factor.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following would most likely increase the tendency for edema to develop in the lower extremities?

questions.question: Which segment of the vasculature has the highest elastic recoil?
questions.explanation: A — arteries. Elastic arteries recoil strongly to maintain diastolic flow. Veins/venules/capillaries have less elastic recoil.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which segment of the vasculature has the highest elastic recoil? (Repeated)

questions.question: Which component of the circulatory system contains the largest percentage of total blood volume?
questions.explanation: A — veins. Systemic veins contain the largest fraction of blood volume at rest. Arteries, capillaries and arterioles contain less.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which component of the circulatory system contains the largest percentage of total blood volume?

questions.question: If capillary hydrostatic pressure is 18 mmHg, interstitial pressure is –2 mmHg, plasma colloid pressure is 23 mmHg, and interstitial colloid pressure is 3 mmHg, what is the net direction of blood flow?
questions.explanation: A — no net force. NFP=(18−(−2))−(23−3)=20−20=0. B–E incorrectly give a nonzero force.
