questions.sourceQuestion: If capillary hydrostatic pressure is 18 mmHg, interstitial pressure is –2 mmHg, plasma colloid pressure is 23 mmHg, and interstitial colloid pressure is 3 mmHg, what is the net direction of blood flow?

questions.question: Which of the following increases lymph flow?
options: Increase in ECF interstitial fluid pressure
questions.explanation: B — increased interstitial fluid pressure. It promotes lymph entry and flow. Higher plasma oncotic pressure lowers filtration; intracellular volume is not directly the lymph driver.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following increases lymph flow?

questions.question: Which structure has the most compliance?
questions.explanation: C — veins. Their high compliance lets them store volume with little pressure rise. Capillaries and arterial options are less compliant.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which structure has the most compliance?

questions.question: Venous compliance:
questions.explanation: A — sympathetic stimulation decreases venous compliance. Venoconstriction decreases capacity/compliance; B reverses, and parasympathetic choices are not the dominant effect.
questions.sourceQuestion: Venous compliance: (Repeated)

questions.question: A decrease in which one of the following tends to increase pulse pressure?
questions.explanation: C — compliance. Decreasing compliance increases pulse pressure (ΔP≈SV/C). A/B/D are not the stated determinant or tend the other direction.
questions.sourceQuestion: A decrease in which one of the following tends to increase pulse pressure?

questions.question: What causes increased movement of fluid from the pulmonary capillary lumen to the interstitium?
options: Increased hydrostatic pressure in interstitial space
Reduced colloid osmotic pressure in blood
Reduced osmotic pressure in interstitial fluid
questions.explanation: D — reduced plasma colloid osmotic pressure. Lower oncotic opposition increases filtration into pulmonary interstitium. A lowers net filtration; B targets epithelium rather than Starling flux; C/E wording reduces filtration.
questions.sourceQuestion: What causes increased movement of fluid from the pulmonary capillary lumen to the interstitium?

questions.question: Which of the following vessels has the highest elasticity?
questions.explanation: A — aorta. The aorta has the greatest elastic recoil among options; veins are compliant but not the highest-elasticity vessel.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following vessels has the highest elasticity?

questions.question: The Starling forces for a particular capillary are: Capillary hydrostatic pressure: 17 mmHg Interstitial hydrostatic pressure: -1 mmHg Plasma colloid osmotic pressure: 28 mmHg Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure: 4 mmHg What is the net filtration pressure and net movement?
questions.explanation: A — 6 mmHg reabsorption. NFP=(17−(−1))−(28−4)=18−24=−6. Other choices have wrong magnitude/direction.
questions.sourceQuestion: The Starling forces for a particular capillary are: Capillary hydrostatic pressure: 17 mmHg Interstitial hydrostatic pressure: -1 mmHg Plasma colloid osmotic pressure: 28 mmHg Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure: 4 mmHg What is the net filtration pressure and net movement?

questions.question: A 24-year-old volunteer participates in a cardiovascular physiology study. An experimental device is used to safely apply localized external pressure to the anterior neck, mechanically compressing the carotid sinuses to simulate a sudden, severe spike in arterial pressure. Which of the following sets of changes would be observed in this volunteer during the compression?
options: Increased heart rate, increased cardiac output, & increased systemic vascular resistance
Decreased heart rate, increased cardiac output, & increased systemic vascular resistance
Increased heart rate, decreased cardiac output, & decreased systemic vascular resistance
Decreased heart rate, decreased cardiac output, & decreased systemic vascular resistance
Decreased heart rate, increased cardiac output, & decreased systemic vascular resistance
questions.explanation: D — lower HR, CO and SVR. Carotid sinus compression mimics high pressure, increasing baroreceptor firing and suppressing sympathetic while increasing vagal tone. A/C predict tachycardia; B/E have conflicting outputs.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 24-year-old volunteer participates in a cardiovascular physiology study. An experimental device is used to safely apply localized external pressure to the anterior neck, mechanically compressing the carotid sinuses to simulate a sudden, severe spike in arterial pressure. Which of the following sets of changes would be observed in this volunteer during the compression?

questions.question: A hard-working sales clerk worked in a busy department store and stood behind the checkout counter for 8 hours. When he got home, he noticed his ankles were swollen. What physiological issue is most likely to blame in this scenario?
options: Lymphatic blockage of the lower legs
High osmotic pressure in the lower leg capillaries
High hydrostatic pressure in the lower leg capillaries
High venous pumping activity by the skeletal muscle
questions.explanation: C — increased dependent capillary hydrostatic pressure. Prolonged standing raises leg venous/capillary pressure and filtration. A/B/D do not explain gravity-dependent edema.
questions.sourceQuestion: A hard-working sales clerk worked in a busy department store and stood behind the checkout counter for 8 hours. When he got home, he noticed his ankles were swollen. What physiological issue is most likely to blame in this scenario?

questions.question: A patient presented with a diastolic murmur. His end diastolic volume was 70, and also presented with left atrial hypertrophy. Which of the following is the cause for the murmur?
questions.explanation: C — mitral stenosis. It causes a diastolic murmur and LA enlargement; aortic/pulmonic regurgitation are diastolic but do not cause LA hypertrophy, and stenoses of semilunar valves are systolic.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient presented with a diastolic murmur. His end diastolic volume was 70, and also presented with left atrial hypertrophy. Which of the following is the cause for the murmur?

questions.question: What may occur as a result of left sided heart failure?
questions.explanation: A — pulmonary edema. Left failure backs pressure into pulmonary veins; hepatomegaly/jaundice/peripheral edema more suggest systemic venous congestion/right failure.
questions.sourceQuestion: What may occur as a result of left sided heart failure?

questions.question: Closure of which of the following pairs of valves causes S1 heart sound?
questions.explanation: D — mitral and tricuspid. S1 is AV-valve closure; semilunar closure creates S2.
questions.sourceQuestion: Closure of which of the following pairs of valves causes S1 heart sound?

questions.question: A 51 year old man is diagnosed with aortic valve regurgitation. From the attached table which effect does this valve pathology have on the left ventricular end diastolic volume (LVEDV), stroke volume (SV) and pulse pressure (PP)?
options: LVEDV decreased; SV decreased; PP decreased
LVEDV increased; SV increased; PP increased
LVEDV increased; SV increased; PP decreased
LVEDV decreased; SV decreased; PP increased
questions.explanation: B — regurgitation raises LVEDV, total SV and pulse pressure. Backflow adds to diastolic volume and wide PP is typical; other table rows conflict. The table confirms B. The supplied explanation incorrectly says end-diastolic pressure decreases and end-systolic pressure increases as the reason for wide PP; regurgitation produces rapid diastolic pressure runoff and increased systolic ejection. Key right; explanation partly wrong.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 51 year old man is diagnosed with aortic valve regurgitation. From the attached table which effect does this valve pathology have on the left ventricular end diastolic volume (LVEDV), stroke volume (SV) and pulse pressure (PP)?

questions.question: What is the cause of S4 heart sound?
questions.explanation: D — aortic stenosis. S4 reflects atrial kick into a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle, often due to AS; A/B can also stiffen ventricles, making this single choice imperfect. C does not cause S4; E is not typical. Key ambiguous: S4 is not specific to AS.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the cause of S4 heart sound?

questions.question: Which would cause a decrease in the end diastolic volume?
questions.explanation: A — mitral stenosis. Restricted LV filling lowers EDV; aortic stenosis can reduce forward flow but not primarily filling, while regurgitant lesions increase EDV.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which would cause a decrease in the end diastolic volume?

questions.question: Where does the second heart sound happen in the pressure-volume loop of the left ventricle diagram?
questions.explanation: D — Point 7. It marks the upper-left end-ejection corner where the aortic valve closes and S2 begins. Point 1 is mitral opening, 3 mitral closure, and 5 aortic opening.
questions.sourceQuestion: Where does the second heart sound happen in the pressure-volume loop of the left ventricle diagram?

questions.question: During which of the following phases does S3 occur?
questions.explanation: A — rapid filling. S3 occurs in early diastole during rapid passive filling; B/C are isovolumetric phases, D slow filling, E atrial systole/S4.
reasons: Rapid early ventricular filling is the phase associated with S3.
All valves are closed during isovolumetric relaxation, so rapid inflow has not yet begun.
Isovolumetric contraction occurs at the onset of systole and is associated with S1, not S3.
Slow filling occurs later in diastole than the typical S3.
Atrial contraction occurs in late diastole and is associated with S4 when the ventricle is stiff.
questions.sourceQuestion: During which of the following phases does S3 occur?

questions.question: Which of the following causes a diastolic murmur and produces S3 heart sound?
questions.explanation: C — pulmonary regurgitation. It creates a diastolic murmur and may generate an S3 with increased volume loading; mitral stenosis is diastolic but classically produces opening snap, while AS/PS are systolic. Key plausible; S3 is not uniquely diagnostic.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following causes a diastolic murmur and produces S3 heart sound?

questions.question: The first heart sound is caused by?
questions.explanation: A — AV valve closure. S1 follows mitral/tricuspid closure; semilunar closure is S2 and valve opening is normally silent.
questions.sourceQuestion: The first heart sound is caused by?

questions.question: What is the cause of difficulty in breathing due to mitral valve stenosis and constriction of esophagus?
questions.explanation: B — enlarged left atrium. LA enlargement from mitral stenosis can compress esophagus and pulmonary structures; other options are not adjacent cause.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the cause of difficulty in breathing due to mitral valve stenosis and constriction of esophagus?

questions.question: Left systolic heart failure produces which heart sound?
questions.explanation: C — S3. Systolic LV failure commonly causes S3 from rapid filling into a dilated, volume-loaded ventricle. S1/S2 are normal closure sounds; S4 is stiff ventricle.
questions.sourceQuestion: Left systolic heart failure produces which heart sound?

questions.question: A person suffering from MI is brought to a hospital but dies soon after. Later it is observed that the muscle that controls closing of valves is affected. Which muscle was affected?
questions.explanation: B — papillary muscle. Papillary muscles tense chordae to prevent AV prolapse during systole; other listed muscles do not control valve closure.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person suffering from MI is brought to a hospital but dies soon after. Later it is observed that the muscle that controls closing of valves is affected. Which muscle was affected?

questions.question: Which of the following conditions decreases pulse pressure?
questions.explanation: A — aortic stenosis. Reduced stroke volume narrows pulse pressure; atherosclerosis/decreased compliance and increased SV widen it.
reasons: Aortic stenosis can limit stroke volume and narrow pulse pressure.
Arterial stiffening with atherosclerosis tends to increase pulse pressure rather than narrow it.
An increased stroke volume tends to increase the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure.
Decreased arterial compliance tends to increase the pressure rise produced by a given stroke volume.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following conditions decreases pulse pressure?

questions.question: A patient who had an episode of syncope and was brought to the hospital by his son. Upon gaining consciousness, he complained of chest pain and difficulty breathing. He was referred to the cardiac lab where an echocardiograph was made and showed a murmur. What type of murmur is shown?
questions.explanation: A — Aortic stenosis. The tracing has a diamond-shaped crescendo–decrescendo systolic ejection murmur. B causes an early diastolic decrescendo, C a diastolic rumble, and D a typically holosystolic murmur.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient who had an episode of syncope and was brought to the hospital by his son. Upon gaining consciousness, he complained of chest pain and difficulty breathing. He was referred to the cardiac lab where an echocardiograph was made and showed a murmur. What type of murmur is shown?

questions.question: When does the third heart sound occur in the ventricular pressure/volume relationship?
options: Between point A and point B
Between point B and point C
Between point C and point D
Between point D and point A
questions.explanation: B — Between A and B. S3 occurs early on the filling limb after mitral opening. A (point D) is end ejection, C (B to C) is isovolumetric contraction, D (C to D) is ejection, and E (D to A) is isovolumetric relaxation.
questions.sourceQuestion: When does the third heart sound occur in the ventricular pressure/volume relationship?

questions.question: A 65-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath, she describes being fatigued and weak for months. A murmur was heard at the upper right sternal border. Her arterial blood pressure is 154/63. Which of the following pathologies best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: A — aortic regurgitation. Wide pulse pressure (154/63) and right upper sternal border murmur support AR; other options usually do not widen PP this way.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 65-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath, she describes being fatigued and weak for months. A murmur was heard at the upper right sternal border. Her arterial blood pressure is 154/63. Which of the following pathologies best explains these findings?

questions.question: Which of the following will happen at a late stage of mitral stenosis?
options: Decreased pressure in the pulmonary artery
questions.explanation: A — pulmonary arteriolar constriction. Chronic LA/pulmonary venous hypertension causes reactive pulmonary vasoconstriction; LV hypertrophy is not typical of isolated MS, and PA pressure rises rather than falls.
reasons: Reactive pulmonary arteriolar constriction can occur downstream of chronic pulmonary venous hypertension.
Decreased total blood volume is not the defining late pulmonary vascular response to mitral inflow obstruction.
Isolated mitral stenosis does not directly create the LV outflow pressure overload that produces concentric LV hypertrophy.
Advanced pulmonary vascular disease tends to raise, not lower, pulmonary arterial pressure.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following will happen at a late stage of mitral stenosis?

questions.question: A person with aortic stenosis is most likely to have?
questions.explanation: B — increased blood volume (as printed). This is not a characteristic consequence of aortic stenosis; classic findings are pressure-loaded LV and reduced stroke volume, not increased total blood volume. A is also unsupported; C is not inevitable. Key wrong/unsupported; no valid answer as worded.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person with aortic stenosis is most likely to have?

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the production of the first and second heart sounds respectively?
options: Closure of the AV valves followed by closure of the semilunar valves
Closure of the AV valves followed by the opening of the semilunar valves
Opening of the semilunar valves followed by the closure of the AV valves
Closure of the semilunar valves followed by the closure of the AV valves
questions.explanation: A — AV closure then semilunar closure. S1 then S2. Other options reverse or substitute valve opening.
reasons: AV closure generates S1, followed later by semilunar closure generating S2.
Semilunar opening begins ejection but does not normally generate S2.
This sequence reverses the normal ordering and incorrectly attributes a sound to opening.
Semilunar closure occurs after AV closure in the normal systolic sequence, not before it.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following best describes the production of the first and second heart sounds respectively? (Repeated)

questions.question: The second heart beat (dub) is created by which one of the following?
options: Vibration of the chordae tendineae during ventricular systole
questions.explanation: E — semilunar closure. S2 (“dub”) is aortic and pulmonary closure; other options relate to S1 or are not sound-generating events.
questions.sourceQuestion: The second heart beat (dub) is created by which one of the following? (Repeated)

questions.question: Which of the following heart murmurs is heard only during diastole?
questions.explanation: B — mitral stenosis. It causes a diastolic rumble; AS is systolic, MR holosystolic, PDA continuous and VSD holosystolic.
reasons: Aortic stenosis produces a systolic ejection murmur during LV outflow.
Mitral stenosis produces a diastolic inflow murmur while the mitral valve should be open.
Mitral regurgitation produces a systolic murmur as LV pressure drives blood back into the atrium.
A patent ductus arteriosus can produce continuous flow and a continuous murmur across systole and diastole.
A ventricular septal defect usually produces a systolic murmur from the LV-to-RV pressure gradient.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following heart murmurs is heard only during diastole?

questions.question: During mitral regurgitation, which of the following will increase?
questions.explanation: A — EDV. Regurgitated blood returns to LA then LV, increasing filling volume; afterload is not increased, and ESV may vary.
questions.sourceQuestion: During mitral regurgitation, which of the following will increase?

questions.question: Which of the following is the diagnosis according to the attached PV Loop?
questions.explanation: B — Aortic stenosis. The yellow loop shows substantially higher LV systolic pressure and a smaller stroke volume. A and E lose clear isovolumetric limbs through regurgitation, C usually reduces LV filling, and D loads the right ventricle.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is the diagnosis according to the attached PV Loop?

questions.question: A 38 year-old man is participating in a clinical trial of a new drug. This drug leads to an increase in venous compliance and a decrease in cardiac contractility. The star is the intersection point under normal conditions. If only these effects were manifested, which new intersection point would be achieved following administration of the drug?
questions.explanation: D — Point N. Less contractility selects the lower cardiac function curve and higher venous compliance selects the left-shifted venous return curve. M and H retain a less left-shifted venous curve, while D and A lie above the depressed cardiac function curve.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 38 year-old man is participating in a clinical trial of a new drug. This drug leads to an increase in venous compliance and a decrease in cardiac contractility. The star is the intersection point under normal conditions. If only these effects were manifested, which new intersection point would be achieved following administration of the drug?

questions.question: A person was severely dehydrated and was rushed to the hospital. Upon entering the hospital his heart rate was 130 bpm and blood pressure was 80/50. He was rehydrated by intravenous injections. Which of the following points best describes his venous return cardiac function Curve?
questions.explanation: D — Point I is the intended intersection. Fluids raise stressed volume and move the venous return curve rightward from the dehydrated state. C/E/G/F correspond to different combinations of filling pressure and cardiac function. The amount of fluid and residual reflex response are unspecified, so an exact point requires the figure’s assumed degree of change.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person was severely dehydrated and was rushed to the hospital. Upon entering the hospital his heart rate was 130 bpm and blood pressure was 80/50. He was rehydrated by intravenous injections. Which of the following points best describes his venous return cardiac function Curve?

questions.question: The Cardiac Output (CO) = 4500 mL/min, Mean Atrial Pressure (MAP) = 94 mmHg, Right atrial pressure (RAP) = 4 mmHg. Which of the following is the Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR)?
questions.explanation: E — 0.02 mmHg·min/mL. SVR=(MAP−RAP)/CO=90/4500=0.02; other values are magnitude/unit errors.
questions.sourceQuestion: The Cardiac Output (CO) = 4500 mL/min, Mean Atrial Pressure (MAP) = 94 mmHg, Right atrial pressure (RAP) = 4 mmHg. Which of the following is the Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR)?

questions.question: Patient with severe haemorrhage, what is his cardiac/venous return state after all compensatory measures are taken?
questions.explanation: B — Point D. The intended compensated hemorrhage state combines reduced filling from blood loss with an elevated cardiac function curve from sympathetic compensation. E lies further left on that curve, C closer to baseline filling, and I/H on a different cardiac function curve. The degree of blood loss and compensation is unspecified.
questions.sourceQuestion: Patient with severe haemorrhage, what is his cardiac/venous return state after all compensatory measures are taken?

questions.question: If there was a positive ionotropic agent and decreased venous compliance, what would be the new point of the star?
questions.explanation: B — Point 1. Positive inotropy raises the cardiac function curve, and reduced venous compliance shifts the venous return curve toward higher mean systemic filling pressure. Points 3, 2 and 6 do not combine both of those directions.
questions.sourceQuestion: If there was a positive ionotropic agent and decreased venous compliance, what would be the new point of the star?

questions.question: A 32-year-old man is taking part in a trial of an experimental drug. The drug simultaneously decreases arteriolar resistance and decreases myocardial contractility. The star on the attached graph represents the intersection point for the patient before administration of the drug. Which new intersection point will be achieved following drug administration?
questions.explanation: D — Point 6 is the intended intersection. Reduced arteriolar resistance decreases resistance to venous return, while reduced myocardial contractility selects the depressed cardiac function curve. Points 1/2/3 do not combine both shifts and point 7 has lower flow without the intended reduction in venous resistance.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 32-year-old man is taking part in a trial of an experimental drug. The drug simultaneously decreases arteriolar resistance and decreases myocardial contractility. The star on the attached graph represents the intersection point for the patient before administration of the drug. Which new intersection point will be achieved following drug administration?

questions.question: A woman puts values into the machine. If CO is 5 and TPR is unknown value, the machine calculates the MAP as 100. If the TPR is halved, what would be the MAP?
questions.explanation: C — MAP 50. MAP≈CO×TPR (ignoring RAP); halving TPR halves MAP from 100 to 50. A doubles, B unchanged, D wrong.
questions.sourceQuestion: A woman puts values into the machine. If CO is 5 and TPR is unknown value, the machine calculates the MAP as 100. If the TPR is halved, what would be the MAP?

questions.question: What will be the reason to shift the curve up/to left ?
questions.explanation: D — increased contractility. Inotropy raises the cardiac function curve; negative inotropy/SVR lower output, and increased MSFP/volume shifts venous return.
questions.sourceQuestion: What will be the reason to shift the curve up/to left ?

questions.question: A patient at rest is given a drug that reduces the venous compliance but has no other cardiac or vascular effects. What effect will this drug have on venous return and venous blood capacity?
options: Venous return increases and venous capacity decreases
Venous return decreases and venous capacity increases
Venous return decreases and venous capacity will not change
Venous return will not change, and venous capacity will not change
Venous return will not change and venous capacity decreases
questions.explanation: A — VR rises, venous capacity falls. Lower compliance constricts veins, mobilizes volume and raises MSFP/return. B reverses both; C–E mismatch at least one.
reasons: Less venous capacitance means less storage at a given pressure and a higher driving pressure for venous return.
Increased capacity describes venodilation, the opposite of the stated compliance reduction.
A compliance reduction changes capacity; treating capacity as unchanged misses the mechanism.
The venous pressure–volume relation changes, so both capacity and the venous-return driving gradient can change.
Capacity decreases, but at fixed volume the resulting pressure rise can increase venous return rather than leave it unchanged.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient at rest is given a drug that reduces the venous compliance but has no other cardiac or vascular effects. What effect will this drug have on venous return and venous blood capacity?

questions.question: A 63-year-old obese woman is treated for hypertension with a drug that antagonizes both alpha – and beta – adrenergic receptors. What direct effect will this drug have on total peripheral resistance and cardiac contraction strength?
options: Total peripheral resistance decreases and cardiac contraction strength decreases
Total peripheral resistance increases and cardiac contraction strength increases
Total peripheral resistance increases and cardiac contraction strength decreases
Total peripheral resistance decreases and cardiac contraction strength increases
Total peripheral resistance will not change, and cardiac contraction strength will not Change
questions.explanation: A — TPR and contractility decrease. Alpha blockade dilates arterioles, beta blockade lowers cardiac inotropy; other options reverse one/both.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 63-year-old obese woman is treated for hypertension with a drug that antagonizes both alpha – and beta – adrenergic receptors. What direct effect will this drug have on total peripheral resistance and cardiac contraction strength?

questions.question: If there is a parallel left shift of the venous return curve, which is true?
questions.explanation: A — decreased MSFP. A parallel left shift of VR curve indicates lower filling pressure/volume; increased CO or venous sympathetic tone shifts right. C is slope change, not parallel shift.
questions.sourceQuestion: If there is a parallel left shift of the venous return curve, which is true?

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the new equilibrium point at D that has been reached after surgical removal of some arterioles?
options: Parallel shifting of venous return due to increased venous compliance
Decreased sympathetic stimulation tone due to normal arterial pressure
Increased mean circulatory filling pressure due to reduced TPR
Increased water and salt retention and contractility of the heart
Increased cardiac output due to decreased arterial pressure
questions.explanation: D per graph. Chronic reduced TPR can lower pressure and trigger renal retention plus increased contractility, shifting curves to new equilibrium; other choices do not describe compensation. Key graph-dependent/context incomplete.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is true regarding the new equilibrium point at D that has been reached after surgical removal of some arterioles?

questions.question: Increased total peripheral resistance will:
options: shift cardiac output curve to left
shift venous return curve to left
questions.explanation: E — VR curve shifts left. Increased TPR increases resistance to venous return (and can reduce CO); it does not raise VR/CO or lower systolic pressure.
questions.sourceQuestion: Increased total peripheral resistance will:

questions.question: Shift cardiac output curve to the left (at this moment ) demonstrates the effect of :
questions.explanation: A — increased contractility. Inotropy elevates cardiac output at a given RAP; B/D lower it, C shifts venous return, E shifts filling pressure.
questions.sourceQuestion: Shift cardiac output curve to the left (at this moment ) demonstrates the effect of :

questions.question: A parallel shifting of venous return curve to right momentarily indicates :
questions.explanation: D — increased MSFP. More stressed volume shifts VR curve right/up in parallel; A/C alter slope/resistance, B alters cardiac curve.
questions.sourceQuestion: A parallel shifting of venous return curve to right momentarily indicates :

questions.question: Cardiac output is decreased when :
questions.explanation: E — decreased EDV. Less filling lowers SV and CO; A–D would generally raise CO (assuming other factors stable).
questions.sourceQuestion: Cardiac output is decreased when :

questions.question: The cardiac output and venous return graphs of a healthy person are shown in solid lines below. Which of the following is the likely cause of the change shown by the dotted lines at any given moment?
questions.explanation: D — myocardial infarction. Weakened contractility depresses cardiac curve; hydration/anaemia tend to increase volume/CO and hemorrhage shifts VR left. Key graph-dependent.
questions.sourceQuestion: The cardiac output and venous return graphs of a healthy person are shown in solid lines below. Which of the following is the likely cause of the change shown by the dotted lines at any given moment?

questions.question: A person suffers from orthostatic hypotension, when he changes his position from supine to standing, which of the following happens?
options: Central venous pressure increased; mean arterial pressure decreased; venous return increased
Central venous pressure increased; mean arterial pressure decreased; venous return decreased
Central venous pressure decreased; mean arterial pressure increased; venous return decreased
Central venous pressure decreased; mean arterial pressure increased; venous return increased
Central venous pressure decreased; mean arterial pressure decreased; venous return decreased
questions.explanation: Printed answer E, but options are missing. Standing lowers venous return and cardiac output before reflex compensation; the question stem is present, but no choice text appears on the page, so E cannot be mapped or audited.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person suffers from orthostatic hypotension, when he changes his position from supine to standing, which of the following happens?

questions.question: A person has been hit by a truck and is bleeding internally due to a hemorrhage, what physiological process is occurring?
questions.explanation: B — carotid baroreceptor firing decreases. Hemorrhage lowers arterial stretch, reducing afferent firing; A is opposite, C/D reverse reflex response.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person has been hit by a truck and is bleeding internally due to a hemorrhage, what physiological process is occurring?

questions.question: When baroreceptors are activated, which of the following takes place?
questions.sourceIssue: The corrected booklet accepts multiple answers: B/C. Self-check; excluded from single-answer grading.
questions.explanation: B and C — sympathetic inhibition and parasympathetic activation. Both occur when baroreceptors fire more; A/D are opposite. Key correctly lists two answers.
questions.sourceQuestion: When baroreceptors are activated, which of the following takes place?

questions.question: Which of the following is elicited in response to the activation of baroreceptors?
questions.printedAnswer: D (second best choice is E, A also works)
questions.explanation: D — decreased HR. Baroreflex raises vagal output and lowers sympathetic tone; vasodilation and reduced CO also occur, so A and E are both true. B/C are false. Key ambiguous; printed note correctly recognizes multiple true answers.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is elicited in response to the activation of baroreceptors?

questions.question: Which of the following would cause a decrease in venous return?
options: Increase in mean systemic filling pressure
Decrease in resistance to venous return
a change in right atrial pressure from 0 to -2 mmHg
questions.explanation: D — decreased sympathetic stimulation. Venodilation/capacitance lowers MSFP and VR; A/C increase VR, B reduces resistance and increases VR, and lower RAP increases VR.
reasons: Higher systemic filling pressure increases the gradient driving blood toward the right atrium.
Lower resistance to venous return increases flow at a given pressure gradient.
Greater blood volume tends to raise filling pressure and support venous return.
Less sympathetic venoconstriction increases venous storage and can reduce the venous-return driving pressure.
Lowering right atrial pressure from 0 to −2 mmHg can increase the driving gradient before venous-collapse limitations dominate.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following would cause a decrease in venous return?

questions.question: What happens to the HR, TPR, and carotid sinus impulses, when the carotid artery is blocked?
options: Increased HR, Decreased TPR, increase of impulses
Decreased HR, Increased TPR, decrease of impulses
Increased HR, Increased TPR, increase OF impulses
Increase HR, Increase TPR, Decrease of impulses
questions.explanation: D — HR↑, TPR↑, carotid impulses↓. Blocking sinus stretch reduces afferent firing and drives sympathetic compensation. A/B/C each reverse one or more effects.
questions.sourceQuestion: What happens to the HR, TPR, and carotid sinus impulses, when the carotid artery is blocked? (Repeated)

questions.question: A patient with a highly elevated heart rate had his carotid sinus massaged by a physician, leading to immediate relief of symptoms, how?
options: Increase the time of the AV-bundle delay
questions.explanation: C — increased AV nodal delay. Carotid massage increases baroreceptor firing, slowing AV conduction and often HR; A reverses firing, B is not the mechanism described. Key broadly OK.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient with a highly elevated heart rate had his carotid sinus massaged by a physician, leading to immediate relief of symptoms, how?

questions.question: Which of the following would move the cardiac output curve to the right without changing the amplitude?
questions.explanation: A — positive-pressure breathing/Valsalva. Positive intrathoracic pressure (Valsalva) raises measured right atrial pressure relative to transmural filling pressure, shifting the cardiac function curve right without changing its contractility amplitude; remaining choices have distinct effects. Key wording/graph-dependent; cannot validate “right without amplitude” from text.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following would move the cardiac output curve to the right without changing the amplitude?

questions.question: In the increase of sympathetic stimulation, what will happen when the unstressed blood volume increases?
options: Increase the mean systemic filling pressure
questions.explanation: C — MSFP increases. Sympathetic venoconstriction converts unstressed to stressed volume, raising MSFP. A is opposite; B is not the acute mechanism.
questions.sourceQuestion: In the increase of sympathetic stimulation, what will happen when the unstressed blood volume increases?

questions.question: Activation of the baroreceptors will cause:
options: Stimulation of the cardioaccelerator center in the brain
Increased sympathetic stimulation of the heart
Increased activity by the parasympathetic nervous system
questions.explanation: C — parasympathetic activity increases. Baroreceptor activation inhibits sympathetic and increases vagal output; A/B/D/E are opposite.
reasons: The baroreflex response to increased stretch suppresses rather than stimulates cardiac acceleration.
Sympathetic drive to the heart decreases when arterial baroreceptors are strongly activated.
Increased parasympathetic cardiac activity is a key response to increased baroreceptor firing.
The vasoconstrictor center is inhibited rather than stimulated by increased arterial baroreceptor input.
Heart rate generally falls rather than rises in this pressure-buffering response.
questions.sourceQuestion: Activation of the baroreceptors will cause:

questions.question: What is the effect of hemorrhage on both venous return and cardiac output?
questions.explanation: D — VR↓ and CO↓. Hemorrhage reduces circulating volume/MSFP, lowering return and output. A–C have one or both directions wrong.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the effect of hemorrhage on both venous return and cardiac output?

questions.question: What causes an increase in cardiac output, doesn’t change Psf, and decreases right atrial pressure?
questions.explanation: A — increased contractility. It raises CO and lowers RAP at steady state without changing MSFP. B increases MSFP; C raises afterload/TPR; D lowers CO.
questions.sourceQuestion: What causes an increase in cardiac output, doesn’t change Psf, and decreases right atrial pressure?

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of the aortic arch baroreceptors?
options: They are less sensitive than carotid baroreceptors
questions.explanation: A — less sensitive than carotid baroreceptors. Aortic baroreceptors operate over higher pressures; B/C do not describe them.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is a characteristic of the aortic arch baroreceptors?

questions.question: Which of the following decreases the mean circulatory filling pressure?
questions.explanation: B — increased venous capacitance. More capacity stores blood and lowers mean circulatory filling pressure; A/C tend to raise it.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following decreases the mean circulatory filling pressure?

questions.question: Which of the following would be expected to occur during a Cushing reaction?
questions.explanation: B — sympathetic activity increases. Cushing response to raised intracranial pressure includes sympathetic hypertension; baroreflex may then cause bradycardia, making E also true downstream. Key partly right; incomplete if asking whole reaction.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following would be expected to occur during a Cushing reaction?

questions.question: A healthy 30-year-old man stands up from supine position. Which set of cardiovascular changes is most likely? Heart rate, Sympathetic nerve activity:
questions.explanation: A — HR and sympathetic activity increase. Standing reduces venous return/BP, provoking baroreflex tachycardia and sympathetic drive. Other pairs reverse or omit response.
questions.sourceQuestion: A healthy 30-year-old man stands up from supine position. Which set of cardiovascular changes is most likely? Heart rate, Sympathetic nerve activity:

questions.question: Acute venous dilation will result in :
questions.sourceIssue: The corrected booklet accepts multiple answers: B/E. Self-check; excluded from single-answer grading.
questions.explanation: B and E — CO and BP fall. Acute venodilation raises capacitance, lowers MSFP/VR, then CO and pressure. A/C/D reverse the expected effects. Key correctly lists both consequences.
questions.sourceQuestion: Acute venous dilation will result in :

questions.question: The patient presented with a heart rate of 75, was advised to follow an exercise routine, later on the patient presented after 3 months with a heart rate of 50, what change could be observed in his pulse pressure and cardiac output?
questions.explanation: D — pulse pressure increases, CO unchanged. Training lowers resting HR while increasing SV enough to maintain CO; greater SV tends to raise PP. A/B/C/E inconsistent. Key plausible; PP is not guaranteed without SV/compliance data.
questions.sourceQuestion: The patient presented with a heart rate of 75, was advised to follow an exercise routine, later on the patient presented after 3 months with a heart rate of 50, what change could be observed in his pulse pressure and cardiac output?

questions.question: Calculate the cardiac output given the pulmonary venous pressure is 0.15mL/dl and aortic pressure is 0.10mL/dl and total oxygen consumption is 200 mL/min. (Not included in 19th batch curriculum)
questions.explanation: C — 4,000 mL/min. Fick: VO₂/(arterial−venous O₂ content)=200/(0.20−0.15)=4,000 mL/min. Wording says “pressure” and mL/dL but evidently means content; other choices miscalculate. Key OK with unit correction.
questions.sourceQuestion: 10mL/dl and total oxygen consumption is 200 mL/min. (Not included in 19th batch curriculum)

questions.question: If the mean arterial pressure decrease, what is the effect on the inhibitory input of vasomotor response, nucleus ambiguous and the afferent vagal nerves?
questions.explanation: C — all decrease. Lower MAP reduces baroreceptor firing and inhibitory vagal/vasomotor inputs; A/B/D conflict.
questions.sourceQuestion: If the mean arterial pressure decrease, what is the effect on the inhibitory input of vasomotor response, nucleus ambiguous and the afferent vagal nerves?

questions.question: A tilt test was performed. Which of the following contributes the most in maintaining systolic pressure?
questions.explanation: B — increased TPR. On standing, sympathetic vasoconstriction sustains systolic pressure despite reduced preload. A is transiently reduced, C worsens hypotension.
questions.sourceQuestion: A tilt test was performed. Which of the following contributes the most in maintaining systolic pressure?

questions.question: What initially decreases then increases in the renal graph?
questions.explanation: B — Total peripheral resistance is the printed answer. The booklet omits the referenced graph, so the fall-then-rise trajectory cannot be compared against cardiac output (A) or arterial pressure (C). Missing figure.
questions.sourceQuestion: What initially decreases then increases in the renal graph?
questions.sourceIssue: The source refers to a renal graph, but no graph accompanies this item on PDF page 77. The original printed key is preserved; the missing figure cannot be verified.

questions.question: Which of the following would shift the venous return to the right (Upward)?
options: Increase of mean systemic filling pressure
Decrease of mean systemic filling pressure
questions.explanation: A — increased MSFP. It raises the VR curve in parallel; lower MSFP/capacitance changes shift left, inotropy affects cardiac curve.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following would shift the venous return to the right (Upward)?

questions.question: After partial carotid constriction is removed, which set of changes occurs?
questions.explanation: A — impulses up, CO down, resistance down. Removing carotid constriction restores stretch/firing, raises vagal and lowers sympathetic tone; CO/TPR fall. Others misstate one or more signs.
questions.sourceQuestion: After partial carotid constriction is removed, which set of changes occurs?

questions.question: During hemorrhage, reflex activation of the sympathetic nervous system will cause vasoconstriction. Which of the following will most likely occur as a result?
options: A decrease in systemic arterial pressure and a decrease in capillary pressure
An increase in systemic arterial pressure and a decrease in capillary pressure
A decrease in systemic arterial pressure and increase in capillary pressure
An increase in systemic arterial pressure and an increase in capillary pressure
questions.explanation: B — arterial pressure rises, capillary pressure falls. Sympathetic arteriolar constriction supports systemic pressure and reduces downstream capillary hydrostatic pressure. A/C/D each get a direction wrong.
questions.sourceQuestion: During hemorrhage, reflex activation of the sympathetic nervous system will cause vasoconstriction. Which of the following will most likely occur as a result?

questions.question: An increase in mean systemic filling pressure would decrease which of the following?
questions.explanation: C — venous compliance. Higher MSFP (e.g., venoconstriction/volume) is associated with lower compliance; A/B would tend to rise. Key OK, causal wording imprecise.
questions.sourceQuestion: An increase in mean systemic filling pressure would decrease which of the following?

questions.question: In an experimental procedure, blood flow to the leg muscles of a mouse is measured at rest and again during exercise. During exercise, blood flow to the leg muscles triples compared to rest. What is the primary cause of this increase in blood flow?
options: Increased metabolite production in the legs
questions.explanation: A — local metabolites. Exercise metabolites cause active hyperemia in working muscle; parasympathetic/systemic gas changes are not primary.
questions.sourceQuestion: In an experimental procedure, blood flow to the leg muscles of a mouse is measured at rest and again during exercise. During exercise, blood flow to the leg muscles triples compared to rest. What is the primary cause of this increase in blood flow?

questions.question: Which of the following changes would increase vascular resistance?
questions.explanation: A — decreased radius. Poiseuille relation raises resistance sharply; B–E lower it.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following changes would increase vascular resistance?

questions.question: A patient with dehydration has the steady-state operating point labeled B on the cardiac-vascular function curves shown in the figure. The patient's normal operating point is at point A. Administration of a drug producing which of the following changes would help to return the patient's cardiac function to normal (i.e., from point B to point A)?
questions.explanation: B — decreased venous compliance. Venoconstriction raises MSFP and supports VR in dehydration; A/E worsen function, C raises afterload, D improves pump but does not restore volume/VR directly. Key figure-dependent but physiologically plausible.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient with dehydration has the steady-state operating point labeled B on the cardiac-vascular function curves shown in the figure. The patient's normal operating point is at point A. Administration of a drug producing which of the following changes would help to return the patient's cardiac function to normal (i.e., from point B to point A)?

questions.question: A man feels dizzy after standing up, and blood tends to pool in his lower extremities. The man has a defect in which of the following reflexes?
questions.explanation: A — baroreceptor reflex defect. Failure to compensate for venous pooling on standing causes orthostatic dizziness. Other choices are effects, not the reflex defect.
questions.sourceQuestion: A man feels dizzy after standing up, and blood tends to pool in his lower extremities. The man has a defect in which of the following reflexes?

questions.question: Which two statements are correctly paired?
options: decrease cardiac output / increase venous return.
increase cardiac output/ increase total peripheral resistance.
decrease total peripheral resistance/ increased venous return.
questions.explanation: C — decreased TPR / increased VR. Lower arteriolar resistance improves forward flow and reduces opposition to VR; A/B/D pairings reverse relationships.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which two statements are correctly paired?

questions.question: A tie is placed around a carotid artery and then pulled to partially constrict the vessel. When we remove the constriction which one of the following sets of physiological changes happens?
questions.explanation: A — impulses up, CO down, resistance down. On release, baroreceptor firing increases and sympathetic tone falls. Alternatives reverse signs. Repeats question 44. Key OK; duplicated item.
questions.sourceQuestion: A tie is placed around a carotid artery and then pulled to partially constrict the vessel. When we remove the constriction which one of the following sets of physiological changes happens?

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with a 10-year history of untreated essential hypertension has a baseline blood pressure of 160/95 mmg. Which of the following best describes the functional state of his arterial baroreceptors compared with those of a normotensive individual?
options: They have completely ceased firing due to chronic mechanical fatigue.
They exhibit increased firing at the patient's baseline pressure to lower it actively.
They have shifted their set-point lower to protect the brain from hypoperfusion.
They remain unchanged because baroreceptors do not adapt to chronic pressure variations.
They operate at a higher set-point with a decreased sensitivity to pressure changes
questions.explanation: E — higher set point, reduced sensitivity. Chronic hypertension resets arterial baroreceptors; they still fire but adapt. A–D are false.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 65-year-old man with a 10-year history of untreated essential hypertension has a baseline blood pressure of 160/95 mmg. Which of the following best describes the functional state of his arterial baroreceptors compared with those of a normotensive individual?

questions.question: A patient loses a significant amount of blood from a deep wound. Which of the following changes will happen first to the venous return curve?
options: The curve shifts to the left because there is less blood volume to push blood back to the heart.
The curve shifts to the right because the remaining blood flows faster.
The slope of the curve becomes completely flat because blood flow stops entirely.
The curve moves upward because the heart pumps harder to compensate.
The curve stays the same because blood loss only affects the heart.
questions.explanation: A — VR curve shifts left. Acute blood loss lowers stressed volume/MSFP; other directions do not follow.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient loses a significant amount of blood from a deep wound. Which of the following changes will happen first to the venous return curve?

questions.question: A patient is given a medication that makes their heart muscle pump much stronger (a positive inotrope). How does this change the cardiac output curve?
options: The curve shifts downward because the heart tires out faster.
The curve shifts upward because the heart pumps more blood at any given pressure.
The curve shifts to the right without changing its height.
The curve disappears because the drug blocks normal heart function.
questions.explanation: B — curve shifts upward. Positive inotropy increases CO at a given RAP; A/C/D/E are wrong.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient is given a medication that makes their heart muscle pump much stronger (a positive inotrope). How does this change the cardiac output curve?

questions.question: A 68-year-old patient is diagnosed with chronic heart failure, a condition where the heart muscle becomes weakened and cannot pump blood effectively. Which of the following changes will be observed on this patient's cardiac output curve?
options: The curve shifts upward because a weak heart must work harder.
The curve shifts to the right without changing its height.
The curve shifts downward because the weak heart pumps less blood at any given pressure.
The curve becomes a completely vertical straight line.
The curve remains completely unchanged because heart failure only affects the blood vessels.
questions.explanation: C — curve shifts downward. Heart failure lowers output at a given filling pressure; alternatives reverse or misattribute.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 68-year-old patient is diagnosed with chronic heart failure, a condition where the heart muscle becomes weakened and cannot pump blood effectively. Which of the following changes will be observed on this patient's cardiac output curve?

questions.question: Which of the following is induced by a fall in the arterial pressure?
options: Blood flow from atria to ventricles
questions.explanation: B — venous constriction. Falling pressure triggers sympathetic venoconstriction; A/D are opposite reflexes, and C is not the direct response.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is induced by a fall in the arterial pressure?

questions.question: Which of the following decreases total systemic vascular resistance?
options: Decrease cardiac output at the beginning
Decrease cardiac output and venous return
questions.explanation: E — decreased oxygen. Hypoxia locally dilates most systemic arterioles and lowers resistance; A changes MSFP, B/C describe flow, D raises flow without necessarily lowering TPR.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following decreases total systemic vascular resistance?

questions.question: The most important regulator of resistance vessels in skin (cutaneous) is which of the following?
questions.explanation: A — norepinephrine. Cutaneous vessels are chiefly under sympathetic adrenergic control; K⁺/H⁺/adenosine are local metabolic factors.
questions.sourceQuestion: The most important regulator of resistance vessels in skin (cutaneous) is which of the following?

questions.question: Which of the following is released by the endothelium under sheer stress?
questions.explanation: E — nitric oxide. Shear activates endothelial NO synthase; endothelin constricts, other substances are not the classic shear-mediated endothelial dilator.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is released by the endothelium under sheer stress?

questions.question: A person’s mean arterial pressure suddenly dropped by 20mmHg, which of the following rows correctly describes the activities of the following centers?
options: Dorsal vagal neuron increased; vasomotor inhibition decreased; nucleus ambiguus increased
Dorsal vagal neuron decreased; vasomotor inhibition increased; nucleus ambiguus decreased
Dorsal vagal neuron decreased; vasomotor inhibition decreased; nucleus ambiguus decreased
Dorsal vagal neuron increased; vasomotor inhibition increased; nucleus ambiguus increased
Dorsal vagal neuron increased; vasomotor inhibition decreased; nucleus ambiguus decreased
questions.explanation: C — Decreased in all three columns. Lower MAP reduces baroreceptor input, decreases cardioinhibitory vagal activity, and removes inhibition of the vasomotor centre. A/D increase vagal activity, B increases inhibition of the vasomotor centre, and E increases dorsal vagal activity.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person’s mean arterial pressure suddenly dropped by 20mmHg, which of the following rows correctly describes the activities of the following centers?

questions.question: During extreme exercise, which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: B — overall TPR decreases. Exercising muscle vasodilation lowers TPR; SV and HR rise, so A/C/D are false.
questions.sourceQuestion: During extreme exercise, which of the following is correct?

questions.question: During exercise, what local factor would lead to increased arteriolar resistance in your coronary arteries?
questions.explanation: B — sodium, as printed, is wrong. Na⁺ is not a standard local coronary vasoconstrictor. Of choices, protons/lactate are metabolic vasodilators; NO also dilates. No listed factor reliably increases coronary arteriolar resistance during exercise. Key wrong/no valid option.
questions.sourceQuestion: During exercise, what local factor would lead to increased arteriolar resistance in your coronary arteries?

questions.question: An aerobically fit 25-year-old woman is exercising in her local gym. From the attached table, which of the following changes in venous compliance, pulse pressure, and total peripheral resistance will most likely occur during normal hemodynamic response to exercise?
questions.explanation: E — Row 5. Exercise venoconstriction lowers venous compliance, increased stroke volume usually widens pulse pressure, and active muscle vasodilation lowers total peripheral resistance. Rows 1–3 raise venous compliance, row 4 lowers pulse pressure and raises resistance, and row 6 lowers pulse pressure.
questions.sourceQuestion: An aerobically fit 25-year-old woman is exercising in her local gym. From the attached table, which of the following changes in venous compliance, pulse pressure, and total peripheral resistance will most likely occur during normal hemodynamic response to exercise?

questions.question: During exercise, which of the following metabolites contributes the most in increasing blood flow to the coronary arteries?
questions.explanation: B — nitric oxide, though “metabolite” is inaccurate. NO contributes to exercise coronary dilation; H⁺/lactate also vasodilate, and sodium is not the strongest mechanism. The prompt's “most” is not well-posed; adenosine is omitted. Key ambiguous.
questions.sourceQuestion: During exercise, which of the following metabolites contributes the most in increasing blood flow to the coronary arteries?

questions.question: In moderate but continuous exercise, which of the following occurs?
questions.explanation: A — HR increases. Exercise raises HR; diastolic pressure/TPR/venous compliance do not increase as a defining response.
questions.sourceQuestion: In moderate but continuous exercise, which of the following occurs?

questions.question: Shear stress on endothelial cells causes the release of which of the following?
questions.explanation: A — nitric oxide. Endothelial shear releases NO; endothelin constricts and angiotensin/epinephrine are not endothelial shear products.
questions.sourceQuestion: Shear stress on endothelial cells causes the release of which of the following?

questions.question: Which of the following vessel would have highest systolic pressure?
questions.explanation: A — femoral artery. Systemic arterial systolic pressure exceeds right atrial, RV and PA systolic pressures.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following vessel would have highest systolic pressure?

questions.question: Which of the following describes the circulatory changes in response to increased cardiac output during exercise:
questions.explanation: B — pulmonary arterial pressure increases. Exercise increases pulmonary flow and pressure modestly; coronary flow increases, venous return increases, and alveolar pressure is not the key change.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following describes the circulatory changes in response to increased cardiac output during exercise:

questions.question: Local blood vessels (in tissue) dilate in response to an excess of which of the following:
questions.explanation: A — carbon dioxide. Local CO₂ accumulation dilates systemic tissue vessels; oxygen/nutrients generally reduce vasodilator drive, angiotensin constricts.
questions.sourceQuestion: Local blood vessels (in tissue) dilate in response to an excess of which of the following:

questions.question: Which of the following substances is a vasodilator of blood vessels?
questions.explanation: E — nitric oxide. NO is a potent vasodilator; oxygen/angiotensin/vasopressin constrict, “endothelium” is not a substance.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following substances is a vasodilator of blood vessels? (Repeated)

questions.question: Which of the following is a vasoconstrictor that is produced by the endothelial cells and causes severe constriction?
questions.explanation: A — endothelin. Endothelial endothelin is a potent vasoconstrictor; NO dilates and the others are not the endothelial peptide in question.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is a vasoconstrictor that is produced by the endothelial cells and causes severe constriction? (Repeated 2X)

questions.question: Which of the following will dilate blood vessels?
questions.explanation: A — CO₂. CO₂ dilates most systemic vascular beds; vasopressin/endothelin/calcium constrict, epinephrine has receptor-dependent effects.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following will dilate blood vessels?

questions.question: What is the main mechanism to control blood flow in cutaneous tissues (skin)?
questions.explanation: D — norepinephrine. Sympathetic adrenergic tone governs cutaneous flow; local adenosine/CO₂/O₂ are less important in skin.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the main mechanism to control blood flow in cutaneous tissues (skin)?

questions.question: Which of the following vasoactive chemicals increases protein leakage through capillaries?
questions.explanation: C — histamine. It increases capillary permeability and protein leakage; NO/endothelin/NE are not the classic permeability mediator.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following vasoactive chemicals increases protein leakage through capillaries?

questions.question: Which of the following best describes what happens to central venous pressure (CVP) in hypovolemic shock and right sided heart failure (cardiogenic shock)?
options: Cardiogenic shock: CVP increased; hypovolemic shock: CVP increased
Cardiogenic shock: CVP decreased; hypovolemic shock: CVP increased
Cardiogenic shock: CVP increased; hypovolemic shock: CVP decreased
Cardiogenic shock: CVP unchanged; hypovolemic shock: CVP decreased
Cardiogenic shock: CVP decreased; hypovolemic shock: CVP decreased
questions.explanation: C — cardiogenic shock raises CVP; hypovolemic shock lowers it. A/B/D/E give the wrong direction for one or both conditions. Key OK; verified against table.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following best describes what happens to central venous pressure (CVP) in hypovolemic shock and right sided heart failure (cardiogenic shock)?

questions.question: 56-year-old man with a history of left ventricular failure due to diastolic dysfunction, presents due to worsening of dyspnea and fatigue. On further examination, which of the following clinical findings would most likely be observed in this patient?
questions.explanation: D — left atrial dilation. Diastolic LV dysfunction raises filling pressure and enlarges LA; right-sided congestion findings occur later, pulmonary capillary pressure rises rather than falls, EDV may be normal/reduced.
questions.sourceQuestion: 56-year-old man with a history of left ventricular failure due to diastolic dysfunction, presents due to worsening of dyspnea and fatigue. On further examination, which of the following clinical findings would most likely be observed in this patient?

questions.question: What happens in cardiogenic shock?
options: Temperature stays the same, CVP increase
questions.explanation: A — temperature decreases, CVP increases. Low output causes cold extremities and venous congestion. Other choices have wrong direction(s).
questions.sourceQuestion: What happens in cardiogenic shock?

questions.question: A patient experiences angina when he exercises due to blockage/occlusion of the coronary artery. What most probably caused it?
options: Stiffening of the artery due to elastin and collagen
questions.explanation: A — endothelial injury. Atherosclerotic endothelial dysfunction/stenosis limits coronary flow and causes exertional ischemia; B/C are not the primary initiating cause. Key broad but plausible.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient experiences angina when he exercises due to blockage/occlusion of the coronary artery. What most probably caused it?

questions.question: Digitalis is given to a person with heart failure to increase the contractility of the heart. What is the effect of this drug?
options: Inhibit Ca^{2+}/Na^+ exchanger via inhibition of Na^+/K^+ pump
Stimulate Ca^{2+}/Na^+ exchanger via inhibition of Na^+/K^+ pump
Inhibit Ca^{2+}/Na^+ exchanger via stimulation of Na^+/K^+ pump
Stimulate Na^+/K^+ pump via inhibition of Ca^{2+}/Na^+ exchange
questions.explanation: A — inhibits Na⁺/K⁺ pump, indirectly inhibiting Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger. Intracellular Na rises, Ca extrusion falls, and intracellular Ca/contractility rise. B reverses exchanger effect; C/D reverse pump or exchanger.
questions.sourceQuestion: Digitalis is given to a person with heart failure to increase the contractility of the heart. What is the effect of this drug?

questions.question: Which of the following is the main reason for decompensated heart failure?
options: Inability of the kidneys to retain fluids
Increased activity of the sympathetic nerve
Increased activity of the parasympathetic nerve
questions.explanation: C — decreased contractility. Pump failure is the central cause of decompensation; fluid retention/sympathetic activity are compensations, not primary cause; increased EF is opposite.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is the main reason for decompensated heart failure?

questions.question: A 74-year-old man presented to the hospital with episodes of dizziness and breath shortening. He was diagnosed with decompensated heart failure. Which of the following Infusions are most beneficial?
questions.explanation: D — digitalis (digoxin). Positive inotropy can help selected decompensated systolic HF; angiotensin II/aldosterone worsen afterload/retention, whole blood is not indicated absent loss, norepinephrine is for shock/hypotension. Key context-dependent.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 74-year-old man presented to the hospital with episodes of dizziness and breath shortening. He was diagnosed with decompensated heart failure. Which of the following Infusions are most beneficial?

questions.question: Which of the following is immediately noticed after acute myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation: E — decreased CO. Acute MI impairs contractile myocardium and immediately lowers output; renal retention follows, and parasympathetic/vasodilation are not expected universal effects.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is immediately noticed after acute myocardial infarction?

questions.question: Which of the following abnormalities will be found in cardiogenic shock?
questions.sourceIssue: The corrected booklet accepts multiple answers: A/B/D. Self-check; excluded from single-answer grading.
questions.explanation: A, B and D. Cardiogenic shock raises CVP (pump backs up), lowers tissue oxygen delivery, and raises SVR reflexively; C/E are opposite. Printed multiple key appropriate.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following abnormalities will be found in cardiogenic shock?

questions.question: Which of the following is exhibited in a patient with clinical shock (acute circulatory failure), due to a severe hemorrhage?
options: A reduced mean systemic filling pressure
questions.explanation: E — reduced MSFP. Hemorrhage removes circulating volume/stressed volume; other choices conflict with compensatory sympathetic response.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is exhibited in a patient with clinical shock (acute circulatory failure), due to a severe hemorrhage?

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of compensated heart failure:
options: Increases firing rate of the baroreceptors
questions.explanation: A — high RAP. Compensated HF retains volume and raises filling pressures; low CO may persist, but B also can describe it. C/D/E are not characteristic. Key ambiguous: B can also be true.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is a characteristic of compensated heart failure:

questions.question: Which of the following results from an increase in right atrial pressure?
options: A decrease in total peripheral resistance
An increase in mean systemic filling pressure
An increase in pressure gradient for venous return
questions.explanation: E — both A and C (as keyed), but not supported by the stem. Increased RAP reduces venous return gradient; it does not itself lower TPR or raise MSFP. If asking reflex consequences of elevated RAP, baroreflex-mediated HR may fall, but no offered answer states that. Key wrong; no valid answer.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following results from an increase in right atrial pressure?

questions.question: What will help during cardiogenic shock?
questions.explanation: A — increased sympathetic stimulation. It supports pressure/contractility in cardiogenic shock; parasympathetic or beta-blockade would worsen pump output. Key OK as immediate compensation, not definitive treatment.
questions.sourceQuestion: What will help during cardiogenic shock?

questions.question: Which of the following refers to a high cardiac output failure?
options: Weakening heart and dilated peripheral blood vessels
questions.explanation: E — weak heart with dilated peripheral vessels. This describes high-output failure physiology (e.g., low SVR with inadequate effective perfusion); A/C/D are not definition; B is not a phenotype. Key imprecise: “high-output failure” requires elevated CO despite failure symptoms, not merely these descriptors.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following refers to a high cardiac output failure?

questions.question: Administration of a cardiotonic drug during decompensated heart failure aims to:
options: Increase fluid retention by the kidneys
questions.explanation: C — improve contractility. That is the goal of a cardiotonic drug; A/B/D/E worsen preload/edema or rely on nonspecific sympathetic activation.
questions.sourceQuestion: Administration of a cardiotonic drug during decompensated heart failure aims to:

questions.question: Which of the following conditions often occurs in compensated hemorrhagic shock?
options: Decrease absorption of interstitial fluid through the capillaries
questions.explanation: E — CNS ischemic response. Severe compensated hemorrhage can trigger this powerful response when cerebral perfusion falls; A/C/D are wrong directions, B is not the key reflex.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following conditions often occurs in compensated hemorrhagic shock?

questions.question: A patient with a heart rate of 96 bpm presented with the following hemodynamic measurements: ● Right atrial pressure: 8 mmHg ● Right ventricular pressure: 32/5 mmHg ● End-diastolic volume: 70 mL ● End-systolic volume: 40 mL The following ECG was obtained from the patient. Q1) Determine whether the patient has a right axis deviation, left axis deviation, or extreme axis deviation based on the ECG findings.
questions.explanation: A — Right axis deviation. Lead I is predominantly negative, while aVF is positive. Left axis deviation would generally have positive I and negative aVF, extreme deviation both negative, and normal axis usually positive I and aVF.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient with a heart rate of 96 bpm presented with the following hemodynamic measurements: ● Right atrial pressure: 8 mmHg ● Right ventricular pressure: 32/5 mmHg ● End-diastolic volume: 70 mL ● End-systolic volume: 40 mL The following ECG was obtained from the patient. Q1) Determine whether the patient has a right axis deviation, left axis deviation, or extreme axis deviation based on the ECG findings.

questions.question: A 78 year old man came in for a regular check up. Everything was found to be normal. Which of the following decreases compared to when he was 20?
questions.explanation: C — vital capacity decreases with age. RV/FRC tend to rise and TLC changes little; A/B/D therefore do not fit.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 78 year old man came in for a regular check up. Everything was found to be normal. Which of the following decreases compared to when he was 20?

questions.question: After expiration of a normal tidal volume, a subject breathes in as much air as possible. Which of the following represents the volume of air inspired?
questions.explanation: A — inspiratory capacity. From end-tidal expiration, maximal inspiration is TV+IRV (IC); IRV alone starts at end-tidal inspiration, TLC is total volume, FRC is resting expiratory volume.
questions.sourceQuestion: After expiration of a normal tidal volume, a subject breathes in as much air as possible. Which of the following represents the volume of air inspired?

questions.question: A combination of which of the following lung volumes is defined as Inspiratory Capacity?
options: Inspiratory Reserve Volume + Tidal Volume + Expiratory reserve volume
Residual Volume + Expiratory Reserve Volume +Tidal Volume + Inspiratory Reserve Volume
questions.explanation: E — IRV+TV. IC is precisely these two volumes; A/B are larger capacities and C/D expiratory measures.
reasons: Adding ERV gives vital capacity, not inspiratory capacity.
Adding every listed volume gives total lung capacity, including residual volume.
ERV plus RV equals functional residual capacity.
ERV plus tidal volume omits IRV and includes an expiratory component.
Tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume is inspiratory capacity.
questions.sourceQuestion: A combination of which of the following lung volumes is defined as Inspiratory Capacity? (Repeated)

questions.question: A patient was asked to exhale maximally and was then connected to a spirometer containing 10% helium (helium fraction: 0.1). The volume of the spirometer was 5 L. After a rebreathing maneuver, the helium fraction approached a steady value of 0.08. What is the calculated residual volume of this patient in liters?
questions.explanation: C — 1.25 L. Helium conservation: initial He=5×0.10=0.5 L; after mixing final volume=0.5/0.08=6.25 L, so lung RV=6.25−5=1.25 L. A/B/D/E wrong. Key OK; option typo “1.25x”.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient was asked to exhale maximally and was then connected to a spirometer containing 10% helium (helium fraction: 0.1). The volume of the spirometer was 5 L. After a rebreathing maneuver, the helium fraction approached a steady value of 0.08. What is the calculated residual volume of this patient in liters? (Repeated)

questions.question: A person has the following spirometry and respiratory function data test: TV: 500 ml RV: 1500 ml TLC: 6500 ml FRC: 2500 ml What is the IRV?
questions.explanation: B — IRV=3.5 L. TLC=IRV+TV+ERV+RV, so IRV=6.5−0.5−(2.5−1.5)−1.5=3.5 L. Other values fail.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person has the following spirometry and respiratory function data test: TV: 500 ml RV: 1500 ml TLC: 6500 ml FRC: 2500 ml What is the IRV?

questions.question: What is the normal range for Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) in adults?
questions.explanation: B — about 3 L. Typical adult FRC is roughly 2–3 L (varies by body size/sex); others are less representative.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the normal range for Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) in adults?

questions.question: When is FRC achieved?
questions.explanation: D — after normal expiration. FRC is the volume at end-tidal expiration. A/B/C are different volume landmarks.
questions.sourceQuestion: When is FRC achieved?

questions.question: Which of the following decreases from age 25 to 65 ?
questions.explanation: B — vital capacity. Aging lowers VC; TLC is relatively preserved, RV rises, and ERV tends to fall too. Key flawed as single-best: D can also decrease.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following decreases from age 25 to 65 ?

questions.question: What is the average lung volume at Functional Residual Capacity by a normal adult person?
questions.explanation: A — 3 L. Typical adult FRC is near 2.5–3 L; alternatives are less representative.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the average lung volume at Functional Residual Capacity by a normal adult person?

questions.question: Which of the following is most likely the cause of low arterial PO2 (hypoxemia)?
options: Increased dead space ventilation with constant tidal volume
Increased tidal volume with constant dead space ventilation
Increase dead space ventilation with increased tidal volume
questions.explanation: A — increased dead-space ventilation at fixed TV. This reduces alveolar ventilation and can lower PAO₂/raise PaCO₂; B/D increase alveolar ventilation, C may impair mechanics, E is ambiguous. Key broadly OK.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is most likely the cause of low arterial PO2 (hypoxemia)?

questions.question: Emphysema:
options: Has more residual volume than fibrosis
Has less residual volume than fibrosis
questions.explanation: A — emphysema has greater RV than fibrosis. Air trapping raises RV in obstruction; fibrosis restricts volume.
questions.sourceIssue: The source recalls only 2 choices; preserved verbatim.
questions.sourceQuestion: Emphysema:

questions.question: Which of the following remains after maximal expiration?
questions.explanation: B — residual volume. RV remains after maximal expiration; FRC is after normal expiration and IRV/ERV are reserve volumes.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following remains after maximal expiration?

questions.question: Which of the following volumes remains in the lung after normal expiration?
questions.explanation: C — FRC. The volume at end-normal expiration is RV+ERV; other options are component volumes/capacity.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following volumes remains in the lung after normal expiration?

questions.question: What is the volume that can’t be measured by spirometer
questions.explanation: A — RV. Spirometry cannot measure RV or capacities containing RV (e.g. FRC); VC/IC are measurable. Key OK, though FRC also cannot be measured directly.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the volume that can’t be measured by spirometer

questions.question: A person has the following spirometry and respiratory function data test: Total lung capacity= 6500 ml Residual volume= 1500 ml Functional residual capacity= 2500 ml Tidal volume= 500 ml Expiratory reserve volume = 1000 ml What is the inspiratory reserve volume?
questions.explanation: E — IRV=3,500 mL. TLC−(RV+ERV+TV)=6500−(1500+1000+500)=3500. Others incorrect.

questions.question: Residual volume is included in:
questions.explanation: A — FRC includes RV. FRC=RV+ERV; TV/IRV do not include RV.
questions.sourceQuestion: Residual volume is included in:

questions.question: A patient with the following respiratory volume : Functional residual capacity = 2500ml Expiratory reserve volume = 500ml What is the residual volume ?
questions.explanation: C — RV=2,000 mL. RV=FRC−ERV=2500−500=2000. Other choices do not subtract correctly.
reasons: 1000 mL does not equal the supplied FRC minus ERV.
1500 mL is smaller than the calculated remaining volume.
2000 mL is 2500 mL minus 500 mL, applying RV = FRC − ERV.
2500 mL is FRC itself and still includes ERV.
5000 mL adds or scales volumes incorrectly rather than subtracting the ERV from FRC.
