questions.sourceQuestion: A patient with the following respiratory volume : Functional residual capacity = 2500ml Expiratory reserve volume = 500ml What is the residual volume ?

questions.question: After removing the volume of the functional residual capacity from the total lung capacity, which of the following volumes or capacities remain?
questions.explanation: B — inspiratory capacity. TLC−FRC=(IRV+TV+ERV+RV)−(ERV+RV)=IC. Other options do not remain.
questions.sourceQuestion: After removing the volume of the functional residual capacity from the total lung capacity, which of the following volumes or capacities remain?

questions.question: What lung capacity is TV + IRV?
questions.explanation: C — inspiratory capacity. IC=TV+IRV; other answers are expiratory capacities/volumes.
questions.sourceQuestion: What lung capacity is TV + IRV?

questions.question: A man had mild bronchitis which developed into lung emphysema. Which of the following best describes the man’s lung volume?
options: Residual volume increased; FRC decreased; vital capacity decreased
Residual volume increased; FRC increased; vital capacity decreased
Residual volume decreased; FRC decreased; vital capacity decreased
Residual volume increased; FRC increased; vital capacity increased
Residual volume decreased; FRC increased; vital capacity increased
questions.explanation: B — increased RV and FRC, decreased VC. This is the table’s emphysema pattern; A/C/D/E disagree on one or more volumes. Key OK; verified against table.
questions.sourceQuestion: A man had mild bronchitis which developed into lung emphysema. Which of the following best describes the man’s lung volume?

questions.question: Which of the following is a difference between fibrosis and emphysema ?
questions.explanation: A — emphysema has higher RV. Fibrosis restricts lung volumes; B reverses compliance (fibrosis is stiffer).
questions.sourceIssue: The source recalls only 2 choices; preserved verbatim.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is a difference between fibrosis and emphysema ?

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of obstructive pulmonary disease?
questions.explanation: C — smoking. Tobacco exposure is the commonest COPD cause; other exposures/genetic factors contribute but are less common.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is the most common cause of obstructive pulmonary disease?

questions.question: A patient has developed lung fibrosis in their lung. What is the measured value of RV, FRC and VC of the patient?
questions.explanation: C — decreased RV, FRC and VC. Fibrosis is restrictive and lowers all three measured volumes; A/B/D have at least one incorrect increase. Key OK; verified against table.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient has developed lung fibrosis in their lung. What is the measured value of RV, FRC and VC of the patient?

questions.question: A 57 yr old heavy smoker comes to your clinic. You diagnose emphysema. Which of the following results will be consistent with pulmonary function tests?
questions.explanation: C — RV, TLC and RV/TLC all increase. Air trapping and hyperinflation raise residual volume and total capacity; the RV fraction rises. Other table rows conflict. Key OK; verified against table.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 57 yr old heavy smoker comes to your clinic. You diagnose emphysema. Which of the following results will be consistent with pulmonary function tests?

questions.question: What happens to RV, TLC , FRC is obstructive lung disease?
options: RV decreased, TLC decreased, FRC decreased
RV increased, TLC decreased, FRC increased
RV decreased, TLC increased, FRC decreased
RV increased, TLC increased, FRC increased
RV increased, TLC unchanged, FRC decreased
questions.explanation: D — RV, TLC and FRC increase. Obstructive air trapping/hyperinflation raises all three; A–C/E give inconsistent changes.
questions.sourceQuestion: What happens to RV, TLC , FRC is obstructive lung disease?

questions.question: A 65-year-old Caucasian man presents to the clinic for his annual physical examination. Since his last visit, he has noticed progressive worsening of his breathlessness. He can only walk about twenty yards on flat ground without having to stop and get his breath back. He has a 30-year history of smoking two packs of cigarettes per day. He is noted to be using accessory muscles for respiration. Wheezing on expiration is noted upon auscultation. Based on the most likely diagnosis, which combination of changes in total lung capacity (TLC), residual volume (RV), and functional residual capacity (FRC) will be measured in this patient?
questions.explanation: B (profile 2). Emphysema raises TLC, RV and FRC; rows 1/4/5/6 disagree in at least one measurement. Key OK; verified against table.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 65-year-old Caucasian man presents to the clinic for his annual physical examination. Since his last visit, he has noticed progressive worsening of his breathlessness. He can only walk about twenty yards on flat ground without having to stop and get his breath back. He has a 30-year history of smoking two packs of cigarettes per day. He is noted to be using accessory muscles for respiration. Wheezing on expiration is noted upon auscultation. Based on the most likely diagnosis, which combination of changes in total lung capacity (TLC), residual volume (RV), and functional residual capacity (FRC) will be measured in this patient?

questions.question: In restrictive lung diseases, what happens to the TLC, RV, and MEF (maximum expiratory flow)?
questions.explanation: C — all decrease. Restriction lowers TLC and RV and reduces maximal expiratory flow in the stated framework; A/D reverse, B incorrectly raises MEF.
questions.sourceQuestion: In restrictive lung diseases, what happens to the TLC, RV, and MEF (maximum expiratory flow)?

questions.question: A 78-year-old man came in for a regular check-up. Everything was found to be normal. Which of the following decreases compared to when he was 20?
questions.explanation: C — vital capacity. With age VC declines, RV rises, TLC is relatively stable. A/B/D do not fit as well. Key OK; repeats P16 Q1.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 78-year-old man came in for a regular check-up. Everything was found to be normal. Which of the following decreases compared to when he was 20?

questions.question: When is the pleural pressure going to be at its lowest?
questions.explanation: A — after forced inspiration. Deep inspiration makes intrapleural pressure most negative; forced expiration makes it positive, normal breaths less extreme.
questions.sourceQuestion: When is the pleural pressure going to be at its lowest?

questions.question: Alveolar pressure (PA) and intrapleural pressure (Ppl) are measured by a man during a respiratory cycle while his airways are open. Which of the following combinations of PA Ppl will be obtained at the end of inspiration?
questions.explanation: C — Row 3. With an open airway and zero flow at the end of inspiration, alveolar pressure is 0 relative to atmosphere, while pleural pressure is −10 cm H₂O in the table. Rows 1/2 show ongoing inspiratory pressure gradients, and 4/5 show positive alveolar pressure.
questions.sourceQuestion: Alveolar pressure (PA) and intrapleural pressure (Ppl) are measured by a man during a respiratory cycle while his airways are open. Which of the following combinations of PA Ppl will be obtained at the end of inspiration? (Repeated)

questions.question: Due to absence of adequate surfactant, which of the following will result in the alveoli?
questions.explanation: A — alveolar collapse. Surfactant lowers surface tension and stabilizes small alveoli; without it alveoli collapse/shrink. C/D are opposite/no effect.
questions.sourceQuestion: Due to absence of adequate surfactant, which of the following will result in the alveoli?

questions.question: What is the effect of increasing surface tension?
options: It is absent at the air-liquid interface
questions.explanation: D — decreased compliance. Increased surface tension raises elastic recoil and makes expansion harder; A–C reverse, E false.
reasons: Higher surface tension opposes inflation rather than facilitating it.
Surface tension increases, not minimizes, the tendency of alveoli to collapse.
Unopposed surface tension can destabilize smaller alveoli rather than provide the stabilizing effect of surfactant.
Greater inward recoil means less volume change for a given pressure change, reducing compliance.
Surface tension is generated at the air–liquid interface rather than being absent there.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the effect of increasing surface tension?

questions.question: A patient suffering a bilateral pneumothorax is taken into the emergency where doctors need to assess the amount of air entering his pleural cavity, what two volumes can they use?
options: Resting volume of chest wall and resting volume of lung
FRC and resting volume of lung
questions.explanation: B — resting volume of chest wall and resting volume of lung. These are their opposing recoil equilibria after pneumothorax; FRC/TLC/RV combinations do not identify both. Key likely OK; terminology unclear.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient suffering a bilateral pneumothorax is taken into the emergency where doctors need to assess the amount of air entering his pleural cavity, what two volumes can they use?

questions.question: What defines lung compliance
options: Decrease in volume per difference in transmural pressure
Increase in volume per difference in transmural pressure
Decrease in volume per difference in pleural pressure
Decrease in volume per difference in peritoneal pressure
Increase in volume per difference in pleural pressure
questions.explanation: B — increase in volume per change in transmural pressure. Compliance is ΔV/ΔP; A reverses sign, C uses pleural pressure alone, D is irrelevant, E uses nonstandard pressure.
questions.sourceQuestion: What defines lung compliance

questions.question: Which formula relates C(Rs) to C(L) and C(cw)?
questions.explanation: E — reciprocal sum. Lung and chest-wall compliances are in series: 1/CRS=1/CL+1/CCW. A/B equate system to one component; C/D are wrong.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which formula relates C(Rs) to C(L) and C(cw)? (Repeated)

questions.question: What compliance does the graph show?
questions.explanation: A — Chest wall compliance. The curve crosses zero transmural pressure above FRC, consistent with the chest wall’s outward recoil at FRC. A lung-only curve relies on positive transpulmonary pressure and the combined respiratory system crosses zero at FRC. D/E name structures that do not account for the plotted RV-to-TLC relationship.
questions.sourceQuestion: What compliance does the graph show? (Repeated)

questions.question: A student expired until FRC and held their breath. What happens to their chest when they let go of their breath?
options: Recoils inward toward minimum lung volume
questions.explanation: B — recoils outward toward its resting volume. At FRC, lung recoil is inward and chest wall recoil outward; releasing chest wall constraint lets chest expand toward its equilibrium. A/C/D/E point incorrectly. Key likely OK; prompt's “chest” is ambiguous.
questions.sourceQuestion: A student expired until FRC and held their breath. What happens to their chest when they let go of their breath?

questions.question: Which of the following is right about the breathing cycle?
options: Alveolar pressure is equal to barometric pressure during inspiration.
Alveolar pressure is always higher than pleural pressure throughout the cycle
Alveolar pressure is equal to barometric pressure during expiration.
Alveolar pressure is higher than barometric pressure during inspiration.
questions.explanation: B — alveolar pressure exceeds pleural pressure. Transpulmonary pressure stays positive to keep lungs open. At airflow endpoints PA equals barometric; during inspiration PA is below and expiration above barometric, so A/C/D are not true throughout.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is right about the breathing cycle?

questions.question: The smallest compliance of the chest wall (Ccw) can be measured at which lung volume or lung capacity?
questions.explanation: D — RV. Chest-wall compliance is lowest at very low volumes near RV; it is generally greatest around its resting volume. Other volumes are not at the low-volume extreme.
questions.sourceQuestion: The smallest compliance of the chest wall (Ccw) can be measured at which lung volume or lung capacity?

questions.question: What is the effect of surface tension?
options: It is absent at the air-liquid interface
questions.explanation: D — surface tension lowers compliance. It resists alveolar expansion; A–C describe effects of surfactant/reduced tension, and E is false because an air–liquid interface has surface tension.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the effect of surface tension?

questions.question: What happens to compliance when recoil increases?
questions.explanation: B — compliance decreases. Compliance is ΔV/ΔP and inversely related to elastic recoil; A reverses, C ignores the relation.
questions.sourceQuestion: What happens to compliance when recoil increases?

questions.question: A 65-year-old Caucasian man presents to the clinic for his annual physical examination. Since his last visit, he has noticed progressive worsening of his breathlessness. He can only walk about twenty yards on flat ground without having to stop and get his breath back. He has a 30-year history of smoking two packs of cigarettes per day He is noted to be using accessory muscles for respiration. Wheezing on expiration is noted upon auscultation. How will the airway resistance of this patient be affected (as compared to normal)?
options: It is increased during both inspiration and expiration, but more during expiration
It is increased during both inspiration and expiration, but more during inspiration
It is increased equally during inspiration and expiration
It is increased only during expiration
It is increased only during inspiration
questions.explanation: A — resistance rises in both phases, more during expiration. Obstructed airways narrow further with positive pleural pressure during expiration; inspiration's negative pleural pressure splints them more open. B–E are incomplete/reversed.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 65-year-old Caucasian man presents to the clinic for his annual physical examination. Since his last visit, he has noticed progressive worsening of his breathlessness. He can only walk about twenty yards on flat ground without having to stop and get his breath back. He has a 30-year history of smoking two packs of cigarettes per day He is noted to be using accessory muscles for respiration. Wheezing on expiration is noted upon auscultation. How will the airway resistance of this patient be affected (as compared to normal)?

questions.question: When is the pleural pressure going to be at its highest ?
questions.explanation: D — after forced exhalation. Forced expiration makes pleural pressure positive; forced inspiration makes it most negative. A–C are lower.
questions.sourceQuestion: When is the pleural pressure going to be at its highest ? (Repeated)

questions.question: During inspiration what happens to the pressure in the alveoli?
options: It becomes equal to barometric pressure
It becomes more than barometric pressure
It becomes less than barometric pressure
questions.explanation: C — alveolar pressure falls below barometric pressure. This gradient drives inspiratory airflow; at end inspiration it returns to atmospheric, while expiration makes it positive.
questions.sourceQuestion: During inspiration what happens to the pressure in the alveoli?

questions.question: Where is the highest compliance in the lung?
questions.explanation: C — 60% of TLC is the closest listed point to maximal lung compliance. Compliance peaks at intermediate volume, then falls toward RV and TLC. D (“below RV”) is not a normal physiologic volume; A is near FRC but less precise, and B is low compliance. Printed key D is wrong.
questions.sourceQuestion: Where is the highest compliance in the lung?

questions.question: How can the compliances be related to each other?
options: 𝐶 𝑅 = 𝐶 𝑊 + 𝐶 𝐿
𝐶 𝑅 = 𝐶𝑊 ×𝐶 𝐿 𝐶𝑊−𝐶 𝐿
questions.explanation: D — 1/CRS=1/CCW+1/CL. Lung and chest wall act in series; A/B/C/E are incorrect algebraic relations.
questions.sourceQuestion: How can the compliances be related to each other?

questions.question: Compliance of lung is equal to:
options: Transmural pressure multiplied by the change in volume
Transpulmonary pressure divided by the resting residual volume
Change in volume divided by change in transmural pressure
Restoring elastic recoil force divided by total lung capacity
Change in airway resistance divided by the change in intrapleural pressure
questions.explanation: C — compliance=ΔV/Δtransmural pressure. Other options invert or use unrelated quantities.
questions.sourceQuestion: Compliance of lung is equal to:

questions.question: Which one regarding pleural pressure and pB is true in a normal beathing Cycle?
options: Intrapleural pressure becomes greater than 𝑃 midway through a normal expiration. 𝐵
Intrapleural pressure becomes equal to 𝑃 at the very end of a normal expiration. 𝐵
Intrapleural pressure is positive relative to 𝑃 throughout the entire cycle. 𝐵
Intrapleural pressure will always be less than 𝑃 in a normal respiratory cycle. 𝐵
Intrapleural pressure only drops below 𝑃 during active inspiration. 𝐵
questions.explanation: D — pleural pressure remains below atmospheric in quiet breathing. A/B/C describe pressures that normally do not occur in quiet cycle; E is false because it is negative throughout.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which one regarding pleural pressure and pB is true in a normal beathing Cycle?

questions.question: A 65-year-old Caucasian man presents to the clinic for his annual physical examination. Since his last visit, he has noticed progressive worsening of his breathlessness. He can only walk about twenty yards on flat ground without having to stop and get his breath back. He has a 30-year history of smoking two packs of cigarettes per day He is noted to be using accessory muscles for respiration. Wheezing on expiration is noted upon auscultation. If compliances of lung (CL), chest wall (CCW) and respiratory system (CRS) of this patient were measured and compared to corresponding compliances of a healthy person at the same lung volumes, which of the following combinations of changes in these parameters will most likely reflect this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: B — Row 2. The smoking history and obstructive symptoms suggest emphysema. Loss of recoil raises lung compliance, intrinsic chest wall compliance is unchanged in the intended comparison, and combined compliance rises. Rows 1/3/4/5/6 miss at least one of those changes.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 65-year-old Caucasian man presents to the clinic for his annual physical examination. Since his last visit, he has noticed progressive worsening of his breathlessness. He can only walk about twenty yards on flat ground without having to stop and get his breath back. He has a 30-year history of smoking two packs of cigarettes per day He is noted to be using accessory muscles for respiration. Wheezing on expiration is noted upon auscultation. If compliances of lung (CL), chest wall (CCW) and respiratory system (CRS) of this patient were measured and compared to corresponding compliances of a healthy person at the same lung volumes, which of the following combinations of changes in these parameters will most likely reflect this patient's condition?

questions.question: Transpulmonary pressure (Ptp) increases by +2 mmHg during a normal inspiration. In subject A, 500 ml of air is inspired. In subject B, 250 ml of air is inspired for the change in Ptp. Which of the following is true? :(
options: The compliance can not be estimated from the data provided.
The surface tension in the lung of subject B is less than that in subject A.
The compliance of the lung of subject B is less than that of subject A.
The airway resistance of subject A is greater than that of subject B.
The lung of subject A is deficient in surfactant.
questions.explanation: C — subject B has lower compliance. CL=ΔV/ΔP; 250 mL/2 is less than 500 mL/2. A is false; B/E infer unsupported surfactant status; D confuses resistance with compliance.
questions.sourceQuestion: Transpulmonary pressure (Ptp) increases by +2 mmHg during a normal inspiration. In subject A, 500 ml of air is inspired. In subject B, 250 ml of air is inspired for the change in Ptp. Which of the following is true? :(

questions.question: Which one of the following statements regarding the compliance of the respiratory Is the system true?
options: It is greater than the compliance of the chest wall.
It is greater than the compliance of the lungs.
It is equal to the compliance of the chest wall,
It is equal to the compliance of the lungs.
It is less than the compliance of the chest wall.
questions.explanation: E — CRS compliance is less than either component. Series compliances obey reciprocal addition, yielding a smaller combined compliance. A–D are false.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which one of the following statements regarding the compliance of the respiratory Is the system true? (Repeated)

questions.question: Which of the following regarding the transpulmonary pressure of the lung is true?
options: It is equal to intrapleural pressure minus the atmospheric pressure
It is independent of lung volume when the muscles are relaxed
It is equal to alveolar pressure minus the intrapleural pressure
It is equal to intrapleural pressure minus the alveolar pressure
questions.explanation: C — Ptp=PA−Ppl. A/E reverse or misreference atmospheric pressure; B is false because Ptp varies with volume; D false because it is positive in normal lung.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following regarding the transpulmonary pressure of the lung is true?

questions.question: Which of the following will tend to increase edema formation in the pulmonary interstitium?
options: A reduction in the pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
An increase in the compliance of the pulmonary capillary
A decrease in the compliance of the alveoli
An increase in the negativity of pulmonary interstitial fluid pressure
An increase in the compliance of the interstitium
questions.explanation: D — more negative interstitial pressure favors filtration. It increases outward Starling force; lower capillary pressure reduces it, while other compliance choices are not direct edema drivers.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following will tend to increase edema formation in the pulmonary interstitium?

questions.question: Which of the following helps to prevent alveolar collapse?
questions.explanation: D — alveolar interdependence. Radial traction from neighbors stabilizes alveoli; decreased surfactant worsens collapse, and B/C do not explain the mechanism.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following helps to prevent alveolar collapse?

questions.question: Which of the following explains lung compliance ?
options: Greater in both expiration and inspiration
Greater during expiration than during inspiration
Greater during inspiration than during expiration
questions.explanation: B — compliance greater on expiration (deflation limb). Hysteresis yields greater compliance during deflation than inflation at comparable volume. A/C are wrong.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following explains lung compliance ? (Repeated)

questions.question: Which of the following could be the pressure of the alveolar?
options: Can be negative, positive or zero
questions.explanation: D — PA can be negative, positive or zero relative to atmosphere. It is negative during inspiration, positive during expiration and zero at flow endpoints.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following could be the pressure of the alveolar?

questions.question: What is the highest compliance for the respiratory system?
questions.explanation: A — around FRC. Respiratory-system compliance is greatest near its resting equilibrium range; at RV/TLC extremes it falls. Key broadly OK.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the highest compliance for the respiratory system? (Repeated)

questions.question: At which volume does lung compliance reach its lowest?
questions.explanation: E — TLC. Lung compliance falls at high inflation as elastic fibers are stretched; RV is not the lowest compliance point, and below-RV is not a normal volume.
questions.sourceQuestion: At which volume does lung compliance reach its lowest? (Repeated)

questions.question: Which of the following characterizes the conditions associated with obstructive lung disease?
questions.explanation: C — decreased recoil force. Emphysema causes loss of elastic tissue, lower recoil and higher lung compliance; A/B/D/E suggest other disease mechanisms.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following characterizes the conditions associated with obstructive lung disease?

questions.question: A patient is finding difficulty in breathing. Which of the following will decrease airway resistance?
questions.explanation: A — β₂ agonist. It relaxes bronchial smooth muscle; parasympathetic activation/β blockade/low volume raise resistance.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient is finding difficulty in breathing. Which of the following will decrease airway resistance? (Repeated 3x)

questions.question: What increases airway resistance?
questions.explanation: C — low lung volume. Loss of radial traction narrows airways; high volume, sympathetic activation and epinephrine tend to lower resistance.
questions.sourceQuestion: What increases airway resistance?

questions.question: Which of the following will decrease the airway resistance?
questions.explanation: E — sympathetic activation. β₂-mediated bronchodilation reduces resistance; low volume/low CO₂/histamine tend to constrict or increase resistance.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following will decrease the airway resistance?

questions.question: Which of the following can reduce airways resistance?
options: Increasing vagal impulses to the lung
Decreasing the transpulmonary pressure across the lung tissue
questions.explanation: B — increasing lung volume. Radial traction widens airways; β blockade, forced expiration, vagal stimulation and lower transpulmonary pressure increase resistance.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following can reduce airways resistance?

questions.question: A 20 year old 180 cm tall man presented with the following lung volumes: Residual Volume: 0.8 L FEV1/FVC: 90% Which of the following statements best describe his case?
options: Normal for an athletic person his age
questions.explanation: B — restrictive pattern. Low RV with preserved/high FEV₁/FVC fits restriction; obstruction lowers ratio. Age/height alone do not make 0.8 L RV normal. Key likely OK; needs predicted values to diagnose.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 20 year old 180 cm tall man presented with the following lung volumes: Residual Volume: 0.8 L FEV1/FVC: 90% Which of the following statements best describe his case?

questions.question: A man with emphysema is exhaling with pursed lips. How does this help him in exhalation?
questions.explanation: D — raises airway transmural pressure. Pursed lips create back-pressure that splints intrathoracic airways open; A/B/C/E do not describe that benefit.
questions.sourceQuestion: A man with emphysema is exhaling with pursed lips. How does this help him in exhalation?

questions.question: Which of the following would be decreased in a patient with emphysema?
questions.explanation: C — recoil force decreases. Emphysema destroys elastic tissue and raises compliance/RV/TLC; A/B reverse, D is usually elevated rather than decreased.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following would be decreased in a patient with emphysema?

questions.question: An exhalation of a patient having emphysema takes longer than usual. What is the most likely cause of lengthening of exhalation?
options: stronger negative intrapleural pressure due to decreased lung compliance
shift in airway equal pressure point towards the mouth
reduced alveolar pressure due a decrease lung recoil force
questions.explanation: C — reduced alveolar pressure from low recoil. Weak elastic recoil lowers expiratory driving pressure and prolongs emptying; A/B/D/E are unsupported or opposite.
questions.sourceQuestion: An exhalation of a patient having emphysema takes longer than usual. What is the most likely cause of lengthening of exhalation?

questions.question: A patient has emphysema. By what mechanism does lip-pursing aid this patient with exhalation?
options: decreases the pressure inside the airways
prevents a negative transmural pressure across the airways
shifts the equal pressure point closer to the alveolar region
increases alveolar pressure at the beginning of exhalation
decreases alveolar pressure at the beginning of exhalation
questions.explanation: B — prevents negative transmural airway pressure. Pursed-lip back-pressure reduces dynamic airway compression; A/C/E are opposite, D is not the main mechanism.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient has emphysema. By what mechanism does lip-pursing aid this patient with exhalation?

questions.question: Early stages of obstructive lung disease show a decrease in which of the following ?
questions.explanation: A — FEV₁ falls early. Obstruction limits expiratory flow; other quantities are not the earliest consistent decrease.
questions.sourceQuestion: Early stages of obstructive lung disease show a decrease in which of the following ?

questions.question: How would the parameters of a patient with restrictive lung disease be changed?
options: TLC decreased; RV decreased; FEV1 normal; FVC decreased; FEV1/FVC increased
TLC decreased; RV decreased; FEV1 decreased; FVC decreased; FEV1/FVC increased
TLC increased; RV decreased; FEV1 normal; FVC decreased; FEV1/FVC increased
TLC increased; RV decreased; FEV1 decreased; FVC decreased; FEV1/FVC normal
TLC decreased; RV increased; FEV1 normal; FVC decreased; FEV1/FVC increased
questions.explanation: B — restrictive pattern. The table shows TLC, RV, FEV₁ and FVC decreased with FEV₁/FVC increased. Other rows include incompatible increases or normal FEV₁. Key OK; verified against table.
questions.sourceQuestion: How would the parameters of a patient with restrictive lung disease be changed?

questions.question: Patients with emphysema breath by pursing their lips. Which of the following represents the mechanism of this type of breathing?
options: Makes equal pressure point away from the mouth
Equal pressure point stays the same
Equal pressure point moves towards alveoli
Makes equal pressure point towards the mouth
questions.explanation: D — equal-pressure point moves toward mouth. Pursed-lip pressure shifts the equal pressure point centrally into supported larger airways; A/C reverse, B no shift.
questions.sourceQuestion: Patients with emphysema breath by pursing their lips. Which of the following represents the mechanism of this type of breathing?

questions.question: A patient suffers from acute obstructive pulmonary disease. If the patient undergoes a pulmonary function test using a spirometer, an increase in which of the following is mostly likely to be seen?
questions.explanation: D — airway resistance increases. Acute obstruction narrows airways; compliance/recoil/TLC/VC vary by cause and are not the direct universal increase.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient suffers from acute obstructive pulmonary disease. If the patient undergoes a pulmonary function test using a spirometer, an increase in which of the following is mostly likely to be seen?

questions.question: A 50 year old male has a forced expiratory vital capacity (FVC) of 3.6 L, and a forced expiratory volume during first second (FEV1) of 3.1 L. His FEV1/FVC = 0.86 (86%). Which of the following statements best describe this person?
questions.explanation: B — restrictive disease. FEV₁/FVC=0.86 is preserved, with low FVC suggesting restriction; obstruction lowers the ratio, while normal cannot be concluded without predicted FVC. Key plausible, insufficient data.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 50 year old male has a forced expiratory vital capacity (FVC) of 3.6 L, and a forced expiratory volume during first second (FEV1) of 3.1 L. His FEV1/FVC = 0.86 (86%). Which of the following statements best describe this person?

questions.question: Which of the following characterizes the conditions associated with obstructive lung disease?
questions.explanation: C — decreased recoil force. Emphysema is obstructive due to elastic recoil loss; other options describe alternate pathologies.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following characterizes the conditions associated with obstructive lung disease?

questions.question: Change in radius in which of the following would cause the biggest change in which of the following?
questions.explanation: A — proximal terminal bronchiole. Its small radius gives high resistance; a small radius change has a large relative effect via r⁴. Proximal bronchus/trachea have larger radii; alveoli lack comparable conducting airway resistance.
questions.sourceQuestion: Change in radius in which of the following would cause the biggest change in which of the following?

questions.question: A man has a tidal volume of 0.5 L and ventilation frequency of 20 breaths/min. He increased his tidal volume to 0.6 L, but kept ventilation the same. How does this affect his dead space ventilation?
questions.explanation: C — Unchanged only if “ventilation” means respiratory rate. At fixed frequency and anatomic dead space, dead-space ventilation stays fixed. If the stem instead means constant minute ventilation (10 L/min), frequency falls from 20 to 16.7/min and dead-space ventilation falls. A/B would require more dead-space ventilation, and D/E require an unstated dead-space volume to give an exact change. Ambiguous wording.
questions.sourceQuestion: A man has a tidal volume of 0.5 L and ventilation frequency of 20 breaths/min. He increased his tidal volume to 0.6 L, but kept ventilation the same. How does this affect his dead space ventilation?

questions.question: Which of the following patients is most likely experiencing hypoventilation?
questions.explanation: E — Hypoventilation. E alone has high PaCO₂ (50 mmHg), with low PaO₂. A/C/D have PaCO₂ 40. B has PaCO₂ 30, implying hyperventilation relative to metabolic CO₂ production.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following patients is most likely experiencing hypoventilation?

questions.question: A student holds his breath for an extended period of time, he keeps it until their PaCO2 doubles. What happens to their ventilation after he lets go of his breath?
questions.explanation: A — tidal volume and frequency both increase. Elevated PaCO₂ strongly stimulates ventilation after breath holding; other combinations miss the expected hyperpnea.
questions.sourceQuestion: A student holds his breath for an extended period of time, he keeps it until their PaCO2 doubles. What happens to their ventilation after he lets go of his breath?

questions.question: Which of the following has the highest alveolar ventilation?
questions.explanation: Underspecified — printed A can be right. Using a common dead space per breath Vᴅ, A gives 200−5Vᴅ and D gives 300−30Vᴅ. D is higher below 4 volume units, they tie at 4, and A is higher above 4. B shares D’s tidal volume but has a lower rate, and C starts with a much smaller minute volume. The missing dead-space value prevents a unique answer.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following has the highest alveolar ventilation?

questions.question: Alveolar ventilation was 4. PaCO2 is then halved. What is the new alveolar ventilation?
questions.explanation: A — ventilation doubles to 8. At constant CO₂ production PaCO₂ is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation. Other options do not double it.
questions.sourceQuestion: Alveolar ventilation was 4. PaCO2 is then halved. What is the new alveolar ventilation?

questions.question: If alveolar ventilation is 4200 ml/min, respiration frequency is 12 breaths per minute, and tidal volume is 500ml, which is the anatomic dead space ventilation?
questions.explanation: E — dead-space ventilation 1,800 mL/min. Minute ventilation=500×12=6,000; alveolar=4,200, difference=1,800. Other values do not reconcile.
questions.sourceQuestion: If alveolar ventilation is 4200 ml/min, respiration frequency is 12 breaths per minute, and tidal volume is 500ml, which is the anatomic dead space ventilation?

questions.question: The partial pressure of CO2 in arterial blood (PCO2) will decrease when:
options: Alveolar ventilation is decreased, CO2 production is unchanged, and dead space is increased
Alveolar ventilation is increased, and CO2 production and dead space are decreased
Alveolar ventilation and CO2 production are increased, and dead space is increased
Alveolar ventilation and CO2 production and shunted blood are increased
Both alveolar ventilation and CO2 production are decreased, and dead space is increased
questions.explanation: B — VA increases while CO₂ production/dead space decrease. Each change lowers PaCO₂; A/E decrease VA, C increases CO₂ production, D raises shunt but CO₂ terms are ambiguous.
questions.sourceQuestion: The partial pressure of CO2 in arterial blood (PCO2) will decrease when:

questions.question: A person has the following spirometry data: - Respiratory rate: 10 breaths/min - Tidal volume: 500ml - Minute respiratory volume: 5000ml - Physiologic dead space: 200 ml What is this person’s ventilation rate?
questions.explanation: D — alveolar ventilation=3,000 mL/min. (500−200)×10=3,000; A is minute ventilation less one dead-space volume only, B minute ventilation, C is wrong arithmetic, E exceeds minute ventilation.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person has the following spirometry data: - Respiratory rate: 10 breaths/min - Tidal volume: 500ml - Minute respiratory volume: 5000ml - Physiologic dead space: 200 ml What is this person’s ventilation rate?

questions.question: Which of the following would acutely result in most potent hyperventilation?
questions.explanation: B — increased arterial PCO₂. Hypercapnia is the strongest acute ventilatory stimulus; hypoxia matters greatly at low PaO₂, while high pH/low CO₂ suppress ventilation.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following would acutely result in most potent hyperventilation?

questions.question: A student goes on a hike, and the following data is obtained: - Barometric pressure: 447 - Water partial pressure: 47 - PACO2: 28 - Respiratory quotient: 1.0 Calculate his alveolar oxygen partial pressure PAO2
questions.explanation: A — PAO₂=56 mmHg. PAO₂=(447−47)×0.21−28/1=56. Other values mismatch.
questions.sourceQuestion: A student goes on a hike, and the following data is obtained: - Barometric pressure: 447 - Water partial pressure: 47 - PACO2: 28 - Respiratory quotient: 1.0 Calculate his alveolar oxygen partial pressure PAO2

questions.question: A healthy volunteer holds his breath for an extended period of time until his arterial carbon dioxide tension PaCO2 doubles. Which of the following respiratory changes will occur immediately after he stops holding his breath and begins breathing again?
options: Decreased respiratory frequency and decreased tidal volume
Decreased respiratory frequency and increased tidal volume
Increased respiratory frequency and decreased tidal volume
Increased respiratory frequency and increased tidal volume
No change in respiratory frequency or tidal volume
questions.explanation: D — frequency and tidal volume increase. Persistent hypercapnia stimulates both immediately; A/B/C/E do not match. Key OK; duplicate of Q3.
questions.sourceQuestion: A healthy volunteer holds his breath for an extended period of time until his arterial carbon dioxide tension PaCO2 doubles. Which of the following respiratory changes will occur immediately after he stops holding his breath and begins breathing again?

questions.question: In one dry gas the O2 content is 10 ml / 100 ml blood. What will be the partial pressure of oxygen if the total pressure is 1000 mmHg?
questions.explanation: C — key is not justified by the wording. O₂ content (mL/100 mL blood) does not determine PO₂ without the dissociation curve/Hb concentration; “dry gas” plus total pressure may imply 10% O₂, giving 100 mmHg, but that is a different quantity. Key ambiguous/malformed.
questions.sourceQuestion: In one dry gas the O2 content is 10 ml / 100 ml blood. What will be the partial pressure of oxygen if the total pressure is 1000 mmHg?

questions.question: The barometric pressure at mount everest is 247 mmHg. What will be the inspired PO2?
questions.explanation: C — inspired PO₂≈42 mmHg. PIO₂=(247−47)×0.21=42. A/B/D/E are inconsistent.
questions.sourceQuestion: The barometric pressure at mount everest is 247 mmHg. What will be the inspired PO2?

questions.question: What is the PIO2 of a person at an elevation with a barometric pressure of 247 mmhg ?
questions.explanation: B — PIO₂≈42 mmHg. Same calculation as Q13. A/C/D/E are wrong. Key OK; duplicate.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the PIO2 of a person at an elevation with a barometric pressure of 247 mmhg ? (Repeated)

questions.question: While climbing up to a high altitude, a climber started experiencing pulmonary hypertension. Why is that?
questions.explanation: C — alveolar hypoxia. Low alveolar PO₂ constricts pulmonary arterioles, increasing pulmonary pressure; systemic response differs.
questions.sourceQuestion: While climbing up to a high altitude, a climber started experiencing pulmonary hypertension. Why is that?

questions.question: A mountaineer ascends to a high altitude where the atmospheric pressure is 447 mmHg. A baseline arterial blood gas analysis reveals a PCO2 of 40 mmHg. Assuming a respiratory quotient (R) of 1.0 and a constant body temperature where water vapor pressure is 47 mmHg, what is this individual's alveolar oxygen tension (PAO2)?
questions.explanation: B — PAO₂=44 mmHg. PAO₂=(447−47)×0.21−40=44. A/C/D/E mismatch.
questions.sourceQuestion: A mountaineer ascends to a high altitude where the atmospheric pressure is 447 mmHg. A baseline arterial blood gas analysis reveals a PCO2 of 40 mmHg. Assuming a respiratory quotient (R) of 1.0 and a constant body temperature where water vapor pressure is 47 mmHg, what is this individual's alveolar oxygen tension (PAO2)?

questions.question: A 67 year old male with heart failure suffers from a pulmonary embolism which completely blocks the blood flow to the right lung. Which of the following would be the correct values for his PAO2. PAO2 PACO2
questions.explanation: A — PAO₂≈150, PACO₂≈0. Perfusion-blocked alveoli approach inspired humidified gas composition; other pairs imply perfused or unventilated units.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 67 year old male with heart failure suffers from a pulmonary embolism which completely blocks the blood flow to the right lung. Which of the following would be the correct values for his PAO2. PAO2 PACO2

questions.question: Which of the following patients is most likely experiencing hyperventilation?
questions.explanation: B — Hyperventilation. B alone has PaCO₂ 30 mmHg. A, C and D are at 40, while E is hypercapnic at 50. The lower PaO₂ in B can itself stimulate ventilation.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following patients is most likely experiencing hyperventilation?

questions.question: A student goes on a hike on a tall mountain. The barometric pressure was measured to be 447 mmHg, whereas the water partial pressure was 47 mmHg. PACO2 was measured as 28 mmHg with a respiratory quotient of 1.0. Calculate his alveolar oxygen partial pressure (PAO2) in mmHg.
questions.explanation: A — PAO₂=56 mmHg. (447−47)×.21−28=56. B–E are incorrect. Key OK; duplicates Q10.
questions.sourceQuestion: A student goes on a hike on a tall mountain. The barometric pressure was measured to be 447 mmHg, whereas the water partial pressure was 47 mmHg. PACO2 was measured as 28 mmHg with a respiratory quotient of 1.0. Calculate his alveolar oxygen partial pressure (PAO2) in mmHg.

questions.question: A man ventilates a tidal volume of 300 mL with a respiratory frequency (FR) of 16 breaths per minute. He forcefully increases his tidal volume, but his respiratory frequency remains the same. Which of the following changes would occur to his dead space ventilation?
questions.explanation: E — no change. Dead-space ventilation is anatomical dead space×frequency and does not depend on tidal volume; A–D wrongly alter it.
questions.sourceQuestion: A man ventilates a tidal volume of 300 mL with a respiratory frequency (FR) of 16 breaths per minute. He forcefully increases his tidal volume, but his respiratory frequency remains the same. Which of the following changes would occur to his dead space ventilation?

questions.question: Which of the following is most likely the cause of low arterial PO2 (hypoxemia)?
options: Increased dead space ventilation with constant tidal volume
Increased tidal volume with constant dead space ventilation
Increase dead space ventilation with increased tidal volume
questions.explanation: A — increased dead space at fixed total ventilation. It lowers alveolar ventilation, potentially lowering PAO₂; B/D increase VA, while C/E are insufficiently specified. Key broadly OK.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is most likely the cause of low arterial PO2 (hypoxemia)?

questions.question: At which volume will alveolar vessels have their highest resistance?
questions.explanation: A — TLC. Alveolar vessel resistance rises at high lung volume because expanded alveoli compress capillaries; B/C lower lung volumes lessen this component.
questions.sourceQuestion: At which volume will alveolar vessels have their highest resistance?

questions.question: A healthy person is participating in a lab experiment. As he takes a deep breath, lung volume increases. Which of the following changes occur to alveolar and extra alveolar vascular resistance respectively?
questions.explanation: B — alveolar resistance rises, extra-alveolar resistance falls. Inflation compresses alveolar capillaries but radial traction opens extra-alveolar vessels. Other pairs reverse one or both.
questions.sourceQuestion: A healthy person is participating in a lab experiment. As he takes a deep breath, lung volume increases. Which of the following changes occur to alveolar and extra alveolar vascular resistance respectively?

questions.question: Where is the extra alveolar resistance the lowest?
questions.explanation: A — at TLC, extra-alveolar resistance is lowest. Radial traction is greatest at high lung volume; B/C/D have less traction.
questions.sourceQuestion: Where is the extra alveolar resistance the lowest?

questions.question: At which Lung volume is the resistance of extra alveolar vessel the lowest:
questions.explanation: A — TLC. Same principle as Q24. Other volumes have less radial traction. Key OK; duplicate.
questions.sourceQuestion: At which Lung volume is the resistance of extra alveolar vessel the lowest:

questions.question: A healthy person participating in a lab experiment takes a deep breath. As long volume increases towards total lung capacity, which of the following changes occurs to alveolar and extra alveolar resistances?
questions.explanation: B — alveolar resistance rises while extra-alveolar resistance falls. This is row 2 in the table; other rows mismatch at least one response. Key OK; verified against table.
questions.sourceQuestion: A healthy person participating in a lab experiment takes a deep breath. As long volume increases towards total lung capacity, which of the following changes occurs to alveolar and extra alveolar resistances?

questions.question: At which point does alveolar capillary resistance reach its highest?
questions.explanation: C — at 100% lung volume. Alveolar vessel resistance is greatest at high lung volume from capillary compression. Lower-volume choices have less compression.
questions.sourceQuestion: At which point does alveolar capillary resistance reach its highest?

questions.question: According to this graph oxygen uptake is?
questions.explanation: B — Perfusion-limited. The capillary PO₂ reaches the dashed alveolar PO₂ well before the end of transit. A would show persistent disequilibrium, C is unsupported without comparison with a normal curve, and D conflicts with the substantial rise in blood PO₂.
questions.sourceQuestion: According to this graph oxygen uptake is? (Repeated)

questions.question: Which of the following shows the correct sequence and structures an oxygen molecule has to pass to bind with hemoglobin?
options: Surfactant → Endothelium of Alveolus → Endothelium of capillary → Membrane of RBC
Endothelium of capillary → Endothelium of Alveolus → Surfactant → Membrane of RBC
Surfactant → Membrane of RBC → Endothelium of Alveolus → Endothelium of capillary
Membrane of RBC → Endothelium of capillary → Endothelium of Alveolus → Surfactant
questions.explanation: A — intended order begins at surfactant then crosses alveolar lining and capillary barriers to RBC. B–D reverse the physiologic direction. “Alveolar endothelium” is anatomically incorrect (alveolar epithelium); the full barrier also includes interstitium/plasma. Key conceptually right, terminology incomplete.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following shows the correct sequence and structures an oxygen molecule has to pass to bind with hemoglobin?

questions.question: What causes a diffusion limitation in lung fibrosis?
questions.explanation: D — increased air–blood barrier thickness. Fibrosis thickens diffusion distance; A/B/C do not explain diffusion limitation.
questions.sourceQuestion: What causes a diffusion limitation in lung fibrosis?

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the diffusion coefficient of O₂, as compared with that of CO?
options: Less because of lower molecular weight of O₂
Less because O₂ is less soluble
Greater because O₂ combines with hemoglobin
Greater because of higher pressure gradient
questions.explanation: C — O₂ has lower solubility than CO. Diffusivity depends on solubility and molecular weight; A gives wrong reason, B/D/E do not explain the coefficient. Key likely OK.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is true about the diffusion coefficient of O₂, as compared with that of CO?

questions.question: According to Fick’s law, which of the following combinations of changes will have the best diffusion of a gas across the respiratory membrane? (A = Membrane surface area, ΔP = Partial pressure difference of the gas, Δx = Thickness of the membrane, S = Solubility of the gas)
options: A increases, ΔP increases, Δx decreases, and S increases
A increases, ΔP increases, Δx decreases, and S decreases
A decreases, ΔP decreases, Δx decreases, and S increases
A increases, ΔP decreases, Δx increases, and S increases
A increases, ΔP decreases, Δx decreases, and S decreases
questions.explanation: A — larger area and gradient, thinner membrane, greater solubility. All improve Fick diffusion; B/E lower solubility, C reduces area/gradient, D reduces gradient and thickens barrier.
questions.sourceQuestion: According to Fick’s law, which of the following combinations of changes will have the best diffusion of a gas across the respiratory membrane? (A = Membrane surface area, ΔP = Partial pressure difference of the gas, Δx = Thickness of the membrane, S = Solubility of the gas)

questions.question: A patient has severe pneumonia, which has thickened the respiratory membrane. Despite oxygen therapy, he still has rapid respiration and feels as if he is not getting enough air. Which of the following is the main cause of that?
options: Oxygen cannot cross the thickened membrane
The oxygen increases the stimulation of the carotid and aortic bodies
The oxygen stimulates the respiratory center to increase the respiratory rate
His blood pH increased and stimulated an increase in his respiratory rate
Hypocapnia causes the respiratory rate to continue to increase
questions.explanation: A — thickened membrane impairs oxygen transfer. The stated diffusion barrier is the direct limitation; oxygen does not stimulate chemoreceptors, and B–E give unrelated/incorrect drive. Key broadly OK; severe hypoxemia can still partially respond to O₂.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient has severe pneumonia, which has thickened the respiratory membrane. Despite oxygen therapy, he still has rapid respiration and feels as if he is not getting enough air. Which of the following is the main cause of that?

questions.question: An increase in carbon monoxide will result in which of the following?
options: Increased firing from the peripheral chemoreceptors
questions.explanation: A — arterial oxygen content decreases. CO occupies Hb and increases affinity at remaining sites; PaO₂ may remain near normal, so D is wrong. B/C/E are not typical.
questions.sourceQuestion: An increase in carbon monoxide will result in which of the following?

questions.question: Many patients with ventilation-perfusion inequality have low blood PO₂ but no CO₂ retention because of which of the following?
options: The O₂ and CO₂ dissociation curves have different stages
There is hyperventilation due to the elevated PCO₂
These patients have an increased blood flow
The variations in ventilation are more than perfusion in lung zones
The diffusing capacity of CO₂ is much higher than O₂
questions.explanation: A — CO₂ content responds more linearly and has greater diffusivity. This lets CO₂ elimination compensate better than O₂ uptake in V/Q mismatch; B may occur but is not the core reason, C/D/E are unsupported. Key OK, wording “different stages” is vague.
questions.sourceQuestion: Many patients with ventilation-perfusion inequality have low blood PO₂ but no CO₂ retention because of which of the following?

questions.question: Which of the following would result in the highest PaO2?
questions.explanation: D — Increased ventilation and decreased perfusion. This gives the highest regional V/Q and tends to yield the highest alveolar PO₂. A is baseline, B raises V/Q through perfusion alone, C changes both in the same direction, and E lowers V/Q. Wording: the table describes regional changes. Whole-body PaO₂ also depends on how much blood comes from each region.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following would result in the highest PaO2?

questions.question: While climbing up to a high altitude, a climber started experiencing pulmonary hypertension. Why is that?
questions.explanation: C — alveolar hypoxia. It causes pulmonary vasoconstriction and can raise pulmonary arterial pressure; A/B are not the mechanism. Key OK; duplicate P22 Q15.
questions.sourceQuestion: While climbing up to a high altitude, a climber started experiencing pulmonary hypertension. Why is that?

questions.question: An inflated balloon can be used to measure the wedge pressure. In the following image which structure has the pressure that the arrow represents?
questions.explanation: C — Pulmonary artery. The arrow points to the pulsatile segment after RV tracing and before the final wedge tracing. Unlike RV, this segment maintains an elevated diastolic pressure. The subsequent wedge trace estimates LA pressure (A). RA (B) has low pulsations before the ventricular trace, and LV (E) is outside the right-sided catheter path.
questions.sourceQuestion: An inflated balloon can be used to measure the wedge pressure. In the following image which structure has the pressure that the arrow represents?

questions.question: Which of the following is true for the upper region of the lung:
questions.explanation: B — upper lung zone 1 ordering PA>Ppa>Ppv. A/C/D give other/inconsistent pressure relations.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is true for the upper region of the lung:

questions.question: If lung volume is increased , what happens to the PVR of extra alveolar capillaries?
questions.explanation: B — extra-alveolar resistance decreases as lung volume rises. Radial traction opens those vessels; A/C are opposite/no change.
questions.sourceQuestion: If lung volume is increased , what happens to the PVR of extra alveolar capillaries?

questions.question: Alveolar hypoxia causes :
questions.explanation: C — pulmonary vasoconstriction. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction redirects blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli; systemic vessels generally dilate in hypoxia.
questions.sourceQuestion: Alveolar hypoxia causes :

questions.question: What mechanism is used to shunt blood away so O2 is not wasted?
questions.explanation: B — hypoxic vasoconstriction. It diverts perfusion away from low-O₂ units; other choices describe wrong reflexes or airway rather than vascular response.
questions.sourceQuestion: What mechanism is used to shunt blood away so O2 is not wasted?

questions.question: Which of the following explains blood flow to the apex and base of the lungs?
options: Blood flow is more towards the apex than the base with the base having zone one
Blood flow is less towards the apex than the base with the apex having zone one
questions.explanation: B — less flow to apex; zone 1 may occur there. Gravity increases perfusion toward base. A reverses gradient and zone location. Key OK with caveat: in healthy upright lungs, zone 1 often absent at rest.
questions.sourceIssue: The source recalls only 2 choices; preserved verbatim.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following explains blood flow to the apex and base of the lungs?

questions.question: Which of the following is true for the lower lung region:
questions.explanation: C — lower lung zone 3: Ppa>Ppv>PA. A/B/D give wrong relationships.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is true for the lower lung region:

questions.question: A man’s pulmonary artery pressure was measured at sea level and then again at a higher altitude. The barometers showed an increase in pulmonary artery pressure from 20 mmHg to 50 mmHg. Which of the following best explains this pulmonary hypertension?
options: Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system
Activation of rapidly activating stretch receptors
questions.explanation: A — alveolar hypoxia. Low inspired/alveolar oxygen at altitude causes pulmonary vasoconstriction; B–E are not the primary cause.
questions.sourceQuestion: A man’s pulmonary artery pressure was measured at sea level and then again at a higher altitude. The barometers showed an increase in pulmonary artery pressure from 20 mmHg to 50 mmHg. Which of the following best explains this pulmonary hypertension?

questions.question: Which of the following will cause an increase in p50 in the hemoglobin dissociation curve?
options: An increase in H+ concentration causing an decrease in pH
A decrease in Carbon dioxide concentration
questions.explanation: A — increased H⁺/lower pH raises P50. Bohr shift right reduces Hb O₂ affinity; lower temperature/CO₂/2,3-DPG shift left.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following will cause an increase in p50 in the hemoglobin dissociation curve?

questions.question: How is CO2 mostly transported in the blood?
questions.explanation: C — bicarbonate. Most CO₂ is converted to HCO₃⁻; dissolved and carbamino forms are smaller fractions.
questions.sourceQuestion: How is CO2 mostly transported in the blood? (Repeated)

questions.question: A person leaves his car running in his garage and is now suspected of CO poisoning, what is true about CO poisoning?
options: Is dark red similar to deoxy mixed venous blood
CO increase O2 affinity to haemoglobin other sites
CO prevents other O2 from binding onto free heme molecules
CO prevents other CO from binding onto free heme molecules
questions.explanation: B — CO increases O₂ affinity at remaining Hb sites. It shifts the dissociation curve left; A misstates color, C wrongly says other O₂ binding is blocked, D is false.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person leaves his car running in his garage and is now suspected of CO poisoning, what is true about CO poisoning?

questions.question: A patient was administered BPG, how does it affect affinity?
options: Increase affinity and shifts curve to the right
Decreases affinity and shifts curve to the left
Decreases affinity and shifts curve to the right
increase affinity and shifts curve to the left
questions.explanation: C — 2,3-BPG lowers affinity, shifts right. A/B reverse affinity or direction; D also reverses.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient was administered BPG, how does it affect affinity?

questions.question: A patient is brought to the emergency department with suspected carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning after being found in an enclosed garage with a running vehicle. Which of the following best describes the structural and physiological effect of CO binding on hemoglobin dynamics?
options: CO binds irreversibly to all four heme sites, physically blocking oxygen from attaching to hemoglobin.
CO alters the shape of hemoglobin, decreasing its affinity for oxygen and shifting the curve to the right.
CO binding to a heme site induces a conformational change that increases the oxygen affinity of the remaining sites, preventing oxygen unloading at the tissues.
CO degrades the globin chains, turning the blood a dark maroon color similar to deoxygenated mixed venous blood.
questions.explanation: C — CO binding increases affinity of remaining sites and impairs tissue unloading. A says irreversible all-site binding, B reverses shift, D is false.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient is brought to the emergency department with suspected carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning after being found in an enclosed garage with a running vehicle. Which of the following best describes the structural and physiological effect of CO binding on hemoglobin dynamics?

questions.question: Which of the following parameters would decrease the affinity of O2 in the blood?
options: Adding acid until the pH changes from 7.4 to 7.0
questions.explanation: D — acidification to pH 7.0 lowers affinity. Decreased CO₂/BPG/H⁺ or temperature shifts left/increases affinity.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following parameters would decrease the affinity of O2 in the blood?

questions.question: In arterial blood with PO, of 60 mmHg, which of the following situations will result in the lowest blood oxygen saturation? (2,3-biphosphoglycerate: BPG)
options: Decreased body temperature, alkalosis, and increased BPG.
Decreased BPG with normal body temperature and blood pH.
Elevated body temperature, acidosis, and increased BPG.
questions.explanation: C — fever, acidosis and increased BPG lower saturation at a given PO₂. All shift curve right; A/B/D/E include left-shifting factors.
questions.sourceQuestion: In arterial blood with PO, of 60 mmHg, which of the following situations will result in the lowest blood oxygen saturation? (2,3-biphosphoglycerate: BPG)

questions.question: The Bohr effect refers to which of the following?
options: Mechanism involved in diffusion of nitrogen into the blood.
Chemical equilibrium between carbonic acid and bicarbonate in the blood
Physical laws governing the solubility of gases in fluids.
Effect of pH on the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.
Effect of temperature on the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.
questions.explanation: D — effect of pH on Hb–O₂ curve. Other choices define unrelated gas laws/equilibria or temperature effect.
questions.sourceQuestion: The Bohr effect refers to which of the following?

questions.question: A 62-year old woman is admitted to the hospital with fever and pneumonia. How does her clinical status influence her O2 dissociation curve?
questions.explanation: E — right shift. Fever and acidosis during pneumonia reduce O₂ affinity and shift curve right; A/B/D reverse or misname shift, C no change.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 62-year old woman is admitted to the hospital with fever and pneumonia. How does her clinical status influence her O2 dissociation curve?

questions.question: A 10-year-old female patient with primary pulmonary hypertension is receiving nitric oxide (NO) therapy for its vasodilatation properties. She presented with a deficiency in O2 carrying capacity with the hemoglobin iron molecule in the ferric acid state and a methemoglobin level of 10%. She most likely has a condition known as:
questions.explanation: D — methemoglobinemia. Ferric Hb cannot bind oxygen normally; other listed diagnoses do not explain ferric iron.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 10-year-old female patient with primary pulmonary hypertension is receiving nitric oxide (NO) therapy for its vasodilatation properties. She presented with a deficiency in O2 carrying capacity with the hemoglobin iron molecule in the ferric acid state and a methemoglobin level of 10%. She most likely has a condition known as:

questions.question: Which is the most common form to transport CO2 in blood?
options: In HCO3- form in red blood cells
Bound to the iron group of hemoglobin
questions.explanation: C — bicarbonate. Most CO₂ travels as HCO₃⁻; dissolved, Hb-bound and heme-bound are lesser/incorrect forms.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which is the most common form to transport CO2 in blood?

questions.question: The binding of CO2 to hemoglobin in the tissues enhance the release of O2 to the tissues, this is explained by?
questions.explanation: A — Bohr effect. CO₂/H⁺ lowers Hb affinity for O₂ in tissue; Haldane effect is oxygenation's effect on CO₂ carriage.
questions.sourceIssue: The source recalls only 2 choices; preserved verbatim.
questions.sourceQuestion: The binding of CO2 to hemoglobin in the tissues enhance the release of O2 to the tissues, this is explained by?

questions.question: Which of the following happens when there is an increase in blood CO2 ?
options: Left shift of haemoglobin dissociation curve
An increase of P50 of the O2
questions.explanation: B — P50 increases. Higher CO₂/H⁺ shifts the O₂ curve right; A is opposite.
questions.sourceIssue: The source recalls only 2 choices; preserved verbatim.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following happens when there is an increase in blood CO2 ?

questions.question: If the patient has low arterial PO2, high arterial PCO2 and alveolar arterial difference is normal, what is the problem?
questions.explanation: A — hypoventilation. High PaCO₂ plus normal A–a gradient indicates reduced ventilation; low inspired O₂ also tends to preserve A–a but typically does not raise CO₂, while V/Q mismatch/shunt widen it.
questions.sourceQuestion: If the patient has low arterial PO2, high arterial PCO2 and alveolar arterial difference is normal, what is the problem?

questions.question: A patient presented with symptoms of hypoxia. He was placed on 100% O2 but PaO2 did not increase. What is the most probable cause of the hypoxia?
questions.explanation: A — right-to-left shunt. Shunted blood bypasses ventilated alveoli and responds poorly to 100% O₂; other causes usually improve more.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient presented with symptoms of hypoxia. He was placed on 100% O2 but PaO2 did not increase. What is the most probable cause of the hypoxia?

questions.question: Severe ventilation-perfusion inequalities lead to hypoxemia because of which of the following?
options: Increases in ventilation cannot normalize PCO.
A decrease in ventilation-perfusion matching in a lung region causes pulmonary arteriolar vasodilation in that region.
Shunted blood reduces the overall arterial O2 content due to mixing of blood from areas with low ventilation-perfusion matching.
The relationship between PCO2 and the content of CO2 in blood is sigmoidal.
Pulmonary blood vessels are not sensitive to changes in PO.
questions.explanation: C — mixing with low-V/Q/shunted blood lowers arterial O₂ content. A is not a complete mechanism; B/E are false, D irrelevant.
questions.sourceQuestion: Severe ventilation-perfusion inequalities lead to hypoxemia because of which of the following?

questions.question: A patient was admitted to the hospital because of hypoxemia. His partial pressure of O2 in arterial blood (PaO2) is 50 mmHg with an oxygen saturation of 82%. While breathing 100% oxygen through a mask, his PaO2 is 83 mmHg with an oxygen saturation of 92%. The cause of this man’s hypoxemia is most likely:
questions.explanation: A — intrapulmonary shunt, though not proven by these data. PaO₂ rises only modestly on 100% O₂, supporting shunt; other listed causes usually respond substantially. But PaO₂ rises 50→83, so the response is partial rather than absent; low-V/Q disease can also fit. Key likely, not definitive.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient was admitted to the hospital because of hypoxemia. His partial pressure of O2 in arterial blood (PaO2) is 50 mmHg with an oxygen saturation of 82%. While breathing 100% oxygen through a mask, his PaO2 is 83 mmHg with an oxygen saturation of 92%. The cause of this man’s hypoxemia is most likely:

questions.question: A man’s pulmonary artery pressure was measured at sea level and then again at a higher altitude. The barometers showed an increase in pulmonary artery pressure from 20 mmHg to 50 mmHg. Which of the following best explains this pulmonary hypertension?
options: Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system
Activation of rapidly activating stretch receptors
questions.explanation: A — alveolar hypoxia. Same altitude pulmonary vasoconstriction mechanism as prior items; B–E are secondary/incorrect. Key OK; duplicate.
questions.sourceQuestion: A man’s pulmonary artery pressure was measured at sea level and then again at a higher altitude. The barometers showed an increase in pulmonary artery pressure from 20 mmHg to 50 mmHg. Which of the following best explains this pulmonary hypertension?

questions.question: Which of the following is most likely the cause of low arterial PO2 (hypoxemia)?
options: Increased dead space ventilation with constant tidal volume
Increased tidal volume with constant dead space ventilation
Increase dead space ventilation with increased tidal volume
questions.explanation: A — increased dead space at fixed tidal volume can lower effective ventilation. B/D increase alveolar ventilation; C/E are not sufficient as phrased.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is most likely the cause of low arterial PO2 (hypoxemia)?

questions.question: A person has low arterial PO2 and high arterial PCO2. He was treated with 100% oxygen which fixed his rapid breathing. When the patient was put on an artificial ventilator, his mechanical breathing stops. What is the most likely reason for this?
options: Increase in right to left shunt
questions.explanation: D — hypoventilation. High CO₂ indicates inadequate ventilation; oxygen can relieve hypoxic drive but not correct the ventilatory cause. A–C/E do not explain hypercapnia and ventilator dependence.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person has low arterial PO2 and high arterial PCO2. He was treated with 100% oxygen which fixed his rapid breathing. When the patient was put on an artificial ventilator, his mechanical breathing stops. What is the most likely reason for this?

questions.question: Which of the following is the main contributor to getting rid of CO2?
questions.explanation: B — hypercapnia. Raised arterial CO₂ is the main stimulus driving its own elimination by increasing ventilation; hypoxia is a separate ventilatory stimulus, low H⁺ suppresses drive, and forced breathing is a response rather than the trigger.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is the main contributor to getting rid of CO2?

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of ventilation and perfusion will give the highest PO2
questions.explanation: D — Increased ventilation with decreased perfusion. That combination raises regional V/Q most clearly. A is baseline, B raises V/Q via perfusion alone, C changes both in the same direction, and E lowers V/Q.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following pairs of ventilation and perfusion will give the highest PO2

questions.question: Which of the following patients is hyperventilating?
questions.explanation: B — PaCO₂ 30 mmHg. Hyperventilation relative to CO₂ production lowers PaCO₂. A/C/D have PaCO₂ 40, and E has PaCO₂ 50, suggesting inadequate ventilation relative to metabolic demand.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following patients is hyperventilating?

questions.question: Which of the following is correct about ventilation perfusion mismatch?
options: The alveolar arterial difference of PO2 increases.
The alveolar arterial difference of PO2 decreases.
questions.explanation: A — A–a PO₂ difference increases. V/Q mismatch creates units with different alveolar gases and widens the gradient; B is opposite.
questions.sourceIssue: The source recalls only 2 choices; preserved verbatim.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is correct about ventilation perfusion mismatch?

questions.question: Which of the following would acutely result in most potent hyperventilation?
questions.explanation: B — increased arterial PCO₂. Hypercapnia is the strongest acute ventilatory stimulus; other choices suppress ventilation or are less potent. Key OK; repeats P22 Q9.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following would acutely result in most potent hyperventilation?

questions.question: Which of the following is responsible for terminating inhalation and initiating exhalation?
questions.explanation: B — slowly adapting stretch receptors. Their vagal inflation feedback contributes to Hering–Breuer inspiratory termination; A/J/central chemoreceptors serve other roles.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is responsible for terminating inhalation and initiating exhalation?

questions.question: A man presents with hypoxia and hypocapnia. Which of the following receptors will mainly work?
questions.explanation: D — peripheral chemoreceptors in carotid bodies. They sense hypoxemia and arterial pH/CO₂; central receptors respond mainly to CSF H⁺/CO₂, and are not at carotid bodies.
questions.sourceQuestion: A man presents with hypoxia and hypocapnia. Which of the following receptors will mainly work?

questions.question: Peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated to the greatest extent by?
questions.explanation: B — hypercapnic, hypoxic. Both stimuli maximally activate peripheral chemoreceptors; other combinations omit one or oppose stimulation.
questions.sourceQuestion: Peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated to the greatest extent by?

questions.question: A person starts an episode of rapid shallow breaths, which receptor is responsible for this?
questions.explanation: A — J/C-fiber receptors. Pulmonary edema stimulates juxtacapillary receptors, producing rapid shallow breathing; irritant/slow stretch/chemoreceptors have different triggers. Key plausible; “rapid shallow” more classically J-receptor response.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person starts an episode of rapid shallow breaths, which receptor is responsible for this?

questions.question: Which receptor is activated due to pulmonary edema?
questions.explanation: C — J receptors. Interstitial edema stimulates juxtacapillary receptors; A/B/D do not identify that edema sensor.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which receptor is activated due to pulmonary edema?

questions.question: Which receptor or fibers is activated due to low PO2 and shallow breathing?
questions.explanation: D — C fibers. J/C-fiber stimulation can cause rapid shallow breathing; low PO₂ itself is sensed chiefly by peripheral chemoreceptors (not offered), so the stem combines distinct clues. Key ambiguous.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which receptor or fibers is activated due to low PO2 and shallow breathing?

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the ventral respiratory group?
options: Stimulates the intercostal and abdominal muscles
Is part of the pontine respiratory group
questions.explanation: D — intercostal and abdominal muscles. VRG includes inspiratory/expiratory motor neurons for accessory muscles; it is medullary, not only expiratory/diaphragmatic or pontine.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is true about the ventral respiratory group?

questions.question: Direct stimulation of neurons within the dorsal respiratory group would cause an increase in the frequency of action potential in which of the following nerves?
questions.explanation: B — phrenic nerve. DRG inspiratory drive activates diaphragm through phrenic output; glossopharyngeal/vagus are afferent, and intercostals are more VRG/accessory.
questions.sourceQuestion: Direct stimulation of neurons within the dorsal respiratory group would cause an increase in the frequency of action potential in which of the following nerves?

questions.question: The impulse rate of the peripheral chemoreceptors:
options: Is particularly sensitive to changes in arterial PO2 in the range of 30-60 mmHg
Is constant between arterial PO2 s of 50-100 mmHg
Increases linearly between arterial PO2 s of 50-200 mmHg
Is affected mainly by changes in pH
Is most sensitive when arterial PO2 is above 100 mmHg
questions.explanation: A — greatest sensitivity at PaO₂ 30–60 mmHg. Peripheral chemoreceptor firing rises steeply below ~60; B–E describe incorrect ranges.
questions.sourceQuestion: The impulse rate of the peripheral chemoreceptors:

questions.question: Which of the following conditions would produce the greatest stimulation of the chemosensitive areas in the medulla?
questions.explanation: B is the intended choice, but the wording is scientifically imprecise. Central chemoreceptors respond to local CSF H⁺, generated mainly when arterial CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier; arterial H⁺ itself crosses poorly. B is the only acidifying option, but increased PaCO₂ would be the cleaner stimulus. A/C/D/E reduce central drive or are not the proximate stimulus. Key intended, stem imprecise.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following conditions would produce the greatest stimulation of the chemosensitive areas in the medulla?

questions.question: Which of the following occurs after 2-3 days of acclimatization to lower atmospheric PO2 levels?
options: Alveolar ventilation remains the same as before acclimatization
Sensitivity of the respiratory center to changes in PCO2 increases
Alveolar ventilation often increases to 400% of normal
questions.explanation: C — ventilation may rise several-fold after acclimatization. Renal bicarbonate loss permits sustained hypoxic hyperventilation; A/D are wrong, B is not the main change, E is incomplete. Key plausible; “400%” is an imprecise blanket value.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following occurs after 2-3 days of acclimatization to lower atmospheric PO2 levels?

questions.question: The pneumotaxic center:
options: Directly inhibits the ventral respiratory nucleus
When stimulated it increases duration of inspiration
When stimulated it increases the rate of respiration
Is the sensory termination of the glossopharyngeal nerve
questions.explanation: D — stimulation increases respiratory rate. The pontine pneumotaxic center limits inspiration and can raise rate; A/B/C/E are false.
questions.sourceQuestion: The pneumotaxic center:

questions.question: Peripheral Chemoreceptors:
options: Respond more to changes in blood H+ than to blood O2
Respond more to changes in blood CO2 than blood O2
Are exposed always to venous blood
Their afferent nerve fibers pass through the hypoglossal nerve to the respiratory center
