questions.explanation: D (sternal angle) — It marks carina around T4/5 plane; xiphoid, jugular notch, T6, and 8th cartilage are not the surface landmark.
questions.sourceQuestion: During physical examination, the medical resident identifies the point where the trachea bifurcates into the right and left main bronchi. This anatomical landmark is known as:

questions.question: A 34 year old man presented to the ER with a stab in the right 3rd intercostal space. Which part of the lung did the knife most probably pierce?
options: Superior lobe of the right lung
questions.explanation: A (right superior lobe) — At right 3rd ICS the lung is upper lobe; middle lobe is mainly anterior lower chest, left upper lobe is contralateral.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 34 year old man presented to the ER with a stab in the right 3rd intercostal space. Which part of the lung did the knife most probably pierce?

questions.question: A 72-year-old patient vomited and then aspirated some of the vomitus while under anesthesia. On bronchoscopic examination, partially digested food is observed blocking the origin of the right superior lobar bronchus. Which of the following groups of bronchopulmonary segments will be affected by this obstruction?
questions.explanation: B (apical, anterior, posterior) — These are right upper-lobe segments supplied distal to its lobar bronchus; others mix segments from middle/lower lobes. Key issue: answer choices contain duplicate “medial/lateral” errors but B is clear.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 72-year-old patient vomited and then aspirated some of the vomitus while under anesthesia. On bronchoscopic examination, partially digested food is observed blocking the origin of the right superior lobar bronchus. Which of the following groups of bronchopulmonary segments will be affected by this obstruction?

questions.question: A child eats a chocolate bar with nuts and it accidentally enters the conducting system. Where is it probably stuck?
questions.explanation: A (right main bronchus) — Aspirated material most often enters right main bronchus; left branches/carina are less common.
questions.sourceQuestion: A child eats a chocolate bar with nuts and it accidentally enters the conducting system. Where is it probably stuck?

questions.question: A 45-year old woman is admitted to the hospital with severe dyspnea. Radiographic examination confirms the presence of a Pancoast tumor. Physical examination reveals that the patient has miosis of the pupil, partial ptosis of the eyelid, and anhidrosis of the face. Which of the following structure has most likely been injured?
questions.explanation: A (sympathetic chain) — Pancoast tumor can compress sympathetic pathway and produce Horner syndrome; vagus/phrenic/aortic arch do not explain triad.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 45-year old woman is admitted to the hospital with severe dyspnea. Radiographic examination confirms the presence of a Pancoast tumor. Physical examination reveals that the patient has miosis of the pupil, partial ptosis of the eyelid, and anhidrosis of the face. Which of the following structure has most likely been injured?

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy had been playing with his little race cars. Soon after he put a wheel from one of the cars in his mouth, he began choking and coughing. Where in the tracheobronchial tree is the most common site for a foreign object to lodge?
questions.explanation: A (right primary bronchus) — Right bronchus is wider, shorter, more vertical; left primary/tertiary, carina and trachea are less common lodgment sites.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 5-year-old boy had been playing with his little race cars. Soon after he put a wheel from one of the cars in his mouth, he began choking and coughing. Where in the tracheobronchial tree is the most common site for a foreign object to lodge?

questions.question: A 60 year old with with a tumor in apex of lung had constricted eye and no sweating due to compression of:
questions.explanation: A (sympathetic nerve) — Apical lung tumor can disrupt sympathetic pathway causing miosis/anhidrosis; subclavian artery compression is not the mechanism.
questions.sourceIssue: The source recalls only 2 choices; preserved verbatim.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 60 year old with with a tumor in apex of lung had constricted eye and no sweating due to compression of:

questions.question: A 4 year old girl was brought to the emergency department with coughing. She aspirated a bead while playing with a necklace. Where would the bead be most likely found?
options: Apicoposterior segmental bronchus of left lung
Terminal bronchiole of the right lung
questions.explanation: D (right main bronchus) — Right main bronchus is the common aspiration site; left main/segments are less likely. Key issue: stem says bead and choices include terminal bronchiole; D is supported.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 4 year old girl was brought to the emergency department with coughing. She aspirated a bead while playing with a necklace. Where would the bead be most likely found?

questions.question: A young child was eating chocolate with nuts. A large nut fell into his respiratory tract. In which major structure is it most likely to get lodged in?
questions.explanation: C (right primary bronchus) — Same right-sided aspiration preference; left primary, carina, larynx/pharynx are less likely.
questions.sourceQuestion: A young child was eating chocolate with nuts. A large nut fell into his respiratory tract. In which major structure is it most likely to get lodged in? (Repeated)

questions.question: A 36-year old man is brought to the emergency room after suffering a deep stabbing wound directly through the 5th right intercostal space in the midclavicular line. Which part of the lung is most likely damaged?
questions.explanation: A (middle lobe) — Right 5th ICS MCL overlies middle lobe anteriorly; upper lobe is above, inferior lobe more posterolateral, lingula is left-sided.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 36-year old man is brought to the emergency room after suffering a deep stabbing wound directly through the 5th right intercostal space in the midclavicular line. Which part of the lung is most likely damaged?

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital with difficulty breathing. Radiologic examination reveals a tumor invading the lung surface anterior to the hilum. Which nerve is most likely compressed by the tumor?
questions.explanation: D (phrenic nerve) — Anterior to lung root; intercostal, splanchnic, recurrent laryngeal and vagus do not occupy that relation.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 58-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital with difficulty breathing. Radiologic examination reveals a tumor invading the lung surface anterior to the hilum. Which nerve is most likely compressed by the tumor?

questions.question: A 36-year-old man is brought to the emergency room after suffering a deep stabbing wound directly through the right 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line. Which of the following structures is most likely pierced?
questions.explanation: B (middle lobe) — Right 5th ICS MCL is over middle lobe; lower lobe more inferior/posterior, lingula left, apex/superior lobe upper.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 36-year-old man is brought to the emergency room after suffering a deep stabbing wound directly through the right 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line. Which of the following structures is most likely pierced?

questions.question: A patient is getting a thoracentesis. If the procedure is done at the midaxillary line, between which ribs should the chest tube go through in the procedure?
questions.explanation: B (8th–10th ribs) — Pleural fluid is commonly accessed around 8th/9th ICS midaxillary with needle above rib; 2–4, 4–6 too high, 11–12 risk diaphragm/abdominal organs. Key issue: range wording imprecise; safe site depends on imaging and current procedural guidance.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient is getting a thoracentesis. If the procedure is done at the midaxillary line, between which ribs should the chest tube go through in the procedure?

questions.question: A person complained of sharp localized pain in his chest. He was diagnosed with a pleural effusion. Which of the following nerves will carry the pain signal?
questions.explanation: C (intercostal nerves) — Costal pleura is somatically innervated by intercostal nerves and gives localized pain; phrenic supplies mediastinal/central diaphragmatic pleura, vagus/splanchnic do not.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person complained of sharp localized pain in his chest. He was diagnosed with a pleural effusion. Which of the following nerves will carry the pain signal?

questions.question: A 72 year old woman with a history of metastatic breast cancer presents with a difficulty breathing. An X-ray reveals a massive pleural effusion. The physician chooses to drain the fluid. Which of the following is the correct insertion point of the needle?
questions.explanation: A (MAL 9th ICS) — This is a traditional dependent-fluid landmark, inserting above rib; 6th ICS is high, parasternal/MCL options are inappropriate. Key issue: modern thoracentesis is image-guided; landmark-only answer is potentially unsafe and should not be treated as procedural instruction.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 72 year old woman with a history of metastatic breast cancer presents with a difficulty breathing. An X-ray reveals a massive pleural effusion. The physician chooses to drain the fluid. Which of the following is the correct insertion point of the needle?

questions.question: A patient is getting a thoracentesis, where should the chest tube go through in the procedure?
questions.explanation: A (superior border of lower rib) — Main intercostal neurovascular bundle runs under upper rib, so enter just superior to the lower rib; inferior border/midspace/diaphragm risk injury.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient is getting a thoracentesis, where should the chest tube go through in the procedure?

questions.question: When inserting a chest tube, the main (not collateral) intercostal vessels and nerves are avoided by placing the tube immediately:
options: above the margin of a rib
below the margin of a rib
questions.explanation: A (above rib margin) — Same VAN protection principle; below margin risks the main bundle.
questions.sourceIssue: The source recalls only 2 choices; preserved verbatim.
questions.sourceQuestion: When inserting a chest tube, the main (not collateral) intercostal vessels and nerves are avoided by placing the tube immediately:

questions.question: A 25-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department with a bullet wound in the neck just above the middle of the right clavicle and first rib. Radiographic examination reveals collapse of the right lung and a tension pneumothorax. Injury to which of the following respiratory structures resulted in the pneumothorax?
questions.explanation: B (cervical pleura/cupula) — It projects above first rib into root of neck, vulnerable to supraclavicular wound; costal/mediastinal pleura and bronchi are not as exposed there.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 25-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department with a bullet wound in the neck just above the middle of the right clavicle and first rib. Radiographic examination reveals collapse of the right lung and a tension pneumothorax. Injury to which of the following respiratory structures resulted in the pneumothorax?

questions.question: A man got stabbed near the first rib and clavicle and had a collapsed lung. What was damaged?
questions.explanation: B (cervical pleura) — Same cupula injury; other choices are lower/deeper airway/pleural structures.
questions.sourceQuestion: A man got stabbed near the first rib and clavicle and had a collapsed lung. What was damaged?

questions.question: A 17-year-old semi-conscious student was brought to ER with a stab injury in the chest during a fight. On physical examination his neck veins were grossly engorged. A radiograph of the chest showed collapsed right lung and a tracheal deviation to the left side. Which of the following is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation: B (tension pneumothorax) — Collapsed lung, contralateral tracheal shift and JVD indicate pressure compressing mediastinum; simple pneumothorax, tamponade, contusion, pneumonia do not fit all signs.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 17-year-old semi-conscious student was brought to ER with a stab injury in the chest during a fight. On physical examination his neck veins were grossly engorged. A radiograph of the chest showed collapsed right lung and a tracheal deviation to the left side. Which of the following is the most likely condition?

questions.question: A 42 year old man presented to the ER and it was found that he has exudative pleural effusion. What is the most appropriate landmark for performing thoracentesis?
questions.explanation: B (MAL 8th ICS) — Typical dependent pleural-fluid access is lower lateral chest, above rib and image-guided; other sites are too high/medial or unsafe. Key issue: same procedural caveat as Q3.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 42 year old man presented to the ER and it was found that he has exudative pleural effusion. What is the most appropriate landmark for performing thoracentesis?

questions.question: A 49-year old man was brought to the ER with a stab wound of the thoracic wall in the right fourth costal cartilage. Which of the following pulmonary structures is present at this site?
options: The horizontal fissure of the right lung
The oblique fissure of the left lung
The horizontal fissure of the left lung
The root of the left lung
The apex of the right lung
questions.explanation: A (horizontal fissure of right lung) — It meets anterior chest wall around 4th costal cartilage; left lung has no horizontal fissure, other locations do not fit.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 49-year old man was brought to the ER with a stab wound of the thoracic wall in the right fourth costal cartilage. Which of the following pulmonary structures is present at this site?

questions.question: A 34- year old man with a complaint of sharp, localized pain over the thoracic wall is diagnosed with pleural effusion. What is the most appropriate landmark for performing thoracentesis?
questions.explanation: B (MAL 8th ICS) — Same traditional thoracentesis landmark; other listed sites are not appropriate dependent lateral pleural access. Key issue: image guidance is standard; “best landmark” is underspecified.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 34- year old man with a complaint of sharp, localized pain over the thoracic wall is diagnosed with pleural effusion. What is the most appropriate landmark for performing thoracentesis?

questions.question: Which of the following best explains the surface projection of the horizontal lung fissure?
options: From the 4th costal cartilage extending laterally.
From the 2nd rib at the midclavicular to the 6th rib at the midaxillary.
From the 2nd thoracic vertebra anteriorly to the 6th rib.
From the 4th thoracic vertebra to the 6th rib.
From the 4th rib to the posterior pudendal nerve at the T10 segment
questions.explanation: A (from 4th costal cartilage laterally) — Right horizontal fissure begins at 4th costal cartilage and runs laterally; rib 2-to-6 describes other projection, vertebral landmarks are incorrect. Key issue: A is a simplified projection, not the full course.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following best explains the surface projection of the horizontal lung fissure?

questions.question: A 41-year-old female is admitted to the emergency department with a complaint of severe, sharp, but poorly localized pain on the chest wall. Radiographic examination gives evidence of pleural effusion. What is the location of the neuronal cell bodies responsible for the nerve fibers that carry this pain to the central nervous system (CNS)?
options: Dorsal horn of the spinal cord
Lateral horn of the spinal cord
Ventral horn of the spinal cord
questions.explanation: A (dorsal root ganglia) — Sensory neuron bodies carrying pleural somatic pain sit in DRG; sympathetic chain is autonomic relay, spinal horns are CNS neuron locations.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 41-year-old female is admitted to the emergency department with a complaint of severe, sharp, but poorly localized pain on the chest wall. Radiographic examination gives evidence of pleural effusion. What is the location of the neuronal cell bodies responsible for the nerve fibers that carry this pain to the central nervous system (CNS)?

questions.question: A person experiences an increased heart rate. The preganglionic cell bodies of the neurons responsible for this increased heart rate are located where?
questions.explanation: B (T1–T4 IML) — Cardiac sympathetic preganglionic neurons arise upper thoracic IML; T5–9 mainly greater splanchnic outflow, DRG/trunk/ventral horn are wrong.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person experiences an increased heart rate. The preganglionic cell bodies of the neurons responsible for this increased heart rate are located where?

questions.question: A 17-year-old was involved in a gang fight and a stab wound severed the thoracic splanchnic nerve at the level of the 3rd thoracic vertebra. Which of the following fibers do the thoracic splanchnic nerves contain?
questions.explanation: B — Postganglionic sympathetic at the stated T3 level. This best fits a cardiopulmonary splanchnic branch. D would apply to greater/lesser/least splanchnic nerves going to abdominal ganglia. A/C are somatic fibre classes and E is parasympathetic. Wording: “thoracic splanchnic” alone usually means the abdominal-bound group. Thoracic autonomic anatomy (https://anatomy.ttuhscep.edu/schemes/lungs_ans.html)
questions.sourceQuestion: A 17-year-old was involved in a gang fight and a stab wound severed the thoracic splanchnic nerve at the level of the 3rd thoracic vertebra. Which of the following fibers do the thoracic splanchnic nerves contain?

questions.question: A patient was told that her nerve in the thoracic cavity is damaged. Which of the following nerves is responsible for parasympathetic innervation of the thoracic organs?
questions.explanation: C (vagus) — Vagus supplies parasympathetic fibers to thoracic organs; phrenic/intercostal somatic, splanchnics sympathetic.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient was told that her nerve in the thoracic cavity is damaged. Which of the following nerves is responsible for parasympathetic innervation of the thoracic organs?

questions.question: A patient is having problems with sympathetic innervation of the heart. Where are the cell bodies of the preganglionic sympathetic part located?
questions.explanation: B (T1–T4 IML) — Same cardiac sympathetic origin; other locations are sensory ganglia, relay ganglia, lower thoracic outflow, or somatic motor horn.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient is having problems with sympathetic innervation of the heart. Where are the cell bodies of the preganglionic sympathetic part located?

questions.question: A 41-year-old female is admitted to the emergency department with severe, sharp, poorly localized chest wall pain. Radiographic examination shows pleural effusion. Where are the neuronal cell bodies carrying this pain?
options: Dorsal horn of the spinal cord
Lateral horn of the spinal cord
Ventral horn of the spinal cord
questions.explanation: A (dorsal root ganglia) — Same sensory cell-body location; autonomic chain and spinal cord horns are not primary afferent somata.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 41-year-old female is admitted to the emergency department with severe, sharp, poorly localized chest wall pain. Radiographic examination shows pleural effusion. Where are the neuronal cell bodies carrying this pain?

questions.question: A 17-year-old boy had a stab wound that severed the thoracic splanchnic nerve at T3. The thoracic splanchnic nerves contain which type of fibers?
options: Axons of neurons located in the sympathetic ganglia
Axons of neurons located in the intermediolateral (IML) cell column
questions.explanation: A — Sympathetic ganglion axons at the stated T3 level. Upper thoracic cardiopulmonary branches carry postganglionic fibres. D would describe the preganglionic fibres in the abdominal-bound thoracic splanchnic nerves. B/C are somatic and E is parasympathetic. Wording is ambiguous for the same reason as Q3.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 17-year-old boy had a stab wound that severed the thoracic splanchnic nerve at T3. The thoracic splanchnic nerves contain which type of fibers?

questions.question: Which of the following provides sympathetic stimulation to the heart?
questions.explanation: D — Upper thoracic cardiac sympathetic branches. Upper thoracic cardiopulmonary splanchnic nerves carry postganglionic fibres to the cardiac plexus. A/C name abdominal-bound nerves, and B supplies cardiac parasympathetic fibres.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following provides sympathetic stimulation to the heart?

questions.question: A 5-year-old male is admitted with cough and severe dyspnea. Examination reveals expiratory wheezes from bronchospasm of bronchial smooth muscle. Blocking which nerve will relax this smooth muscle?
questions.explanation: B (vagus nerve) — Vagal parasympathetic activity causes bronchoconstriction; blocking it relaxes airway smooth muscle. Sympathetic fibers already promote bronchodilation; intercostal/phrenic/recurrent laryngeal do not supply bronchial smooth muscle.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 5-year-old male is admitted with cough and severe dyspnea. Examination reveals expiratory wheezes from bronchospasm of bronchial smooth muscle. Blocking which nerve will relax this smooth muscle?

questions.question: A person suffered from angina. Pain was felt in:
questions.explanation: A (T1–T4) — Cardiac visceral afferents refer angina pain to upper thoracic dermatomes; C3–5 is phrenic referral, T10/T12/L1 are not typical.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person suffered from angina. Pain was felt in:

questions.question: What is the location of postganglionic parasympathetic neurons to innervate thoracic viscera?
options: Ventral horn of the spinal cord
Lateral horn of the spinal cord
questions.explanation: E (terminal/intramural ganglia) — Parasympathetic postganglionic cell bodies lie near/in target organ; spinal horns and sympathetic ganglia are not parasympathetic relays.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the location of postganglionic parasympathetic neurons to innervate thoracic viscera?

questions.question: A person experiences an increased heart rate. The preganglionic cell bodies of the neurons responsible for this increased heart rate are located in which region?
questions.explanation: B (T1–T4 IML) — Same cardiac sympathetic preganglionic source; other options are sensory/relay/somatic motor sites or wrong thoracic levels.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person experiences an increased heart rate. The preganglionic cell bodies of the neurons responsible for this increased heart rate are located in which region?

questions.question: A 17-year-old boy was involved in a gang fight, and a stab wound severed the thoracic splanchnic nerve at the level of his third thoracic vertebra. The thoracic splanchnic nerves contain which of the following types of fibers?
options: Axons of neurons located in the intermediolateral (IML) cell column
Axons of neurons located in sympathetic ganglia
Axons of neurons located in the ventral horn of the spinal cord
questions.explanation: D (sympathetic ganglion neuron axons) — Preganglionic fibers have cell bodies in IML and postganglionic axons arise in sympathetic ganglia; other options are somatic/IML/ventral-horn. Printed key D is correct.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 17-year-old boy was involved in a gang fight, and a stab wound severed the thoracic splanchnic nerve at the level of his third thoracic vertebra. The thoracic splanchnic nerves contain which of the following types of fibers?

questions.question: Based on the examination at her doctor's office, the patient is told that her parasympathetic nerve in the thoracic cavity is damaged. Which of the following nerves is responsible for parasympathetic innervation of thoracic organs?
questions.explanation: B (vagus) — Vagus supplies thoracic parasympathetics; intercostal/phrenic somatic, splanchnic sympathetic.
questions.sourceQuestion: Based on the examination at her doctor's office, the patient is told that her parasympathetic nerve in the thoracic cavity is damaged. Which of the following nerves is responsible for parasympathetic innervation of thoracic organs?

questions.question: A 75-year-old man presented to the ER with nonspecific chest pain. Imaging revealed a cancer of the mesothelium of the heart. Which of the following structures became cancerous?
questions.explanation: C (epicardium) — Epicardium is visceral serous pericardium, lined by mesothelium; myocardium/endocardium/Purkinje/subendocardium are not mesothelium.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 75-year-old man presented to the ER with nonspecific chest pain. Imaging revealed a cancer of the mesothelium of the heart. Which of the following structures became cancerous?

questions.question: Which of the following structures is the primary feature used to identify the endocardium in the ventricles of the heart?
questions.explanation: E (Purkinje fibers) — Subendocardial conducting fibers identify ventricular endocardial region; coronary vessels, intercalated discs, striations, adipose do not specifically identify it.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following structures is the primary feature used to identify the endocardium in the ventricles of the heart?

questions.question: A 50-year-old female died from a myocardial disease associated with mutations in the connexin43 gap-junction gene. Her diagnosis was confirmed with a pathological biopsy. Which structure of her myocardium looked impaired under the electron microscope?
questions.explanation: E (intercalated disc) — Connexin 43 forms gap junctions in intercalated discs; tubules, SR, mitochondria, nucleus are not the intercellular junction complex.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 50-year-old female died from a myocardial disease associated with mutations in the connexin43 gap-junction gene. Her diagnosis was confirmed with a pathological biopsy. Which structure of her myocardium looked impaired under the electron microscope?

questions.question: An 80-year-old man arrived at the emergency department with visibly swollen neck veins, suggesting a significant buildup of fluid in his pericardial cavity. Which type of cells is linked to this particular condition?
questions.explanation: C (mesothelium) — Pericardial serous surfaces are mesothelium and produce lubricating fluid; endocardial/endothelial/cardiomyocyte/fibroblast cells do not line the pericardial cavity.
questions.sourceQuestion: An 80-year-old man arrived at the emergency department with visibly swollen neck veins, suggesting a significant buildup of fluid in his pericardial cavity. Which type of cells is linked to this particular condition?

questions.question: The central part of the mitral valve was deficient. What composes that part ?
questions.explanation: D (fibroelastic sheath) — Valve core is dense fibroelastic connective tissue; myocardium, loose areolar CT, and reticular fibers are not the load-bearing central layer.
questions.sourceQuestion: The central part of the mitral valve was deficient. What composes that part ?

questions.question: Which of the following represents the central core of the mitral valve?
questions.explanation: B (fibroelastic tissue) — Same valve core; endothelium covers its surfaces, myocardium is absent from normal valve core.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following represents the central core of the mitral valve?

questions.question: Deficiency of which of the following tissues can cause a defect in the mitral valve and chordae tendenae?
questions.explanation: A (fibroelastic tissue) — Valve leaflets and chordae depend on collagen/elastin-rich fibrous tissue; areolar/dense regular/irregular labels are not the principal valve core, endothelium is covering layer.
questions.sourceQuestion: Deficiency of which of the following tissues can cause a defect in the mitral valve and chordae tendenae?

questions.question: A patient comes with mitral valve inflammation, which layer is damaged?
questions.explanation: A (endothelium) — Valve surfaces are covered by endothelium; valves have no cardiac or smooth muscle layer.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient comes with mitral valve inflammation, which layer is damaged?

questions.question: A patient has Cardiac mesothelioma, which structure of the following is most likely damaged?
questions.explanation: C (epicardium) — Cardiac mesothelium lies on epicardium; endocardium and myocardium are inner lining/muscle, septum is not mesothelium.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient has Cardiac mesothelioma, which structure of the following is most likely damaged?

questions.question: What would you see if you cut the myocardium transversely?
questions.explanation: C (rich capillary network) — Myocardium is highly vascular; chordae/valve lamina/Purkinje are specialized structures, dense irregular CT is not the dominant transverse myocardial feature.
questions.sourceQuestion: What would you see if you cut the myocardium transversely?

questions.question: Which of the following intercellular junctions is the site of transmission of contractile forces between adjacent cells at the level of intercalated discs?
questions.explanation: D (fascia adherens) — Anchors actin and transmits contractile force cell-to-cell; gap junctions conduct ions, desmosomes provide spot adhesion, hemidesmosomes attach cells to basal lamina, tight junctions seal epithelia.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following intercellular junctions is the site of transmission of contractile forces between adjacent cells at the level of intercalated discs? (Repeated)

questions.question: The low resistance pathway between myocardial cells that allow for the spread of action potential?
questions.explanation: C (gap junctions) — Connexons form low-resistance ionic pathways; desmosomes and fascia adherens are mechanical junctions, hemidesmosomes attach to basal lamina.
questions.sourceQuestion: The low resistance pathway between myocardial cells that allow for the spread of action potential?

questions.question: The intercalated discs are made from?
questions.explanation: B (desmosome + gap junction + fascia adherens) — These are the main intercalated-disc junctions; alternatives omit electrical coupling or mechanical anchoring, or include epithelial tight/hemidesmosomal junctions.
questions.sourceQuestion: The intercalated discs are made from?

questions.question: While using a light microscope, which of the following is shown between the myocardial fibers, in a transverse section of the myocardium?
questions.explanation: A (network of capillaries) — Myocardial cross-sections show abundant capillaries between fibers; chordae/lamina/papillary muscle/vasa nervorum are not the interstitial network.
questions.sourceQuestion: While using a light microscope, which of the following is shown between the myocardial fibers, in a transverse section of the myocardium?

questions.question: Which of the following is responsible for the pale microscopic appearance of Purkinje fibers?
questions.explanation: B (glycogen) — Glycogen-rich Purkinje cytoplasm stains pale; smooth muscle and neuroendocrine cells do not explain the appearance.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is responsible for the pale microscopic appearance of Purkinje fibers?

questions.question: Which of the following forms the core of the heart valves?
questions.explanation: A (fibroelastic tissue) — Valve core is fibroelastic connective tissue; endothelium/mesothelium cover different surfaces, smooth/cardiac muscle are not normal valve core.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following forms the core of the heart valves?

questions.question: What is the characteristic feature to identify Purkinje fibers under microscope?
questions.explanation: B (large pale-staining cytoplasm) — Purkinje fibers are large, pale, glycogen-rich subendocardial cells; subendocardial location alone, branching, striation, or discs are not uniquely diagnostic.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the characteristic feature to identify Purkinje fibers under microscope?

questions.question: What type of tissue is located in the center of the valves?
questions.explanation: E (fibroelastic tissue) — Same valve-core composition; endothelial covering and mesothelium are surface epithelia, muscle is absent from valve core.
questions.sourceQuestion: What type of tissue is located in the center of the valves?

questions.question: A person has been diagnosed with capillary leak syndrome, which is a condition that causes fluid and proteins to leak out of the blood vessels. What structure is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: C (endothelium) — Endothelial barrier regulates permeability; pericytes support microvessels, sphincters regulate flow, basement membrane supports, elastic membrane is not the principal leak barrier.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person has been diagnosed with capillary leak syndrome, which is a condition that causes fluid and proteins to leak out of the blood vessels. What structure is most likely affected?

questions.question: A patient comes into the ER with symptoms suggesting cardiac tamponade, where excess fluid builds up in the pericardial sac. Which of the following epithelium lines the cells that normally produce fluid in this location?
questions.explanation: A (simple squamous epithelium) — Mesothelium lining pericardial sac is simple squamous; pseudostratified/columnar/cuboidal types are not serous cavity lining.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient comes into the ER with symptoms suggesting cardiac tamponade, where excess fluid builds up in the pericardial sac. Which of the following epithelium lines the cells that normally produce fluid in this location?

questions.question: In which layer of the heart are the Purkinje fibers found?
questions.explanation: D (subendocardium) — Purkinje network lies in subendocardial connective tissue; epicardium, mesothelium and bulk myocardium are not the principal location.
questions.sourceQuestion: In which layer of the heart are the Purkinje fibers found?

questions.question: A 69-year-old man developed inflammation of the heart associated with COVID-19. After his death, microscopic examination showed inflammatory cells in the middle layer of both ventricular walls and in the interventricular septum. Which tissue of the heart is primarily affected?
questions.explanation: C (cardiac muscle tissue) — Middle heart layer is myocardium; mesothelium/endothelium line surfaces, smooth muscle/areolar CT are not ventricular wall middle layer.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 69-year-old man developed inflammation of the heart associated with COVID-19. After his death, microscopic examination showed inflammatory cells in the middle layer of both ventricular walls and in the interventricular septum. Which tissue of the heart is primarily affected?

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman diagnosed with infective endocarditis suddenly died. After her death, examination of the heart showed a large, infected mass attached to the mitral valve. Which tissue normally covers the mitral valve at the site where the infected mass was attached?
questions.explanation: A (endothelium) — Valve leaflets are endothelial-lined; core is CT, not mesothelium, cardiac muscle, or smooth muscle.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 22-year-old woman diagnosed with infective endocarditis suddenly died. After her death, examination of the heart showed a large, infected mass attached to the mitral valve. Which tissue normally covers the mitral valve at the site where the infected mass was attached?

questions.question: Which of the following tissues is specific and unique to the tunica externa of the superior and inferior vena cava?
questions.explanation: A (longitudinal smooth muscle) — Large vena cava tunica externa contains prominent longitudinal smooth muscle; connective tissue is widespread, endothelium is intima, circular muscle is media, adipose is not unique.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following tissues is specific and unique to the tunica externa of the superior and inferior vena cava? (Repeated)

questions.question: A woman presented with an infection of the aorta. Which type of cell is affected in the tunica media of the aorta?
questions.explanation: A (smooth muscle) — Aortic tunica media contains smooth muscle cells among elastic lamellae; fibroblasts/adipose/Purkinje/striations are not the main media cell.
questions.sourceQuestion: A woman presented with an infection of the aorta. Which type of cell is affected in the tunica media of the aorta? (Repeated)

questions.question: Vasa vasorum is located in which layer?
questions.explanation: B (tunica externa) — Vasa vasorum supply walls of large vessels, mainly adventitia and outer media; intima and inner media are nourished by lumen diffusion.
questions.sourceQuestion: Vasa vasorum is located in which layer? (Repeated)

questions.question: A stent is placed inside a blood vessel. What is the layer that the stent is touching?
questions.explanation: C (endothelium) — Blood-contacting surface of lumen is endothelial; collagen/smooth muscle lie deeper, cartilage absent.
questions.sourceQuestion: A stent is placed inside a blood vessel. What is the layer that the stent is touching?

questions.question: In which of the following layers can vasa vasorum be found?
questions.explanation: C (tunica externa of aorta) — Vasa vasorum are prominent in large-vessel adventitia; small arteries/arterioles/venous intima do not fit.
questions.sourceQuestion: In which of the following layers can vasa vasorum be found?

questions.question: Deficiency of collagen fibres (Ehler Dahlos syndrome) Weak arteries translucent skin. Which layer is affected?
questions.sourceIssue: The corrected booklet accepts multiple answers: D / E (Double Keyed). Self-check; excluded from single-answer grading.
questions.explanation: D/E (tunica externa or media) — Ehlers–Danlos collagen defects affect collagen-containing vessel wall, and both media and adventitia contain collagen; options do not specify collagen subtype. Printed double key is defensible; the question cannot uniquely select one layer.
questions.sourceQuestion: Deficiency of collagen fibres (Ehler Dahlos syndrome) Weak arteries translucent skin. Which layer is affected?

questions.question: How do we differentiate between middle muscular and small muscular Artery?
options: Middle muscular artery has one elastic layer and small muscular artery has two elastic layers
Middle muscular artery has only internal elastic lamellae and small muscular artery has only external elastic lamellae
Middle muscular artery has both external and internal elastic lamellae. Small muscular artery has no elastic lamellae.
Middle muscular artery has both external and internal elastic lamellae. Small muscular artery has internal elastic lamellae.
questions.explanation: D (both elastic lamellae in medium artery; internal lamina in small artery) — Medium muscular arteries typically have internal and external elastic laminae; small muscular arteries may retain internal but have indistinct/absent external lamina. A–C reverse or wrongly omit the internal lamina.
questions.sourceQuestion: How do we differentiate between middle muscular and small muscular Artery?

questions.question: Which blood vessel has the thinnest wall?
questions.explanation: C (capillaries) — Capillaries have a one-cell endothelial wall and no tunics; venules and arteries have additional wall layers.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which blood vessel has the thinnest wall?

questions.question: What is the characteristic under a microscope of the muscular artery?
questions.printedAnswer: A (C can also be correct but the question asks for a specific characteristic that is specific to a
questions.explanation: A (internal elastic lamina) — A conspicuous IEL is a defining histologic landmark of muscular arteries; circular smooth muscle (C) is also present in many vessels, so not specific; longitudinal collagen and myointimal cells are not defining. Printed key A accepted; item’s own note correctly recognizes C is nonspecific.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the characteristic under a microscope of the muscular artery?

questions.question: Through which type of epithelium is the oxygen diffusion rate the highest in the tunica intima?
questions.explanation: B (simple squamous) — Endothelium is simple squamous, minimizing diffusion distance; cuboidal, pseudostratified, columnar and stratified epithelia are thicker/nonvascular lining types.
questions.sourceQuestion: Through which type of epithelium is the oxygen diffusion rate the highest in the tunica intima?

questions.question: In which of the following can smooth muscles be seen?
options: Tunica externa of medium muscular arteries
Tunica externa of small muscular arteries
Tunica Intima of medium muscular arteries
questions.explanation: C (tunica media of arterioles) — Arteriolar media has smooth muscle regulating resistance; externa is mostly connective tissue and intima is endothelial.
questions.sourceQuestion: In which of the following can smooth muscles be seen?

questions.question: Which of the following microscopic features of the aorta helps to accommodate the force exerted upon its wall by the contraction of the heart?
questions.explanation: A (fenestrated elastic sheets) — Aortic elastic lamellae stretch/recoil to damp systolic pressure; collagen adds tensile strength but not elastic recoil, smooth muscle/adventitia/intima are not the primary mechanism.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following microscopic features of the aorta helps to accommodate the force exerted upon its wall by the contraction of the heart? (Repeated)

questions.question: Which vein may rarely show the internal elastic lamina?
questions.explanation: A (small veins) — Small veins may show a faint internal elastic lamina; muscular venules and postcapillary venules generally lack one.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which vein may rarely show the internal elastic lamina?

questions.question: Which of the following is the characteristic microscopic feature of tunica intima of muscular arteries?
questions.explanation: B (internal elastic lamina) — Muscular artery intima is distinguished by IEL; circular muscle belongs media, fenestrated elastic lamellae characterize elastic arteries, longitudinal collagen/adipocytes are not intimal hallmarks.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is the characteristic microscopic feature of tunica intima of muscular arteries?

questions.question: Which represents the aging process of a muscular artery?
options: Accumulation of fat between collagen and elastic layers
questions.explanation: A (calcification of media) — Medial calcification is a recognized age-related change; arteriosclerosis is broad, fat accumulation is atherosclerosis/plaque, reduced elasticity may result but is less specific. Key issue: question is imprecise; age-related arterial change is not uniquely medial calcification.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which represents the aging process of a muscular artery?

questions.question: What characteristic allows the aorta to withstand the high pressure?
questions.explanation: C (fenestrated elastic sheets) — Elastic lamellae stretch and recoil under pulsatile pressure; collagen resists tearing, smooth muscle regulates tone, vasa vasorum nourishes wall.
questions.sourceQuestion: What characteristic allows the aorta to withstand the high pressure?

questions.question: Tunica media in elastic arteries is comprised of:
questions.explanation: C (fenestrated elastic lamellae) — Elastic artery media has many fenestrated elastic sheets plus smooth muscle; circular muscle alone is incomplete, longitudinal fibers/myointimal cells are not defining.
questions.sourceQuestion: Tunica media in elastic arteries is comprised of:

questions.question: Which blood vessel has both inner and outer elastic lamellae?
questions.explanation: B (medium muscular arteries) — They usually have distinct internal and external elastic laminae; veins/capillaries lack both, small arteries often lack a clear external lamina, arterioles have scant elastic layers.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which blood vessel has both inner and outer elastic lamellae?

questions.question: Which cell synthesizes the collagen and elastin in tunica media?
questions.explanation: C (smooth muscle cell) — Vascular smooth muscle synthesizes extracellular matrix including collagen and elastin in media; endothelial/pericyte/myointimal/fibroblast are not the principal medial matrix source. Key issue: myointimal cells are modified smooth muscle cells, so terminology overlaps; C is intended.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which cell synthesizes the collagen and elastin in tunica media?

questions.question: In atherosclerosis, which of the following cells is responsible for accumulation of fat in between with the progression of age?
questions.explanation: B (modified smooth muscle cells) — Smooth muscle cells migrate into the intima and become foam-like cells in atherosclerotic lesions; smooth muscle cells (A) is less precise, while elastic fibers and fibroblasts do not accumulate lipid as the stated cell type. Printed key B is correct.
questions.sourceQuestion: In atherosclerosis, which of the following cells is responsible for accumulation of fat in between with the progression of age?

questions.question: Which of the following structures in the tunica media depends on the vasa vasorum to receive O2 and nutrient supply?
questions.explanation: A (smooth muscle) — Outer/central tunica media is too far from lumen for diffusion in a large vessel and depends on vasa vasorum; fibroblasts/adipose are not the media’s principal cells, striations and Purkinje fibers are irrelevant.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following structures in the tunica media depends on the vasa vasorum to receive O2 and nutrient supply?

questions.question: Smooth muscle damage in large veins, such as the superior and inferior vena cava, affects which parts of the blood vessel structure?
options: Tunica intima, tunica externa, and tunica media
questions.explanation: B (tunica externa and media) — Large venae cavae have longitudinal smooth muscle in externa and circular smooth muscle in media; intima is endothelial.
questions.sourceQuestion: Smooth muscle damage in large veins, such as the superior and inferior vena cava, affects which parts of the blood vessel structure?

questions.question: A patient presented with blurred vision and severely elevated blood pressure. Examination of the retina revealed narrowing of the arterioles. Which of the following describes the normal arrangement of elastic layers in typical small arterioles?
questions.explanation: C (absence of elastic laminae) — Typical small arterioles lack a distinct elastic lamina; elastic lamellae and dual IEL/EEL occur in larger vessels. Key issue: some larger arterioles may have a faint IEL, but “small arterioles” supports C.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient presented with blurred vision and severely elevated blood pressure. Examination of the retina revealed narrowing of the arterioles. Which of the following describes the normal arrangement of elastic layers in typical small arterioles?

questions.question: A 71-year-old woman presents with headache scalp tenderness localized to the temporal region. A temporal artery biopsy reveals inflammation of the arterial wall and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina. Which cell type primarily synthesizes the internal elastic lamina (IEL), the inner border of the tunica media?
questions.explanation: B (vascular smooth muscle cells) — Smooth muscle produces elastin in arterial media, including IEL; pericytes support capillaries, fibroblasts synthesize adventitial matrix, macrophages degrade, and endothelial cells line lumen.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 71-year-old woman presents with headache scalp tenderness localized to the temporal region. A temporal artery biopsy reveals inflammation of the arterial wall and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina. Which cell type primarily synthesizes the internal elastic lamina (IEL), the inner border of the tunica media?

questions.question: During vascular surgery, a tissue specimen is collected from a large blood vessel. Histological examination reveals a thin tunica media and a thick tunica externa. Which additional histological feature would support identification of this vessel as a large vein rather than a medium muscular artery?
options: Circular vascular smooth muscle in the tunica media
Collagen fibers in the tunica externa
Longitudinal smooth muscle bundles in the tunica externa
questions.explanation: D (longitudinal smooth muscle bundles in tunica externa) — Large veins have thick adventitia with longitudinal smooth muscle; muscular arteries have thicker media, prominent IEL, collagen also occurs widely, and endothelium is common to both.
questions.sourceQuestion: During vascular surgery, a tissue specimen is collected from a large blood vessel. Histological examination reveals a thin tunica media and a thick tunica externa. Which additional histological feature would support identification of this vessel as a large vein rather than a medium muscular artery?

questions.question: Students are drawing leukocyte migration during inflammation. What is the most accurate statement out of all?
options: Smooth muscle and post capillary venule
questions.explanation: A (endothelium + postcapillary venule) — Leukocytes cross endothelium chiefly in postcapillary venules; arterioles/metarterioles are not the main emigration site, smooth muscle is not the barrier.
questions.sourceQuestion: Students are drawing leukocyte migration during inflammation. What is the most accurate statement out of all?

questions.question: Students are studying diabetes and vasocirculatory issues that affect and cause dysfunction in microcirculation. What structure should the students focus on?
questions.sourceIssue: The corrected booklet accepts multiple answers: A & B. Self-check; excluded from single-answer grading.
questions.explanation: A and B (pericytes and endothelium) — Both regulate microvascular stability/permeability and are implicated in diabetic microvascular injury; mesothelium lines serosa, smooth muscle regulates larger vessels. Printed double key is reasonable.
questions.sourceQuestion: Students are studying diabetes and vasocirculatory issues that affect and cause dysfunction in microcirculation. What structure should the students focus on?

questions.question: Which blood vessel has the thinnest wall?
questions.explanation: C (capillaries) — A single endothelial layer plus basal lamina is thinnest; venules/arterioles/small arteries have additional wall layers.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which blood vessel has the thinnest wall?

questions.question: Through which type of epithelium, the oxygen diffusion rate is the highest in the tunica intima?
questions.explanation: B (simple squamous) — Thin endothelial lining permits diffusion; other epithelia are thicker or not vascular linings.
questions.sourceQuestion: Through which type of epithelium, the oxygen diffusion rate is the highest in the tunica intima?

questions.question: Which Organ of the following has Continuous Capillaries?
questions.explanation: B (lungs) — Pulmonary capillaries are continuous; spleen/liver are sinusoidal, kidney glomeruli are fenestrated.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which Organ of the following has Continuous Capillaries?

questions.question: Which of the following is widely believed to be contractile in capillaries?
questions.explanation: A (pericytes) — Pericytes can contract and regulate capillary flow; fenestrae are endothelial pores, diaphragm is unrelated, myofibroblasts are not the classic capillary mural cell.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is widely believed to be contractile in capillaries?

questions.question: Where would you find the least leakage of capillaries?
questions.explanation: B (brain) — Blood–brain barrier continuous capillaries have tight junctions and low permeability; liver/spleen are highly permeable sinusoids, kidney filters selectively.
questions.sourceQuestion: Where would you find the least leakage of capillaries?

questions.question: Which organ has fenestrated capillaries?
questions.explanation: A (kidney) — Glomerular capillaries are fenestrated; liver/spleen are sinusoidal, brain continuous.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which organ has fenestrated capillaries? (Repeated)

questions.question: A person has been diagnosed with capillary leak syndrome, which is a condition that causes fluid and proteins to leak out of the blood vessels. What structure is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: C (endothelium) — Endothelial barrier injury increases vascular leak; pericytes support vessels, sphincters control flow, basement membrane supports but is not the primary barrier named, elastic membrane is irrelevant.
questions.sourceQuestion: A person has been diagnosed with capillary leak syndrome, which is a condition that causes fluid and proteins to leak out of the blood vessels. What structure is most likely affected?

questions.question: The endothelium in the capillaries are formed from which epithelium?
questions.explanation: B (simple squamous) — Capillary endothelium is simple squamous; other listed epithelia are not found lining capillaries.
questions.sourceQuestion: The endothelium in the capillaries are formed from which epithelium?

questions.question: Where can fenestrated capillaries without diaphragm be found?’
questions.explanation: E (kidney) — Renal glomerular fenestrae are generally without diaphragms; lung/muscle are continuous, liver/spleen have discontinuous sinusoidal endothelium.
questions.sourceQuestion: Where can fenestrated capillaries without diaphragm be found?’

questions.question: Where are sinusoids found?
questions.sourceIssue: The corrected booklet accepts multiple answers: A & D (Double keyed). Self-check; excluded from single-answer grading.
questions.explanation: A and D (liver and spleen) — Both contain sinusoids; kidney and small intestine primarily have fenestrated capillaries. Printed double key is correct.
questions.sourceQuestion: Where are sinusoids found?

questions.question: Which structure is found surrounding the basement membrane of the capillaries?
questions.explanation: B (pericytes) — Pericytes lie outside endothelial tube, sharing/abutting its basement membrane; neutrophils/mast cells are mobile/interstitial, smooth muscle surrounds larger vessels.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which structure is found surrounding the basement membrane of the capillaries?

questions.question: When a tissue is injured, white blood cells migrate from the blood into the connective tissue. Which of the following vessels facilitate this migration?
questions.explanation: E (postcapillary venules) — They are the principal site of leukocyte diapedesis; capillaries, arterioles, shunts and collecting venules are not the main site. Repeated three times in source set.
questions.sourceQuestion: When a tissue is injured, white blood cells migrate from the blood into the connective tissue. Which of the following vessels facilitate this migration? (Repeated 3X)

questions.question: A 61-year-old woman presented with numerous small, visible blood vessels (redpurple spots) on her arms and legs. A skin biopsy and histology shows white blood cells (WBC) surrounding small blood vessels in her connective tissue. Through which of the following blood vessels did the WBCs observed in this patient's skin biopsy migrate from the blood into the surrounding connective tissue?
questions.explanation: E (postcapillary venules) — Leukocytes exit at postcapillary venules; continuous/fenestrated/sinusoidal describe capillary types, arterioles are not the principal emigration site.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 61-year-old woman presented with numerous small, visible blood vessels (redpurple spots) on her arms and legs. A skin biopsy and histology shows white blood cells (WBC) surrounding small blood vessels in her connective tissue. Through which of the following blood vessels did the WBCs observed in this patient's skin biopsy migrate from the blood into the surrounding connective tissue?

questions.question: In which of the following organs would you most likely find fenestrated with diaphragm capillaries?
questions.explanation: A (intestines) — Intestinal absorptive capillaries are fenestrated with diaphragms; liver sinusoids are discontinuous, skin/muscle are continuous.
questions.sourceQuestion: In which of the following organs would you most likely find fenestrated with diaphragm capillaries?

questions.question: Which of the following types of epithelium covers the vocal folds?
questions.explanation: E (stratified squamous) — True vocal folds endure abrasion and are stratified squamous; respiratory epithelium lines most nearby airway, simple columnar/stratified columnar are not typical.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following types of epithelium covers the vocal folds?

questions.question: Which of the following cells in the olfactory epithelium of the nasal cavity is responsible for the regeneration of olfactory perception, in a patient who lost his sense of smell.
questions.explanation: A (basal cells) — Basal stem cells replace olfactory receptor neurons; brush/goblet/supporting cells do not regenerate sensory neurons.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following cells in the olfactory epithelium of the nasal cavity is responsible for the regeneration of olfactory perception, in a patient who lost his sense of smell.

questions.question: A patient comes with nasal pain. You find mucus blocked in the paranasal sinuses. The failure of which of the following has led to the mucus block?
questions.explanation: A (mucociliary escalator) — Cilia and mucus clear sinus openings; venous flow, lymph drainage, and blood pressure are not the clearance mechanism.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient comes with nasal pain. You find mucus blocked in the paranasal sinuses. The failure of which of the following has led to the mucus block?

questions.question: After eating a candy bar with traces of nuts, a 7-year-old child was taken to the emergency room with breathing difficulty, and the doctor noticed marked edema of his epiglottis. What type of epithelium is present on the lingual (upper) surface of the epiglottis?
questions.explanation: E (stratified squamous) — Lingual surface of epiglottis faces food and is stratified squamous; ciliated/simple types line other respiratory areas.
questions.sourceQuestion: After eating a candy bar with traces of nuts, a 7-year-old child was taken to the emergency room with breathing difficulty, and the doctor noticed marked edema of his epiglottis. What type of epithelium is present on the lingual (upper) surface of the epiglottis?

questions.question: Ciliary escalator movement in bronchus is towards which structure ?
questions.explanation: C (pharynx) — Cilia move mucus upward toward pharynx; terminal/respiratory bronchioles and alveoli are distal.
questions.sourceQuestion: Ciliary escalator movement in bronchus is towards which structure ?

questions.question: What is the epithelium on the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis?
questions.explanation: B (pseudostratified columnar) — Laryngeal surface is mostly respiratory epithelium; stratified squamous is most characteristic of lingual side, cuboidal/simple columnar are not typical.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the epithelium on the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis?

questions.question: What type of epithelium do true vocal cords have?
questions.explanation: A (stratified squamous) — True vocal folds are stratified squamous; other epithelia are respiratory/ductal types.
questions.sourceQuestion: What type of epithelium do true vocal cords have?

questions.question: What makes up the epithelium of the upper surface of epiglottis ?
questions.explanation: A (nonkeratinized stratified squamous) — Upper/lingual epiglottis faces bolus and has nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium; respiratory lining is on laryngeal side.
questions.sourceQuestion: What makes up the epithelium of the upper surface of epiglottis ?

questions.question: What is the epithelium of lingual epiglottis
questions.explanation: A (nonkeratinized stratified squamous) — Same lingual epiglottis epithelium; pseudostratified ciliated lines laryngeal surface, transitional/simple cuboidal are wrong.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the epithelium of lingual epiglottis

questions.question: What is the epithelium of vocal folds
questions.explanation: A (stratified squamous) — Vocal folds resist friction; simple squamous/columnar and pseudostratified options are not true-fold lining.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the epithelium of vocal folds

questions.question: Which of the following structures in the upper respiratory tract is responsible for the humidification of inhaled air?
questions.explanation: D (serous glands) — Serous secretions humidify inhaled air; AV plexuses warm it, goblet cells make mucus, sinuses/vibrissae have other roles. Key issue: humidification is also aided by airway mucus and mucosal surface; answer is intended among choices.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following structures in the upper respiratory tract is responsible for the humidification of inhaled air?

questions.question: Which of the following cells in the respiratory epithelium act as stem cells?
questions.explanation: A (basal cells) — Basal cells serve as progenitors in respiratory epithelium; brush/ciliated/goblet/serous cells are differentiated.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following cells in the respiratory epithelium act as stem cells?

questions.question: Which of the following is the function of the olfactory receptor cells?
questions.explanation: D (binding odor molecules) — Olfactory receptor neurons detect odorants; metabolic support/insulation/protein production are not their primary receptor function.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is the function of the olfactory receptor cells?

questions.question: What structure has an elastic core, stratified squamous epithelium on one side, and pseudostratified ciliated columnar on the other?
questions.explanation: A (epiglottis) — Elastic cartilage core has stratified squamous on lingual side and respiratory epithelium on laryngeal side; trachea/bronchi/nasopharynx lack this paired lining pattern.
questions.sourceQuestion: What structure has an elastic core, stratified squamous epithelium on one side, and pseudostratified ciliated columnar on the other?

questions.question: A DNA virus targets stratified squamous epithelium. Which part of the respiratory tract is most prominently affected?
questions.explanation: C (true vocal cords) — True vocal folds carry stratified squamous epithelium; nasal cavity/trachea/false folds are mostly respiratory epithelium.
questions.sourceQuestion: A DNA virus targets stratified squamous epithelium. Which part of the respiratory tract is most prominently affected?

questions.question: In the respiratory mucosa, what is responsible for heating and humidifying the air entering the respiratory tract?
questions.explanation: B (lamina propria with blood vessels) — Vascular plexuses warm and humidify mucosa; glands add moisture, cilia move mucus, vibrissae filter, brush cells are sensory.
questions.sourceQuestion: In the respiratory mucosa, what is responsible for heating and humidifying the air entering the respiratory tract?

questions.question: A 32-year old patient recovering from a viral infection experiences temporary loss of smell. A biopsy reveals selective loss of the cells that produce odorant-binding proteins. Which cell type in the olfactory epithelium is primarily affected?
questions.explanation: C (sustentacular cells) — Supporting cells produce odorant-binding proteins; receptor neurons detect odor, basal cells regenerate, brush/small granule cells have other roles.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 32-year old patient recovering from a viral infection experiences temporary loss of smell. A biopsy reveals selective loss of the cells that produce odorant-binding proteins. Which cell type in the olfactory epithelium is primarily affected?

questions.question: A 24-year old patient with seasonal allergic rhinitis experiences severe nasal congestion. Histological examination of the respiratory region of the nasal cavity shows marked swelling of the mucosa. Which structure within the lamina propria is primarily responsible for this nasal congestion?
questions.explanation: D (venous plexuses and capillary loops) — Vascular engorgement of nasal conchae causes congestion; nerves/mucous glands/loose CT/lymphatics are not the primary erectile component.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 24-year old patient with seasonal allergic rhinitis experiences severe nasal congestion. Histological examination of the respiratory region of the nasal cavity shows marked swelling of the mucosa. Which structure within the lamina propria is primarily responsible for this nasal congestion?

questions.question: Which of the following cells is responsible for detoxifying noxious agents?
questions.explanation: A (Club/Clara cells) — Club cells detoxify inhaled substances with cytochrome enzymes; goblet cells secrete mucus, macrophages phagocytose particles.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following cells is responsible for detoxifying noxious agents?

questions.question: A 12 year old boy visits the doctor due to a persistent cough and difficulty breathing. His symptoms get worse when playing sports or running. During the examination, the doctor hears wheezing sounds in his chest. He is diagnosed with asthma. Which of the following features distinguishes an intrapulmonary bronchus from a bronchiole?
questions.explanation: D (irregular cartilage plates) — Intrapulmonary bronchi have cartilage plates; bronchioles have none. Key issue: stem asks to distinguish bronchus from bronchiole; D is best, while C-shaped cartilage is tracheal, not intrapulmonary bronchus.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 12 year old boy visits the doctor due to a persistent cough and difficulty breathing. His symptoms get worse when playing sports or running. During the examination, the doctor hears wheezing sounds in his chest. He is diagnosed with asthma. Which of the following features distinguishes an intrapulmonary bronchus from a bronchiole? (Repeated)

questions.question: Which of the following structures does not have cartilage?
questions.explanation: B (bronchiole) — Bronchioles lack cartilage; bronchus/secondary bronchi and larynx/epiglottis contain cartilage.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following structures does not have cartilage?

questions.question: Which of the following cells produces a surfactant like material and are located in the terminal bronchiole?
questions.explanation: B (Club cells) — Club cells in terminal bronchioles secrete surfactant-like material; pneumocytes are alveolar, type I are gas-exchange, brush/goblet are not the classic source.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following cells produces a surfactant like material and are located in the terminal bronchiole?

questions.question: Which cells in the respiratory system are responsible for engulfing and clearing inhaled carbon particles (such as smoke and dust)?
questions.explanation: C (alveolar macrophage) — Dust cells engulf inhaled particles; pneumocytes/Club cells/brush cells have other functions.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which cells in the respiratory system are responsible for engulfing and clearing inhaled carbon particles (such as smoke and dust)?

questions.question: Which of the following structures is involved in both air conduction and gas exchange?
questions.explanation: C (respiratory bronchiole) — It conducts air and has alveoli in its walls for gas exchange; terminal bronchiole and bronchi only conduct, alveolar duct is exchange region but not typically counted as conducting airway.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following structures is involved in both air conduction and gas exchange?

questions.question: A 62-year-old man was admitted to the hospital due to trouble breathing. He used to smoke two packs of cigarettes every day. He was diagnosed with emphysema. Which of the following cells cover the largest surface of the alveoli?
questions.explanation: C (type I alveolar cells) — Type I pneumocytes cover most alveolar surface area; type II are more numerous but cover less area, others do not line most alveoli.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 62-year-old man was admitted to the hospital due to trouble breathing. He used to smoke two packs of cigarettes every day. He was diagnosed with emphysema. Which of the following cells cover the largest surface of the alveoli?

questions.question: Which of the following lists the components of the Air-Blood barrier?
options: Alveolar epithelial cells, capillary endothelial cells, and their basal lamina (basement membrane)
Mucus layer, ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelial cells, and muscularis layer
Mucus layer, ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelial cells, muscularis layer, and cartilage
Visceral pleura, parietal pleura, and serous fluid
Surfactant layer, alveolar epithelial cells, capillary endothelial cells, and their basal lamina (basement membrane)
questions.explanation: E (surfactant + type I epithelial cell + fused basal lamina + capillary endothelium) — These form the thin air–blood barrier; option A omits surfactant, other choices describe conducting airway or pleura.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following lists the components of the Air-Blood barrier?

questions.question: A 68-year-old smoker with a history of progressive dyspnea. Biopsy shows squamous cells lining most of the alveolar surface, and a cuboidal cell population has lamellar bodies. Which cell forms the air-blood barrier?
questions.explanation: C (type I pneumocyte) — Thin type I cells form most alveolar surface and gas barrier; type II produce surfactant, macrophages clear particles, club/ciliated cells are airway cells.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 68-year-old smoker with a history of progressive dyspnea. Biopsy shows squamous cells lining most of the alveolar surface, and a cuboidal cell population has lamellar bodies. Which cell forms the air-blood barrier?

questions.question: In which of the following structures is smooth muscle absent?
questions.explanation: D (alveoli) — Alveoli lack smooth muscle; trachea has trachealis, bronchi and bronchioles have smooth muscle.
questions.sourceQuestion: In which of the following structures is smooth muscle absent?

questions.question: Which alveolar cell type covers the largest surface area?
options: Type I pneumocytes (Alveolar type I cells)
Type II pneumocytes (Alveolar type II cells)
questions.explanation: A (type I pneumocytes) — They cover the largest alveolar surface; type II, macrophages, endothelium and brush cells cover less/do not line alveolar air surface.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which alveolar cell type covers the largest surface area?

questions.question: How does a pathologist know he’s viewing bronchioles not bronchus?
options: Presence of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
Presence of a well-developed smooth muscle layer
Complete absence of hyaline cartilage plates and glands
Presence of elastic fibers in the lamina propria
questions.explanation: C (absence of cartilage plates and glands) — Bronchioles lack both cartilage and submucosal glands; bronchial epithelium and muscle alone are not sufficient to distinguish them.
questions.sourceQuestion: How does a pathologist know he’s viewing bronchioles not bronchus?

questions.question: What is the last part of the air conducting system?
questions.explanation: C (terminal bronchiole) — It is final conducting airway before respiratory bronchioles; respiratory bronchiole/alveolar duct exchange gas, segmental bronchus is proximal.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the last part of the air conducting system?

questions.question: The cells which aid in surfactant production is present in which of the following:
questions.explanation: E (respiratory bronchiole) — Type II pneumocytes producing surfactant are in alveolarized respiratory region; terminal bronchioles instead have Club cells, bronchi are proximal. Key issue: wording says “cells which aid in surfactant production”; if referring specifically to Club cells, terminal bronchiole would also be plausible. Printed E is intended for alveolar type II cells.
questions.sourceQuestion: The cells which aid in surfactant production is present in which of the following:

questions.question: Cartilage that prevents collapse of airways are not present in?
questions.explanation: D (bronchioles) — Bronchioles lack cartilage; trachea, primary/segmental bronchi and larynx contain cartilage.
questions.sourceQuestion: Cartilage that prevents collapse of airways are not present in?

questions.question: Carbon dioxide (CO2) molecules, in order to pass from capillary lumen to the lumen of alveoli, must pass through which of the following layers?
options: Endothelial cells, a fused basement membrane and type-l pneumocytes
Endothelial cells, a fused basement membrane and Clara cells
Endothelial cells, fused basement membrane and Type-Il pneumocytes
questions.explanation: B (endothelium + fused basal lamina + type I pneumocyte) — Capillary-to-alveolus gas crosses these thin layers; club cells/type II are not the exchange barrier, interstitial connective tissue is minimal/usually fused lamina.
questions.sourceQuestion: Carbon dioxide (CO2) molecules, in order to pass from capillary lumen to the lumen of alveoli, must pass through which of the following layers?

questions.question: In chronic interstitial lung diseases (interstitial lung disease), the alveolar septa become thick due to fibrosis thus impeding the gaseous exchange. Which of the following cells most likely stimulate the fibroblasts to cause this condition?
questions.explanation: C (septal macrophages) — Alveolar macrophages can promote inflammatory/fibrotic signaling; dust cells are same macrophage family, making C/A terminology ambiguous. Key issue: A “fixed dust cells” and C “septal macrophages” substantially overlap; key C is not uniquely distinguishable.
questions.sourceQuestion: In chronic interstitial lung diseases (interstitial lung disease), the alveolar septa become thick due to fibrosis thus impeding the gaseous exchange. Which of the following cells most likely stimulate the fibroblasts to cause this condition?

questions.question: A 48-year-old man was presented to the ER with severe dyspnea for the last few hours. Bronchoscopy reveals that the carina is distorted and widened. Enlargement of which one of the following groups of lymph nodes is most likely responsible for altering the carina?
questions.explanation: D (inferior tracheobronchial nodes) — These lie below carina and enlargement can widen it; paratracheal, pulmonary, bronchopulmonary nodes are not directly at bifurcation; plexus is neural.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 48-year-old man was presented to the ER with severe dyspnea for the last few hours. Bronchoscopy reveals that the carina is distorted and widened. Enlargement of which one of the following groups of lymph nodes is most likely responsible for altering the carina?

questions.question: Which of the following respiratory airways contains cells in their lining epithelium contributing to the secretion of a substance required to prevent collapse of alveoli?
questions.explanation: C (respiratory bronchioles) — Their walls contain type II pneumocytes that make surfactant; larger bronchi/trachea lack alveolar surfactant-secreting cells.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following respiratory airways contains cells in their lining epithelium contributing to the secretion of a substance required to prevent collapse of alveoli?

questions.question: Presence of cilia in the respiratory epithelium helps to propel mucous upwards towards the pharynx. They extend up to which of the following airways?
questions.explanation: B (respiratory bronchioles) — Ciliated cells extend to respiratory bronchioles, with decreasing cilia distally; alveolar ducts/sacs/alveoli lack cilia, terminal bronchioles are proximal.
questions.sourceQuestion: Presence of cilia in the respiratory epithelium helps to propel mucous upwards towards the pharynx. They extend up to which of the following airways?

questions.question: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can live particularly well in which of the following cells?
questions.explanation: C (alveolar macrophages) — M. tuberculosis can survive within macrophages; pneumocytes and Club cells are not the main host niche.
questions.sourceQuestion: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can live particularly well in which of the following cells?

questions.question: What is the epithelium of terminal bronchi?
options: Simple cuboidal ciliated, with Clara cells (Club cells)
Pseudostratified columnar ciliated, with Goblet cells
Simple columnar ciliated, with Goblet cells
questions.explanation: A (simple cuboidal ciliated with Club cells) — Terminal bronchioles are mainly simple cuboidal, with Club cells; pseudostratified goblet epithelium belongs larger airways, stratified squamous is not typical.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the epithelium of terminal bronchi?

questions.question: In the respiratory mucosa, what is responsible for heating and humidifying the air entering the respiratory tract?
questions.explanation: B (lamina propria with vessels) — Vascular plexuses warm mucosa and contribute to humidification; glands secrete, cilia transport, vibrissae filter, brush cells are sensory.
questions.sourceQuestion: In the respiratory mucosa, what is responsible for heating and humidifying the air entering the respiratory tract?

questions.question: Upon examination, a patient is found to have a disease in his small bronchioles. Which feature distinguishes small bronchioles from other structures?
questions.explanation: B (relatively thick smooth muscle layer) — Small bronchioles have prominent smooth muscle relative to wall and no cartilage; cartilage/goblet/respiratory epithelium are absent or not defining. Key issue: “small bronchioles” and “relatively thick” are underspecified, but B is intended.
questions.sourceQuestion: Upon examination, a patient is found to have a disease in his small bronchioles. Which feature distinguishes small bronchioles from other structures? (Repeated)

questions.question: An electron micrograph of a terminal bronchiole shows non-ciliated cells with dome-shaped apical surfaces containing secretory granules. Which of the following is a key function of these cells?
options: Acting as progenitor cells for bronchiolar epithelial regeneration
Producing mucus to trap inhaled particles
Transporting mucus toward the upper respiratory tract
Releasing neuropeptides to regulate airway activity
Phagocytosing inhaled microorganisms and cellular debris
