questions.explanation: A (progenitor/regeneration) — Club cells are secretory and progenitor cells for bronchiolar epithelium; mucus secretion/ciliary transport/phagocytosis are other cell roles.
questions.sourceQuestion: An electron micrograph of a terminal bronchiole shows non-ciliated cells with dome-shaped apical surfaces containing secretory granules. Which of the following is a key function of these cells?

questions.question: An autopsy performed on a patient with chronic left-sided heart failure reveals brown-pigmented cells free within the alveolar air spaces. Which of the following cell types are most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: E (alveolar macrophages) — Hemosiderin-laden “heart failure cells” are alveolar macrophages after pulmonary congestion; monocytes circulate, septal macrophages are interstitial, pneumocytes do not phagocytose blood pigment.
questions.sourceQuestion: An autopsy performed on a patient with chronic left-sided heart failure reveals brown-pigmented cells free within the alveolar air spaces. Which of the following cell types are most likely responsible for this finding?

questions.question: A researcher is studying the rate of oxygen diffusion across the thinnest region of the air-blood barrier (respiratory membrane). Which sequence correctly traces the path of an oxygen molecule moving from the alveolar lumen into a red blood cell?
options: Type I pneumocytes→ smooth muscle layer →Endothelial basal lamina → endothelial cells.
Club cell Type 1 pneumocytes → fused basal lamina Capillary endothelial cells.
Surfactant layer→ Type I pneumocytes→ fused basal lamina Capillary endothelial cells.
Capillary endothelial cells → Interstitial connective tissue Type I pneumocytes→ Surfactant layer
Surfactant layer→ Type Il pneumocytes Interstitial connective tissue Endothelial cells.
questions.explanation: C (surfactant → type I pneumocyte → fused basal lamina → capillary endothelium) — This is the air-to-blood diffusion sequence; smooth muscle, Club/type II cells, and reverse direction are incorrect.
questions.sourceQuestion: A researcher is studying the rate of oxygen diffusion across the thinnest region of the air-blood barrier (respiratory membrane). Which sequence correctly traces the path of an oxygen molecule moving from the alveolar lumen into a red blood cell?

questions.question: A neonate presented with a defect that caused the endocardial tube to bend to the left, causing the apex to be on the right side. What is the name of this defect?
questions.explanation: E Dextrocardia — correct. A primitive heart tube looping abnormally leftward can place the apex rightward. A Patent ductus arteriosus is persistent fetal shunting; TOF is a conotruncal malformation; VSD and ASD are septal defects, none specify rightward apex.
questions.sourceQuestion: A neonate presented with a defect that caused the endocardial tube to bend to the left, causing the apex to be on the right side. What is the name of this defect?

questions.question: What is the embryological origin of the smooth part of the right atrium?
questions.explanation: A Sinus venosus — correct, but more precisely its right horn. It is incorporated into the smooth sinus venarum of the right atrium. Truncus arteriosus and bulbus cordis form outflow regions; atrium proper makes trabeculated atrial portions; ventricle proper forms trabeculated ventricles.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the embryological origin of the smooth part of the right atrium? (Repeated 6x)

questions.question: What is the complete embryological origin of the endocardial heart tubes?
questions.explanation: E Visceral (splanchnic) mesoderm — correct. Cardiogenic mesoderm forms paired endocardial tubes. Paraxial mesoderm forms somites; neural tube/neuroectoderm do not form the heart tube; endoderm forms much of gut/respiratory epithelium.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the complete embryological origin of the endocardial heart tubes?

questions.question: What best explains why the foramen ovale closes after birth?
questions.explanation: C Increased left atrial pressure — correct. Lung expansion lowers pulmonary resistance and raises pulmonary venous return, increasing LA pressure above RA and functionally apposing septum primum to septum secundum. Increased RA pressure would keep the flap open; “ventricular pressure” is not the direct mechanism. Key C is supported.
questions.sourceQuestion: What best explains why the foramen ovale closes after birth? (Repeated)

questions.question: What is the reason for the apex of the heart to be directed to the left side?
options: The left ventricle is muscular and the apex is attached to it
The interventricular septum pushes the left ventricle
The embryonic heart develops on the left side of the thorax
The heart grows on the left side more due to the absence of the liver
The embryonic heart bends to the right and the bulbus cordis swells
questions.explanation: E — keyed answer is imprecise. Normal rightward looping (dextral loop) and differential growth position the apex leftward; bulbus cordis expansion contributes to the loop, but option E overstates it as the sole explanation. A is a consequence (LV forms apex), B is not the main mechanism, C is false (heart initially develops ventrally), D is false (liver asymmetry is not causal). No fully precise option.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the reason for the apex of the heart to be directed to the left side?

questions.question: What is the embryological origin of the part of the heart which covers most of the anterior surface (sternocostal surface)?
questions.explanation: A Bulbus cordis — correct. Its proximal part forms the trabeculated right ventricle; truncus arteriosus forms proximal aorta/pulmonary trunk, sinus venosus venous inflow, atrium proper atrial trabeculae, and “ventricle proper” mainly trabeculated LV.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the embryological origin of the part of the heart which covers most of the anterior surface (sternocostal surface)?

questions.question: What Is the origin of the endocardium tube of the heart?
questions.explanation: B Mesoderm — correct. The endocardium and myocardial lineage are mesodermal. Endoderm and ectoderm are other germ layers; hypoblast is extraembryonic endoderm; epiblast is the source of all three germ layers but is not the differentiated heart tissue origin.
questions.sourceQuestion: What Is the origin of the endocardium tube of the heart?

questions.question: What comes from the sinus venosus left horn?
questions.explanation: B Coronary sinus — correct. It derives mainly from the left horn of sinus venosus. Pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins and SVC have different origins.
questions.sourceQuestion: What comes from the sinus venosus left horn?

questions.question: When does foramen ovale close after birth?
questions.explanation: D Immediately — correct as functional closure. First breaths and cord clamping increase LA relative to RA pressure, closing the flap. Anatomical fusion takes months to years in many people, so options A–C confuse functional with anatomical closure.
questions.sourceQuestion: When does foramen ovale close after birth? (Repeated)

questions.question: If the embryonic heart tube bends to the right, the heart and apex are placed to the left. Which one of the following terms justifies the position of the heart?
questions.explanation: D Normal — correct. Rightward looping normally places the apex leftward. A is a location descriptor, B is misspelled/abnormal right-sided heart, C is ectopia cordis, E describes the mediastinum rather than laterality.
questions.sourceQuestion: If the embryonic heart tube bends to the right, the heart and apex are placed to the left. Which one of the following terms justifies the position of the heart?

questions.question: The heart and the apex are placed to the left in normal situations. Dextocardia is the abnormal placement of the heart and the placement to the right. What is the primary cause of the closure of the foramen ovale?
questions.explanation: B Increased LA pressure — correct. It functionally closes the foramen ovale against septum secundum. Heart rate, aortic pressure, or reduced pulmonary pressure do not explain the flap closure.
questions.sourceQuestion: The heart and the apex are placed to the left in normal situations. Dextocardia is the abnormal placement of the heart and the placement to the right. What is the primary cause of the closure of the foramen ovale?

questions.question: If the heart bends towards the left and the Apex is found on the right side?
questions.explanation: E Dextrocardia — correct. Leftward looping may position the apex rightward. The other options are unrelated septal or outflow defects/tamponade.
questions.sourceQuestion: If the heart bends towards the left and the Apex is found on the right side?

questions.question: How does the Transverse Sinus form?
options: Folding of the Heart tube and Bending of the Great vessels
Folding of the heart tube and apoptosis of the Dorsal Mesocardium
Folding of the heart tube and Bending of the Heart 45 degrees Anteriorly
Folding of the Heart tube and Partial apoptosis of the Bulbus cordis
questions.explanation: B Heart-tube folding plus apoptosis of dorsal mesocardium — correct. Loss of the dorsal mesocardium creates the transverse pericardial sinus behind the arterial and in front of venous ends. Other proposed folding/bending mechanisms do not describe this passage.
questions.sourceQuestion: How does the Transverse Sinus form? (Repeated 2x)

questions.question: What is the origin of the heart of a 6 -month infant?
questions.explanation: E Splanchnic mesoderm — correct. Cardiac muscle and connective components arise from splanchnic mesoderm; germ layers/cell types listed otherwise are not the direct tissue origin.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the origin of the heart of a 6 -month infant?

questions.question: What makes the coronary sinus?
questions.explanation: A Sinus venosus — best answer; key C is wrong. The coronary sinus is derived from the left horn of sinus venosus. The left common cardinal vein chiefly accounts for the oblique vein in the conventional teaching description. Some descriptions include a common-cardinal contribution to the coronary sinus, whose primary origin is the left sinus horn. Truncus arteriosus, right umbilical vein and left subclavian vessels have other derivatives. Human embryo sections (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1767797/)
questions.sourceQuestion: What makes the coronary sinus?

questions.question: What are the regions of the early heart tubes that correspond to outflow and inflow of blood, respectively?
options: Aortic arch and inferior vena cava
Bulbus cordis and superior vena cava
Arch of the aorta and superior vena cava
questions.explanation: C Truncus arteriosus and sinus venosus — correct. These are arterial outflow and venous inflow ends. Bulbus cordis is not the full outflow tract; SVC and pulmonary artery/aorta are later vessels, while option E mismatches inflow.
questions.sourceQuestion: What are the regions of the early heart tubes that correspond to outflow and inflow of blood, respectively?

questions.question: What is the clinical importance of the space between the outflow and inflow regions of the initial development of the heart?
options: The space is known for the presence of autonomic nerves
Absence of the space leads to dextrocardia
The covering pericardium needs reflection to expose great vessels
Clamping of big vessels is possible in surgery
Echocardiography reveals oblique sinus at this region
questions.explanation: D Clamping of great vessels is possible — correct. The transverse pericardial sinus permits a surgeon to pass a clamp behind arterial outflow vessels. Other options misstate its contents, clinical effect, or identification.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the clinical importance of the space between the outflow and inflow regions of the initial development of the heart?

questions.question: Which structure of the original heart tube forms the right ventricle of the heart?
options: A part of the primitive atrium
questions.explanation: B Bulbus cordis — correct. The proximal bulbus forms most trabeculated RV. Primitive ventricle forms trabeculated LV; truncus makes great artery roots; sinus venosus and primitive atrium make venous/atrial portions.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which structure of the original heart tube forms the right ventricle of the heart? (Repeated)

questions.question: In which condition does the heart loop to the left, shifting to the right?
questions.explanation: A Dextrocardia — correct. Leftward looping produces right-sided apex. ASD, TOF, and transposition have different developmental bases.
questions.sourceQuestion: In which condition does the heart loop to the left, shifting to the right? (Repeated)

questions.question: The major anterior part of the ventricle comes from sudden swelling of the bulbus cordis. Thus, which of the following parts of the heart makes its anterior surface?
questions.explanation: B Right ventricle — correct. The bulbus cordis contributes most of RV, which forms much of the sternocostal/anterior surface. Atria are posterior/superior; LV mostly forms the left border/diaphragmatic surface; epicardium is a covering.
questions.sourceQuestion: The major anterior part of the ventricle comes from sudden swelling of the bulbus cordis. Thus, which of the following parts of the heart makes its anterior surface?

questions.question: A heart that folds in the opposite direction and points to the right is called?:
questions.explanation: A Dextrocardia — correct. Opposite-direction looping may place the apex rightward. Coarctation and transposition do not define apex orientation; TOF is a conotruncal defect.
questions.sourceQuestion: A heart that folds in the opposite direction and points to the right is called?:

questions.question: During embryological development of the heart, the smooth part of the right atrium develops from?
questions.explanation: C Right horn of sinus venosus — correct. It becomes smooth right atrium. Pulmonary veins incorporate into smooth LA; conus is outflow; truncus becomes great arteries; left horn forms coronary sinus.
questions.sourceQuestion: During embryological development of the heart, the smooth part of the right atrium develops from? (Repeated 2x)

questions.question: Which vein bypasses the liver to reach the heart during fetal life?
questions.explanation: C Left umbilical vein — keyed answer is wrong/ambiguous wording. The ductus venosus bypasses hepatic sinusoids, connecting left umbilical vein to IVC; the left umbilical vein itself carries oxygenated placental blood toward the liver/ductus venosus, not directly to the heart. Right umbilical vein regresses; cardinal veins drain embryo; vitelline vein contributes portal/hepatic system. No offered “ductus venosus.”
questions.sourceQuestion: Which vein bypasses the liver to reach the heart during fetal life?

questions.question: If there were a virus affecting the primitive ventricle, which adult structure would be affected?
questions.explanation: A Left ventricle — correct. Primitive ventricle forms trabeculated LV. Bulbus forms most RV/outflow; atria derive from primitive atrium/sinus venosus; pulmonary trunk from conotruncal outflow.
questions.sourceQuestion: If there were a virus affecting the primitive ventricle, which adult structure would be affected?

questions.question: pregnant woman is exposed to a teratogenic medication during the third week of embryonic development. The embryo develops severe cardiac malformation. Why is this period particularly important for cardiac development?
options: The primitive heart tube is forming
questions.explanation: D Primitive heart tube forming — correct. Cardiac development begins in week 3, making this a sensitive period. Coronary circulation and chamber separation occur later; foramen ovale is prenatal and ductus closure postnatal.
questions.sourceQuestion: pregnant woman is exposed to a teratogenic medication during the third week of embryonic development. The embryo develops severe cardiac malformation. Why is this period particularly important for cardiac development?

questions.question: The coronary sinus normally develops primarily from which embryonic structure?
options: Left horn of the sinus venosus
questions.explanation: B Left horn of sinus venosus — correct. It forms coronary sinus (and oblique vein of LA). Other options contribute arterial, cardinal, atrial, or placental structures.
questions.sourceQuestion: The coronary sinus normally develops primarily from which embryonic structure?

questions.question: In tetralogy of the fallot, which of the following causes the defect in Aorticopulmonary Septum?
questions.explanation: D Neural crest migration defect — best answer. Conotruncal septation depends on neural crest; abnormal alignment/septation contributes to TOF. Pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta and VSD are components, not the embryologic initiating defect.
questions.sourceQuestion: In tetralogy of the fallot, which of the following causes the defect in Aorticopulmonary Septum? (Repeated)

questions.question: In transposition of the great vessels, the pulmonary trunk originates from the left ventricle instead of the right ventricle. To effectively address this condition, it is important to know the normal anatomy. What is the correct anatomical origin of the pulmonary trunk?
questions.explanation: A Truncus arteriosus — correct. The pulmonary trunk arises from the truncus arteriosus after spiral aorticopulmonary septation. Fourth and sixth arches contribute to great-vessel segments, not the pulmonary trunk’s embryonic source.
questions.sourceQuestion: In transposition of the great vessels, the pulmonary trunk originates from the left ventricle instead of the right ventricle. To effectively address this condition, it is important to know the normal anatomy. What is the correct anatomical origin of the pulmonary trunk?

questions.question: What is the most common heart defect?
questions.explanation: A VSD — conventional answer, but “most common heart defect” can vary by population/definition. ASD, TOF and transposition are less common in standard teaching. Key acceptable with wording caveat.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the most common heart defect? (Repeated 3X)

questions.question: Cause of ventricular septum defect in tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.explanation: E Neural crest migration — correct in intended developmental account. TOF is due to anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular/conotruncal septum; neural crest disruption can underlie it. Aortic stenosis, mitral disease and pulmonary stenosis alone do not explain the VSD pattern.
questions.sourceQuestion: Cause of ventricular septum defect in tetralogy of Fallot? (Repeated 3X)

questions.question: If there is a problem in the endocardium cushion material which of the following will happen?
questions.explanation: C ASD — likely intended, but under-specified. Endocardial cushion defects classically produce AV septal (endocardial cushion) defects, not generic ASD. TOF/transposition are conotruncal; mitral stenosis is not the typical defect. Key “ASD” is too broad; best precise answer absent.
questions.sourceQuestion: If there is a problem in the endocardium cushion material which of the following will happen? (Repeated)

questions.question: What forms the aortic valve during embryonic life?
questions.explanation: A — Endocardial cushions of the outflow tract. Conotruncal cushions and intercalated swellings remodel into aortic valve leaflets. D names the region in broad embryology terminology, while A is the better tissue answer. B forms trabeculated atrium and C contributes to venous inflow. Human outflow tract cell atlas (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42345287/)
questions.sourceQuestion: What forms the aortic valve during embryonic life?

questions.question: What is the most common type of embryological cardiovascular defect in patients?
questions.explanation: B VSD — correct under standard prevalence teaching. ASD, PDA, coarctation and TOF are common defects but less frequent than VSD in many series; prevalence varies by surveillance and case definitions.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the most common type of embryological cardiovascular defect in patients?

questions.question: What is present in tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.explanation: A Enlarged RV — correct. RV hypertrophy is one of TOF’s four features. Aortic regurgitation, ASD and aortic stenosis are not defining; aorta overrides the septum rather than simply originating wholly from RV.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is present in tetralogy of Fallot?

questions.question: What is the main cause of tetralogy of fallot?
options: Decrease of the migration of the neural crest
originating of Aorta from the left atrium
less pressure in the right ventricle
questions.explanation: A Reduced/abnormal neural crest migration — acceptable. TOF results from malalignment of the conotruncal septum, often associated with neural crest defects. The distractors do not describe accepted mechanisms.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the main cause of tetralogy of fallot?

questions.question: Which of the following complications is present in Tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.sourceIssue: The corrected booklet accepts multiple answers: A and C. Self-check; excluded from single-answer grading.
questions.explanation: A and C — correct (multiple select). TOF includes pulmonary stenosis and VSD, along with overriding aorta and RV hypertrophy. PDA and ASD are not defining components.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following complications is present in Tetralogy of Fallot?

questions.question: What is the main cause of right ventricular hypertrophy in Tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.explanation: B Pulmonary stenosis — correct. RV pressure overload causes compensatory hypertrophy. Overriding aorta and VSD are associated but not the principal pressure-load cause; systemic hypertension is not the lesion.
questions.sourceQuestion: What is the main cause of right ventricular hypertrophy in Tetralogy of Fallot?

questions.question: A 6-day-old newborn with a diagnosis of patent ductus arteriosus undergoes surgery to ligate the ductus arteriosus. During the repair, the surgeon takes special care to avoid injury to a closely related nerve. The surgeon is protecting which of the following nerves?
questions.explanation: D Left recurrent laryngeal nerve — correct. It loops under the arch of aorta beside the ductus arteriosus/ligamentum arteriosum. Left vagus is the parent nerve; right recurrent nerve loops under right subclavian; phrenic nerves are not endangered at ductal ligation.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 6-day-old newborn with a diagnosis of patent ductus arteriosus undergoes surgery to ligate the ductus arteriosus. During the repair, the surgeon takes special care to avoid injury to a closely related nerve. The surgeon is protecting which of the following nerves?

questions.question: A 50-year old woman had an ECG. The results indicated a thickened right ventricle. Other data indicated that the patient had severely decreased arterial O2 content and equal systolic pressure in both ventricles. What condition is present?
questions.explanation: B Tetralogy of Fallot — correct. VSD equalizes ventricular systolic pressures, RV hypertrophy and low arterial oxygen fit right-to-left shunting from TOF. Isolated septal defect/valve lesions/PDA do not explain the combination.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 50-year old woman had an ECG. The results indicated a thickened right ventricle. Other data indicated that the patient had severely decreased arterial O2 content and equal systolic pressure in both ventricles. What condition is present?

questions.question: Which of the following conditions leads to an aorta coming from the right ventricle and a pulmonary trunk coming from the left ventricle?
questions.explanation: B Transposition — correct. In d-TGA the aorta arises from RV and pulmonary trunk from LV. The other listed lesions do not switch the great arteries.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following conditions leads to an aorta coming from the right ventricle and a pulmonary trunk coming from the left ventricle?

questions.question: Which of the following is a cause for the tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.explanation: D Displacement of aorticopulmonary septum — correct. Anterosuperior displacement causes TOF. RV hypertrophy, VSD and overriding aorta are consequences/components; cushion defect is more associated with AV septal defect.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is a cause for the tetralogy of Fallot?

questions.question: Which of the following structures are involved in the closure of foramen ovale at the time of birth?
questions.explanation: A Septum primum and secundum — correct. After birth, higher LA pressure presses septum primum against secundum. Other listed structures do not form the foramen ovale valve.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following structures are involved in the closure of foramen ovale at the time of birth?

questions.question: What forms the membranous portion of the interventricular septum?
questions.explanation: D Anterior endocardial cushion — incomplete/ambiguous key. The membranous IV septum forms through fusion of conotruncal (bulbar) ridges with endocardial cushions and muscular septum; both superior and inferior cushions contribute. Septa primum/secundum/spurium are atrial. Single cushion option is not a complete answer.
questions.sourceQuestion: What forms the membranous portion of the interventricular septum?

questions.question: Which of the following is a cyanotic congenital heart disease?
questions.explanation: B Tetralogy of Fallot — correct. Right-to-left shunting commonly causes cyanosis. ASD and coarctation are generally acyanotic initially; dextrocardia alone is not a cyanotic lesion.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is a cyanotic congenital heart disease?

questions.question: A fetus has abnormal development of the left atrium. Normally, which embryological structure becomes incorporated into the posterior wall of the left atrium?
questions.explanation: C Pulmonary veins — correct. Incorporation of pulmonary veins forms smooth posterior LA. Bulbus/primitive ventricle/truncus and sinus venosus have other derivatives.
questions.sourceQuestion: A fetus has abnormal development of the left atrium. Normally, which embryological structure becomes incorporated into the posterior wall of the left atrium?

questions.question: A newborn develops severe cyanosis shortly after birth. Echocardiography reveals a single arterial trunk leaving the heart and supplying both the systemic and pulmonary circulations. Which developmental process most likely failed?
options: Incorporation of the pulmonary veins into the left atrium
Fusion of the septum primum and septum secundum
Formation of the muscular interventricular septum
Neural crest cell migration forming the aorticopulmonary septum
questions.explanation: E Neural crest migration forming aorticopulmonary septum — correct. Failure to divide truncus arteriosus causes persistent truncus arteriosus. Other choices produce atrial/AV/septal or pulmonary venous abnormalities, not a common arterial trunk.
questions.sourceQuestion: A newborn develops severe cyanosis shortly after birth. Echocardiography reveals a single arterial trunk leaving the heart and supplying both the systemic and pulmonary circulations. Which developmental process most likely failed?

questions.question: What explains the presence of a double aortic arch?
questions.explanation: C — Intended, with imprecise wording. Double aortic arch results from persistence of the right dorsal aorta distal to the right subclavian origin alongside the left arch. C is the closest choice if “right distal aorta” refers to that segment. A/B name the wrong arches, D refers to the left distal sixth arch (ductus arteriosus), and E describes an intersegmental vessel. Pharyngeal arch developmental anatomy (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10602722/)
questions.sourceQuestion: What explains the presence of a double aortic arch?

questions.question: The ductus arteriosus is a vital structure during fetal development that connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta. From which aortic arch does the ductus arteriosus form?
questions.explanation: B Left sixth arch distal part — correct. It forms ductus arteriosus; right distal sixth regresses, left proximal sixth forms left pulmonary artery, fourth arch contributes systemic arch/subclavian portions, truncus forms arterial roots.
questions.sourceQuestion: The ductus arteriosus is a vital structure during fetal development that connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta. From which aortic arch does the ductus arteriosus form?

questions.question: The proximal part of the left 6th aortic arch will form?
questions.explanation: B Left pulmonary artery — correct. Proximal left sixth arch forms left pulmonary artery; ductus is distal left sixth. Right pulmonary artery derives proximal right sixth; left subclavian vein is unrelated.
questions.sourceQuestion: The proximal part of the left 6th aortic arch will form?

questions.question: Which of the following will cause a double arch of aorta?
options: Presence of the distal part of the right 4th aortic arch.
Presence of the distal part of the right 6th aortic arch.
questions.explanation: A Persistent distal right fourth arch — intended, but imprecise. Double aortic arch classically reflects persistence of right dorsal aorta distal to the right seventh intersegmental artery, not simply distal right fourth arch. Other options do not create a complete double arch. Flag wording/key ambiguity.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following will cause a double arch of aorta?

questions.question: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around the right subclavian artery. What is the embryological basis for this nerve placement?
options: Distal part of the sixth aortic arch disappears on the right side
Right vagus nerve lies initially anterior to the hilum and right subclavian artery
Fourth aortic arch on the right side forms the subclavian artery
Third aortic arch forms the branches of the arch of the aorta
Right recurrent laryngeal nerve originated from the right phrenic nerve
questions.explanation: A — Regression of the distal right sixth arch. This releases the right recurrent laryngeal nerve to ascend and ultimately hook around the right subclavian artery. C correctly identifies the source of the proximal right subclavian but does not describe the asymmetric regression driving the change. B is an initial positional description, D is not the mechanism, and E gives the wrong parent nerve.
questions.sourceQuestion: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around the right subclavian artery. What is the embryological basis for this nerve placement?

questions.question: A patient presents with double aorta. Which of the following abnormally persisted?
questions.explanation: D Right fourth arch — best among offered, but incomplete. Persistence of right dorsal aorta (not the right fourth arch alone) causes double arch. Other arches listed have normal derivatives or are unrelated. Key imprecise.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient presents with double aorta. Which of the following abnormally persisted?

questions.question: The 6th left aortic arch forms?
questions.explanation: A Ductus arteriosus — correct for distal left sixth arch. The proximal segment forms left pulmonary artery; right subclavian is mainly right fourth arch/seventh intersegmental artery; left subclavian from left seventh intersegmental artery.
questions.sourceQuestion: The 6th left aortic arch forms?

questions.question: What embryological defect would cause shortness of breath and dysphagia:
questions.explanation: B Double aortic arch — correct. Vascular ring compresses trachea and esophagus causing dyspnea/dysphagia; dextrocardia and left SVC do not typically compress both.
questions.sourceQuestion: What embryological defect would cause shortness of breath and dysphagia:

questions.question: The double arch of the aorta is often characterized by a vascular ring around the trachea and esophagus. Which one of the following structures is responsible for it?
options: The persistence of the right 4th aortic arch
questions.explanation: D Persistence of right fourth arch — intended but incomplete. The vascular ring requires persistent right dorsal aorta distal to the right subclavian origin, yielding a second arch. Coarctation and other arches/PDA do not cause classic double arch. Same terminology issue as Q1.
questions.sourceQuestion: The double arch of the aorta is often characterized by a vascular ring around the trachea and esophagus. Which one of the following structures is responsible for it?

questions.question: A newborn infant has difficulty breathing and swallowing. Radiographic examination reveals constrictions of both the trachea and esophagus in the same plane. Which of the following congenital malformations is the most likely cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: A Double aortic arch — correct. A complete ring constricts trachea/esophagus. Other choices do not encircle both structures.
questions.sourceQuestion: A newborn infant has difficulty breathing and swallowing. Radiographic examination reveals constrictions of both the trachea and esophagus in the same plane. Which of the following congenital malformations is the most likely cause of this condition?

questions.question: Which aortic arch(es) forms the pulmonary arteries?
options: Distal part of the left 6th aortic arch
Proximal part of the left 6th aortic arch
Proximal parts of the left and right 6th aortic arch
questions.explanation: E Proximal parts of both sixth arches — correct. These form right and left pulmonary arteries. Distal left sixth forms ductus; fourth arch and seventh intersegmental artery have systemic derivatives.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which aortic arch(es) forms the pulmonary arteries? (Repeated)

questions.question: An infant presents with chronic breathing problems, recurrent respiratory infections, and severe feeding difficulties. Imaging reveals a complete vascular ring compressing the trachea and esophagus. Which embryological abnormality leads to a double aortic arch?
options: Persistence of the embryonic right and left second aortic arches
Regression of the left fourth aortic arch with persistence of the right fourth arch
Persistence of both right and left fourth aortic arches
Persistence of right sixth aortic arch
Failure of the fifth aortic arch
questions.explanation: C Persistence of both fourth arches — accepted shorthand, but technically persistence of right dorsal aorta plus left arch creates double arch. Remaining choices do not produce the vascular ring. Key simplified/inexact.
questions.sourceQuestion: An infant presents with chronic breathing problems, recurrent respiratory infections, and severe feeding difficulties. Imaging reveals a complete vascular ring compressing the trachea and esophagus. Which embryological abnormality leads to a double aortic arch?

questions.question: Which embryological arch are the common carotid arteries and a part of the internal carotid arteries derived from?
questions.explanation: B Third arch — correct. It forms common carotid arteries and proximal internal carotids; first/second arches regress or contribute other structures, fourth forms arch/subclavian segments, sixth pulmonary arteries/ductus.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which embryological arch are the common carotid arteries and a part of the internal carotid arteries derived from?

questions.question: Which of the following cells forms the thin gas exchange surface in the alveoli?
questions.explanation: D Type I pneumocytes — correct. They form the thin alveolar gas-exchange lining. Type II cells secrete surfactant; club cells line bronchioles; macrophages phagocytose; brush cells are sensory.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following cells forms the thin gas exchange surface in the alveoli?

questions.question: During which week of development is the blood-air barrier fully formed?
questions.explanation: C — 28 weeks is the booklet’s expected milestone. Thinning of the respiratory epithelium and close capillary contact begin in the canalicular period and progress during the saccular stage. B is far too early, A precedes typical functional maturation, and D is later than the expected teaching landmark. Wording: “fully formed” has no universal week. Human fetal lung morphometry (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2771524/)
questions.sourceQuestion: During which week of development is the blood-air barrier fully formed?

questions.question: The trachea is lined by pseudostratified squamous epithelium, what is the embryological origin of this epithelium?
questions.explanation: A Endoderm — correct. Respiratory epithelial lining derives from foregut endoderm. Mesoderm makes cartilage, muscle, connective tissue/vessels; neural tube is unrelated.
questions.sourceQuestion: The trachea is lined by pseudostratified squamous epithelium, what is the embryological origin of this epithelium?

questions.question: Smooth muscle and cartilage of primary bronchi are derived from which of the following sources?
questions.explanation: C and D — Splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm. These are synonyms in this context and both choices describe the origin of bronchial cartilage and smooth muscle. A/E do not form these tissues and B supplies the mucosal epithelium. Multiple correct choices.
questions.sourceQuestion: Smooth muscle and cartilage of primary bronchi are derived from which of the following sources?

questions.question: A newborn baby girl presents with tachypnea, nasal flaring and cyanosis shortly after birth. She is diagnosed with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following cell types is responsible for reducing the alveolar surface tension to prevent the collapsing of the lung?
questions.explanation: D Type II pneumocyte — correct. They secrete surfactant to lower surface tension. Type I gas-exchange lining; club cells secrete bronchiolar products, not alveolar surfactant; brush cells and elastic fibers do not make surfactant.
questions.sourceQuestion: A newborn baby girl presents with tachypnea, nasal flaring and cyanosis shortly after birth. She is diagnosed with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following cell types is responsible for reducing the alveolar surface tension to prevent the collapsing of the lung?

questions.question: Which of the following is caused by Oligohydramnios?
questions.explanation: A Lung hypoplasia — correct. Oligohydramnios limits fetal lung expansion and may cause pulmonary hypoplasia. ASD, low surfactant, and esophageal fistula are not direct defining outcomes.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is caused by Oligohydramnios?

questions.question: Which of the following represents the terminal sac stage ?
questions.printedAnswer: B (Mentioned 26 in the slides but was written 28 in the exam)
questions.explanation: B — 28 weeks is a typical saccular-stage example. A (16 weeks) is around the pseudoglandular-to-canalicular transition. C (36 weeks) lies near the late saccular-to-alveolar transition and can overlap depending on the staging convention. Wording: stages overlap.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following represents the terminal sac stage ?

questions.question: Which of the following is the beginning of the terminal (end of canalicular) where a premature baby may survive ?
questions.printedAnswer: C (Mentioned 26 in the slides but was written 28 in the exam)
questions.explanation: C — 28 weeks is the intended saccular-stage answer. B (16 weeks) is too early for gas exchange. A (22 weeks) is still canalicular in conventional staging, though survival at that age is possible with intensive neonatal care. The saccular transition is often taught around 24–26 weeks, so 28 weeks is an approximate exam answer. Periviable birth cohort (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2832617)
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following is the beginning of the terminal (end of canalicular) where a premature baby may survive ?

questions.question: A baby was born prematurely at 28 weeks. Which one of the following statements is correct for the survival of a premature baby at this stage?
options: The lung is in pseudo glandular stage
The lung is in canalicular stage
Respiration is active Alveoli are matured
The lung is in terminal sac stage
questions.printedAnswer: D (Mentioned 26 in the slides but was written 28 in the exam)
questions.explanation: D Terminal sac stage — acceptable at 28 weeks. Terminal sacs and surfactant-producing type II cells support survival, though survival depends on maturity/care. Pseudoglandular is earlier; canalicular is usually before terminal sac; mature alveoli are not yet fully developed.
questions.sourceQuestion: A baby was born prematurely at 28 weeks. Which one of the following statements is correct for the survival of a premature baby at this stage?

questions.question: What may be the result of insufficient amniotic fluid in embryonic life?
questions.explanation: C Retarded lung development — correct. Oligohydramnios can restrict thoracic expansion and cause pulmonary hypoplasia. Listed cardiac lesions are not the expected consequence.
questions.sourceQuestion: What may be the result of insufficient amniotic fluid in embryonic life?

questions.question: A premature delivery was performed. A medical student was aware of the problem of lung development in a premature baby. Which one corresponds to the beginning of the terminal sac (or end of canalicular stage) of lung development so that an infant may likely to survive a premature delivery?
questions.explanation: B 26 weeks — correct in standard teaching. Terminal sacs begin around 26 weeks; 18–22 weeks are too early in conventional framing; 36 weeks is later. Survival is not guaranteed at this boundary.
questions.sourceQuestion: A premature delivery was performed. A medical student was aware of the problem of lung development in a premature baby. Which one corresponds to the beginning of the terminal sac (or end of canalicular stage) of lung development so that an infant may likely to survive a premature delivery?

questions.question: A newly born infant chokes and coughs when fed with milk, and a capsule endoscope cannot pass through into the esophagus and an esophageal atresia was present. Which of the following congenital abnormalities is present?
questions.explanation: B Tracheoesophageal fistula — likely. Esophageal atresia commonly coexists with TE fistula, causing choking/coughing with feeds. TOF/PDA/diaphragmatic hernia do not explain esophageal discontinuity; polyhydramnios is an association, not the anomaly.
questions.sourceQuestion: A newly born infant chokes and coughs when fed with milk, and a capsule endoscope cannot pass through into the esophagus and an esophageal atresia was present. Which of the following congenital abnormalities is present? (Repeated)

questions.question: A neonate suffers from lung retardation due to external compression in the uterus by which of the following?
questions.explanation: C Oligohydramnios — correct. Reduced fluid can compress fetus and restrict lung growth. Polyhydramnios is excess fluid; other options do not explain uterine compression.
questions.sourceQuestion: A neonate suffers from lung retardation due to external compression in the uterus by which of the following?

questions.question: Low amniotic fluid is clinically defined as which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: B Oligohydramnios — correct. It means abnormally low amniotic fluid. Polyhydramnios/hydramnios mean excess; anhydramnios means absent fluid (more severe).
questions.sourceQuestion: Low amniotic fluid is clinically defined as which of the following conditions?

questions.question: During early embryonic development (around week 4), the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) appears as an outgrowth. From which primary embryonic germ layer does the epithelial lining of the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and alveoli originate?
questions.explanation: C Endoderm — correct. Foregut endoderm makes respiratory epithelium from larynx to alveoli. Mesoderm forms supportive tissues; ectoderm/neural crest do not line the respiratory tract.
questions.sourceQuestion: During early embryonic development (around week 4), the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) appears as an outgrowth. From which primary embryonic germ layer does the epithelial lining of the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and alveoli originate?

questions.question: A pathology resident is examining lung sections from a human fetus. The bronchi and terminal bronchioles are present, surrounded by loose mesenchyme, but no respiratory bronchioles or alveoli are yet formed. Which weeks of gestation correspond to this pseudoglandular stage?
questions.sourceIssue: The corrected booklet accepts multiple answers: C/B (Doubled Key). Self-check; excluded from single-answer grading.
questions.explanation: C 5–16 weeks — correct. Pseudoglandular stage forms conducting airways through terminal bronchioles but no respiratory bronchioles/alveoli. B is canalicular; D/E terminal sac/alveolar; A is too early.
questions.sourceQuestion: A pathology resident is examining lung sections from a human fetus. The bronchi and terminal bronchioles are present, surrounded by loose mesenchyme, but no respiratory bronchioles or alveoli are yet formed. Which weeks of gestation correspond to this pseudoglandular stage?

questions.question: Right at the beginning of the development of the diaphragm (week 4), where is it Located?
questions.explanation: B C3–C5 — correct. The septum transversum begins cervical (roughly C3–C5), then descends as the embryo elongates. Other spinal levels are not the initial position.
questions.sourceQuestion: Right at the beginning of the development of the diaphragm (week 4), where is it Located?

questions.question: A 1 month old infant presents to your clinic with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. A defect in formation of which of the following caused this hernia?
questions.explanation: B Pleuroperitoneal membrane — correct. Failure of closure, commonly posterolateral, causes congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Esophageal mesentery forms crura; lateral body-wall ingrowth and central tendon contribute other components.
questions.sourceQuestion: A 1 month old infant presents to your clinic with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. A defect in formation of which of the following caused this hernia?

questions.question: A new-born was diagnosed as having a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The abdominal contents were seen in thorax. Which of the following structures is associated with this developmental problem?
questions.explanation: C Pleuroperitoneal membrane — correct. It closes the pericardioperitoneal canals; failure permits abdominal contents into thorax. Other diaphragm components are not the usual posterolateral hernia defect.
questions.sourceQuestion: A new-born was diagnosed as having a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The abdominal contents were seen in thorax. Which of the following structures is associated with this developmental problem?

questions.question: A defect in which of the following would lead to a congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
options: Muscle ingrowth from the body wall
questions.explanation: A Pleuroperitoneal membrane — correct. The posterolateral defect is classically Bochdalek hernia. Body-wall muscle and central tendon defects are not the usual cause.
questions.sourceQuestion: A defect in which of the following would lead to a congenital diaphragmatic hernia?

questions.question: The reason that abdominal contents move to the thorax is due to a defect in?
questions.explanation: A Pleuroperitoneal membrane — correct. Incomplete closure leaves communication between abdominal and thoracic cavities. Other options form crura/central tendon but do not typically cause this defect.
questions.sourceQuestion: The reason that abdominal contents move to the thorax is due to a defect in?

questions.question: Why is the diaphragm innervated by intercostal nerves?
options: A major part is derived from the intercostal muscle.
Intercostal nerves give rise to the diaphragm.
A part of the diaphragm comes from the lateral wall muscles.
The diaphragm is derived partly from the pleuroperitoneal membrane.
questions.explanation: C — Intended association with lateral body-wall contribution. The phrenic nerves supply all diaphragmatic motor fibres and central sensation. Lower intercostal nerves carry sensation from the periphery. A overstates the contribution, B gives a nerve as the tissue source, and D names a structural primordium without explaining innervation. Underspecified: the stem needs to specify peripheral sensation.
questions.sourceQuestion: Why is the diaphragm innervated by intercostal nerves? (Repeated 4x)

questions.question: What will the persistence of the left anterior cardinal vein give rise to?
questions.explanation: A Double SVC — correct. Persistence of left anterior cardinal/common cardinal venous channels can create persistent left SVC. Other choices describe unrelated IVC, arterial, or ductal anomalies.
questions.sourceQuestion: What will the persistence of the left anterior cardinal vein give rise to?

questions.question: Which of the following vessels forms the ductus venosus bypassing the liver?
questions.explanation: D Left umbilical vein — correct. Ductus venosus channels placental blood from left umbilical vein to IVC bypassing hepatic sinusoids. Other listed veins do not provide this fetal route.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following vessels forms the ductus venosus bypassing the liver?

questions.question: Which vein bypasses the liver to reach the heart during fetal life?
questions.explanation: C Left umbilical vein — keyed wording is inaccurate. The ductus venosus bypasses most liver circulation; the umbilical vein enters it and then blood reaches IVC/heart. It does not itself bypass liver. Other veins do not fit. No option names the ductus venosus.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which vein bypasses the liver to reach the heart during fetal life?

questions.question: Which of the following will cause a double superior vena cava ?
options: Presence of left anterior cardinal vein.
Presence of right anterior cardinal vein.
questions.explanation: A Persistence of left anterior cardinal vein — correct in intended sense. The left anterior cardinal system regresses normally except for cross-connection; persistence can leave a left SVC and double SVC. Other options do not explain this anomaly.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following will cause a double superior vena cava ?

questions.question: The left brachiocephalic vein is larger than the right one as it comes from which of the following embryological structures?
questions.explanation: B Anterior communicating vein — correct. The transverse anastomosis between anterior cardinal veins forms the left brachiocephalic vein. Other listed channels contribute different veins.
questions.sourceQuestion: The left brachiocephalic vein is larger than the right one as it comes from which of the following embryological structures?

questions.question: A surgeon found a double IVC in a patient at the OR. This is due to what?
questions.explanation: D Left postrenal supracardinal vein — correct. Persistence yields left-sided IVC, sometimes with duplicated IVC. Other listed veins form different segments/portal system.
questions.sourceQuestion: A surgeon found a double IVC in a patient at the OR. This is due to what?

questions.question: Which vein is connected to ductus venosus to bypass portal circulation?
questions.explanation: C Left umbilical vein — correct. It connects to ductus venosus, shunting placental blood around hepatic sinusoids. Vitelline veins form portal/hepatic components; right umbilical regresses.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which vein is connected to ductus venosus to bypass portal circulation?

questions.question: The right IVC occurs due to:
options: Persistence of the left postrenal supracardinal vein
Persistence of the right prerenal subcardinal vein
Persistence of the right postrenal supracardinal vein
Persistence of the left prerenal subcardinal vein
questions.explanation: C Right postrenal supracardinal vein — correct. It forms the infrarenal IVC. Other choices represent anomalous left-sided or different segments.
questions.sourceQuestion: The right IVC occurs due to:

questions.question: The doctor saw a second SVC. Where would it drain?
questions.explanation: B Coronary sinus — correct. Persistent left SVC commonly drains into coronary sinus then right atrium. Other vessels are not the usual route.
questions.sourceQuestion: The doctor saw a second SVC. Where would it drain?

questions.question: If two inferior vena cavae are present, where does the second IVC drain?
questions.explanation: D Left renal vein — correct. A duplicated/left IVC commonly crosses via left renal vein into the right IVC. Other options do not describe its usual drainage.
questions.sourceQuestion: If two inferior vena cavae are present, where does the second IVC drain?

questions.question: You open the chest and you find a vessel that opens to the coronary sinus, what is this structure called?
questions.explanation: A Left SVC — correct. Persistent left SVC drains to coronary sinus in most cases. Other listed vessels do not normally open there.
questions.sourceQuestion: You open the chest and you find a vessel that opens to the coronary sinus, what is this structure called?

questions.question: A medical student was performing a dissection on a cadaver only to find a left superior vena cava but no right superior vena cava. What is the connection between the left superior vena cava to the right side of the heart? (How does it drain into the right side?)
questions.explanation: D Coronary sinus — correct. Persistent left SVC usually drains through coronary sinus to right atrium. IVC, azygos and hemiazygos are not the usual connection.
questions.sourceQuestion: A medical student was performing a dissection on a cadaver only to find a left superior vena cava but no right superior vena cava. What is the connection between the left superior vena cava to the right side of the heart? (How does it drain into the right side?)

questions.question: In a routine dissection on a cadaver, a medical student found a double inferior vena cava. The persistence of left inferior vena cava is possible as a result of existence of which of the following veins?
options: Right infrarenal component of subcardinal vein
Left infrarenal component of supracardinal vein
Right suprarenal component of supracardinal vein
questions.explanation: C Left infrarenal supracardinal component — correct. Persistence of the left supracardinal vein can form a left IVC/duplicated IVC. Other choices do not supply the left infrarenal channel.

questions.question: The left brachiocephalic vein develops from the anastomosis between which structure?
questions.explanation: A Anterior cardinal veins — correct. Their cross-anastomosis forms left brachiocephalic vein. Posterior, subcardinal, supracardinal systems form other venous segments; C/E duplicate.
questions.sourceQuestion: The left brachiocephalic vein develops from the anastomosis between which structure?

questions.question: Which of the following happens when the left sacro-cardinal vein fails to lose its connection with the left subcardinal vein?
questions.explanation: A Double IVC — intended; phrasing “left sacro-cardinal” is nonstandard. Persistence of left supracardinal/posterior venous channel can produce duplicated IVC. SVC/aortic anomalies are unrelated; “left IVC” alone is a related but less complete label.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following happens when the left sacro-cardinal vein fails to lose its connection with the left subcardinal vein?

questions.question: Which of the following contributes to the development of a major part of superior vena cava?
options: Part of left anterior cardinal vein
Part of right anterior cardinal vein
Part of right posterior cardinal vein
questions.explanation: C Part of right anterior cardinal vein — correct. Right anterior cardinal plus right common cardinal forms most SVC. Left-sided counterpart normally regresses; posterior cardinal is not the principal SVC source.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following contributes to the development of a major part of superior vena cava?

questions.question: A patient has double superior vena cava, which of the following persistent causes this condition?
questions.explanation: A Left anterior cardinal vein — correct. Persistence produces left SVC, often in addition to right SVC. Other named systems do not.
questions.sourceQuestion: A patient has double superior vena cava, which of the following persistent causes this condition?

questions.question: Which of the following form the renal segment of inferior vena cava?
options: Anastomosis between the two subcardinal veins
questions.explanation: B Subcardinal–supracardinal anastomosis — correct. It forms renal IVC segment. Other options form alternative segments or are not the renal cross-connection.
questions.sourceQuestion: Which of the following form the renal segment of inferior vena cava?

questions.question: Portal vein develops from the
questions.explanation: D Right vitelline vein — correct. Vitelline veins form portal venous system (with remodeling). Cardinal and umbilical veins have other derivatives.
questions.sourceQuestion: Portal vein develops from the

questions.question: Hepatic segment of inferior vena cava develops from:
questions.explanation: A Right vitelline vein — correct. Its hepatocardiac channel forms hepatic IVC segment. Subcardinal/supracardinal veins form prerenal/postrenal components.
questions.sourceQuestion: Hepatic segment of inferior vena cava develops from:

questions.question:
SAQ & Clinical Scenarios
Physiology
SAQ 1) An 80-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after
fainting during a church service. Her ECG trace in the emergency department is shown in the
accompanying image. Which of the following answer choices best describes the irregularity noted on this
patient's ECG?
A) Atrial fibrillation
B) Premature atrial complexes
C) Second-degree heart block type I
D) Second-degree heart block type II
E) Third-degree heart block
questions.sourceExplanation: C — Second-degree AV block, Mobitz I. The strip shows grouped beats and a nonconducted P wave after increasing PR intervals. A (atrial fibrillation) lacks organized P waves. B (premature atrial complexes) would show early atrial beats. D (Mobitz II) has a fixed PR before dropped beats, and E (complete AV block) shows independent atrial and ventricular rhythms.

questions.question: SAQ 2) What are points A and B representing?
questions.printedAnswer:
A: Bradycardia on expiration
B: Tachycardia on inspiration
questions.sourceExplanation: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia reflects vagal modulation: vagal tone rises during expiration (slowing the heart) and falls during inspiration (speeding it).

questions.question:
SAQ 3) Dixon, a 63-year-old man presented to the ER with progressive shortness of breath for the last
five years. He fatigues easily and has lost all his energy to do anything. He also complains of anorexia.
Last night he awoke suddenly from sleep because of shortness of breath and developed a dry cough. The
breathing problem improved when he sat on the edge of his bed for an hour. Previously, he had
myocardial infarction, mitral stenosis and hypertension. He generally sleeps with two, sometimes three
pillows. He has not experienced chest pain, leg pain or fainting spells. His CXR showed enlarged heart
with pulmonary congestion. He is taking Digitalis (cardiac glycoside, an inotropic agent) and Furosemide
tablets (diuretic) for his ongoing condition.
1. What is your diagnosis?
questions.sourceExplanation: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, pulmonary congestion and cardiomegaly support decompensated heart failure.

questions.question: 2. Why does he fatigue easily?
questions.caseText:
SAQ 3) Dixon, a 63-year-old man presented to the ER with progressive shortness of breath for the last
five years. He fatigues easily and has lost all his energy to do anything. He also complains of anorexia.
Last night he awoke suddenly from sleep because of shortness of breath and developed a dry cough. The
breathing problem improved when he sat on the edge of his bed for an hour. Previously, he had
myocardial infarction, mitral stenosis and hypertension. He generally sleeps with two, sometimes three
pillows. He has not experienced chest pain, leg pain or fainting spells. His CXR showed enlarged heart
with pulmonary congestion. He is taking Digitalis (cardiac glycoside, an inotropic agent) and Furosemide
tablets (diuretic) for his ongoing condition.
questions.sourceExplanation: Reduced cardiac reserve limits the ability to increase cardiac output during activity, causing fatigue.

questions.question: 3. What is the reason for shortness of breath?
questions.caseText:
SAQ 3) Dixon, a 63-year-old man presented to the ER with progressive shortness of breath for the last
five years. He fatigues easily and has lost all his energy to do anything. He also complains of anorexia.
Last night he awoke suddenly from sleep because of shortness of breath and developed a dry cough. The
breathing problem improved when he sat on the edge of his bed for an hour. Previously, he had
myocardial infarction, mitral stenosis and hypertension. He generally sleeps with two, sometimes three
pillows. He has not experienced chest pain, leg pain or fainting spells. His CXR showed enlarged heart
with pulmonary congestion. He is taking Digitalis (cardiac glycoside, an inotropic agent) and Furosemide
tablets (diuretic) for his ongoing condition.
questions.sourceExplanation: Raised left-sided filling pressure increases pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure and causes congestion or edema.

questions.question: 4. How does Digitalis (as an inotropic agent) work?
questions.printedAnswer:
Digitalis bonds to ATPase (Na-K pump) and inhibits it, thus sodium is retained inside the
cardiomyocytes and do not leave the cell. This affects the Na-Ca exchanger that normally brings sodium and let
calcium out. Due to the high concentration of sodium inside, morecalcium accumulates inside the cell
improving heart contractility
questions.caseText:
SAQ 3) Dixon, a 63-year-old man presented to the ER with progressive shortness of breath for the last
five years. He fatigues easily and has lost all his energy to do anything. He also complains of anorexia.
Last night he awoke suddenly from sleep because of shortness of breath and developed a dry cough. The
breathing problem improved when he sat on the edge of his bed for an hour. Previously, he had
myocardial infarction, mitral stenosis and hypertension. He generally sleeps with two, sometimes three
pillows. He has not experienced chest pain, leg pain or fainting spells. His CXR showed enlarged heart
with pulmonary congestion. He is taking Digitalis (cardiac glycoside, an inotropic agent) and Furosemide
tablets (diuretic) for his ongoing condition.
questions.sourceExplanation: Digoxin inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, increasing intracellular Na⁺ and reducing Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange; intracellular Ca²⁺ rises and strengthens contraction.

questions.question: 5. Why do you give diuretic?
questions.printedAnswer:
To prevent pulmonary edema. Diuretics lower blood volume and arterial
pressure for hypertension.

questions.question:
SAQ 4) If the respiratory rate was 10 breaths per minute and the tidal volume was 500 ml , answer the
following questions :
1 : Calculate minute ventilation
questions.printedAnswer:
Respiratory rate x Tidal volume = minute ventilation
10 x 500 = 5000 ml
questions.sourceExplanation: Minute ventilation is respiratory rate × tidal volume: 10 × 500 = 5,000 mL/min.

questions.question: 2 : Calculate alveolar ventilation:
questions.caseText:

following questions :
questions.sourceExplanation: Alveolar ventilation is rate × (tidal volume − dead space): 10 × (500 − 150) = 3,500 mL/min.

questions.question:
SAQ 5) During normal spontaneous breathing, the respiratory parameters of a healthy 25-year-old male
are measured as: Tidal volume (VT) =500 ml and Respiratory frequency (FR) =16 breaths/min.
Following a thorax injury, breathing becomes very painful for this individual. To reduce the magnitude
of chest movement by breathing and reduce pain, the physician decides to ventilate him artificially (using
a ventilator) with a smaller tidal volume but with a higher frequency than his spontaneous breathing. His
VT is set to 250 ml and FR to 32 breaths/min. (Repeated)
1. What is Total ventilation, Alveolar ventilation, and Dead space Ventilation of this person before and
after artificial ventilation?
questions.printedAnswer:
Before artificial ventilation:
- Total ventilation: 500 × 16 = 8000 mL
- Alveolar ventilation: 350 × 16 = 5600 mL
- Dead ventilation: 150 × 16 = 2400 mL
After artificial ventilation:
- Total ventilation: 250 × 32 = 8000 mL
- Alveolar ventilation: 100 × 32 = 3200 mL
- Dead ventilation: 150 × 32 = 4800 mL
questions.sourceExplanation: At equal minute ventilation, smaller breaths waste a larger fraction in anatomic dead space: alveolar ventilation falls 5.6 to 3.2 L/min and dead-space ventilation rises 2.4 to 4.8 L/min.

questions.question: 2. What change in arterial PO2 will occur after the transition to artificial ventilation?
questions.printedAnswer: PO2 will decrease because of decreased alveolar ventilation.
questions.caseText:

questions.sourceExplanation: Lower alveolar ventilation tends to lower alveolar and arterial PO₂, assuming other conditions are stable.

questions.question: 3. What change in pulmonary vascular resistance will occur after the transition to artificial ventilation?
questions.printedAnswer:
Hypoxia (decreased PO2) will cause vasoconstriction, which would in turn increase pulmonary
vascular resistance.

questions.question:
SAQ 7) A man traveled to a high-altitude location where the barometric pressure was 580 mmHg,
compared to the normal 760 mmHg at sea level.
Q1) How does the partial pressure of inspired oxygen (PᵢO₂) change at this altitude compared to sea
level?
questions.printedAnswer:
At higher altitudes, the barometric pressure decreases, leading to a reduction in the
partial pressure of inspired oxygen.
questions.sourceExplanation: Lower barometric pressure lowers inspired oxygen partial pressure (humidified PIO₂ = 0.21 × (PB − 47)).

questions.question: Q2) What effect does this altitude have on alveolar ventilation?
questions.printedAnswer:
Alveolar ventilation increases at high altitudes due to hypoxemia, which stimulates the peripheral
chemoreceptors. These receptors signal the respiratory center to increase the rate and depth of breathing
(hyperventilation) to improve oxygen uptake.
questions.caseText:
SAQ 7) A man traveled to a high-altitude location where the barometric pressure was 580 mmHg,
compared to the normal 760 mmHg at sea level.
questions.sourceExplanation: Hypoxemia stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors and usually increases alveolar ventilation.

questions.question: Q3) How does the activity of peripheral chemoreceptors respond to this change in altitude?
questions.printedAnswer:
Peripheral chemoreceptors become more active in response to the reduced partial
pressure of oxygen in arterial blood (PaO₂). They detect hypoxemia and stimulate the respiratory center to
increase ventilation. This response helps mitigate the effects of low oxygen availability at high altitudes.
questions.caseText:
SAQ 7) A man traveled to a high-altitude location where the barometric pressure was 580 mmHg,
compared to the normal 760 mmHg at sea level.
questions.sourceExplanation: Carotid and aortic bodies increase firing as arterial oxygen falls, particularly with substantial hypoxemia.

questions.question:

questions.sourceExplanation: The listed 100.4 and 149.7 mmHg values correctly calculate humidified inspired PO₂ at PB 525 and 760 mmHg; they are not alveolar PO₂.

questions.question: Q2. What changes in regards to his peripheral chemoreceptor activity take place?
questions.printedAnswer:
His chemoreceptor activity would increase due to the hypoxia detected and would

questions.sourceExplanation: Reduced arterial oxygen activates peripheral chemoreceptors, increasing ventilatory drive.

1. Determine whether the patient has a right axis deviation, left axis deviation, or extreme axis deviation

questions.printedAnswer: Right axis deviation due to negative lead 1 and positive AVF
questions.sourceExplanation: Negative lead I with positive aVF places the frontal axis in the right-axis-deviation quadrant; confirm the absent ECG figure.

questions.question: 2. Identify the type of murmur present in this patient.

questions.sourceExplanation: The printed pulmonary-stenosis diagnosis cannot be established from the axis alone; the murmur or figure is needed.

questions.question: 3. Calculate the cardiac output.
questions.printedAnswer:
CO= SV x HR
SV= EDV-ESV , 70 ml/min - 40 ml/min = 30 ml/min
30 x 96 = 2880 ml/min

questions.sourceExplanation: Sepsis commonly causes vasodilation and reduced total peripheral resistance, with compensatory tachycardia; low preload may coexist.

Arterial oxygen 200 ml/L
Venous oxygen 100 mL/L
questions.sourceExplanation: Fick: CO = VO₂/(CaO₂−CvO₂) = 240 mL/min ÷ 100 mL/L = 2.4 L/min.

questions.question: 3. According to the P-V loop what will the effect be on cardiac output

questions.question:

increase in blood pressure]
questions.printedAnswer:
The P-V loop will be taller and narrower
Explanation: The End-systolic volume (ESV) ,corresponding to the top left
corner of the loops, will increase along the ESPVR line making the loop
taller and narrower, less stroke volume and cardiac output.

questions.question: 3.Which phase of respiration is mostly affected?
questions.caseText: SAQ 13) A patient presents with emphysema.

questions.question: 4. What type of breathing do patients with emphysema do to make breathing easier?
questions.caseText: SAQ 13) A patient presents with emphysema.
questions.sourceExplanation: Pursed-lip, slow expiration creates positive airway pressure that helps keep small airways open; shallow breathing is not the key mechanism.

questions.sourceExplanation: Aortic valve disease is plausible if the described murmur is systolic ejection, but the case does not specify the valve lesion clearly.

questions.question: 2. What is the most common cause of valvular disease, list the two most commonly damaged valves.
questions.printedAnswer:
Rheumatic fever is the most common cause. Most commonly damaged valves are aortic and mitral
valves.
questions.caseText:

significant systolic murmur. The patient was diagnosed with a valvular lesion. An ECG later reveals an

questions.sourceExplanation: Calcific degeneration is a common cause of aortic stenosis in older adults; rheumatic disease remains important globally. Aortic and mitral valves are commonly affected.

questions.question:

questions.question: SAQ 16) Give 2 factors that causes shift of VR curve
questions.printedAnswer:
1) Right atrial pressure

questions.sourceExplanation: Venous-return curve shifts mainly with mean systemic filling pressure (volume/venous tone) and resistance to venous return. Right atrial pressure sets the operating point along the curve, not its shift.

family physician had him several times to check his blood pressure; his blood pressure had been
consistently found to be in the range of 180 systolic and 118 mmHg diastolic pressures. The family
physician discussed the matter with Ahmad and asked him to follow a no salt and no coffee diet, a weight
reduction program, and daily physical exercise regimen. The physician also prescribed an
antihypertensive drug, Amlodipine.
After two weeks of taking the medication and sincerely following the instructions of the physician,
Ahmad had just finished one hour of exercise on the treadmill, got a shower, and was about to get dressed
and leave. He bent to tie his shoes and while standing up, he felt dizzy; the world started to spin, then he
blacked out and fell to the floor. The physician on-duty in the fitness center examined Ahmed, his blood
pressure was recorded to be 110/60 mmHg.
1. What are the factors that determine blood pressure?
questions.printedAnswer:
1) The degree of pressure shift in the renal output curve for salt and water
2) The level of the water and salt intake.
questions.sourceExplanation: Blood pressure is directly related to cardiac output × total peripheral resistance; renal salt/water handling and intake regulate long-term pressure.

questions.question:
SAQ 19) A person was complaining of dizziness while standing up from bed every morning. On
examination, his blood pressure was 150/95 mmHg. Further investigations revealed hyperlipidemia with
sustained increase in blood pressure 155/100 mmHg. An MRI showed significant atherosclerotic plaques
at the carotid sinus with severe renal artery stenosis.
1. While standing, what causes the dizziness in this patient?
questions.printedAnswer: Because of the decreased blood flow to the brain due to gravity pull
questions.sourceExplanation: Standing can pool blood in the legs, briefly reducing venous return and cerebral perfusion; this is plausible but not proven as the cause.

questions.question: 2. Which reflex is evoked when standing from a supine position?
questions.caseText:
SAQ 19) A person was complaining of dizziness while standing up from bed every morning. On
examination, his blood pressure was 150/95 mmHg. Further investigations revealed hyperlipidemia with
sustained increase in blood pressure 155/100 mmHg. An MRI showed significant atherosclerotic plaques
at the carotid sinus with severe renal artery stenosis.
questions.sourceExplanation: The baroreceptor reflex responds to reduced stretch on standing by increasing sympathetic tone and heart rate.

questions.question: 3. Why would this patient be irresponsive to the sit-to-stand baroreceptor reflex?
questions.printedAnswer:
As a result of the atherosclerotic plaque, the carotid sinus will be hardened and less
stretchable, thus changes in pressure will not be detected, as there will be no stretch of
baroreceptors
questions.caseText:

examination, his blood pressure was 150/95 mmHg. Further investigations revealed hyperlipidemia with
sustained increase in blood pressure 155/100 mmHg. An MRI showed significant atherosclerotic plaques
at the carotid sinus with severe renal artery stenosis.
questions.sourceExplanation: Carotid atherosclerosis may stiffen the sinus and blunt its stretch response, but does not prove absent reflexes; aortic baroreceptors remain.

questions.question: 4. What is the most prevalent form of hypertension to develop?
questions.caseText:
SAQ 19) A person was complaining of dizziness while standing up from bed every morning. On
examination, his blood pressure was 150/95 mmHg. Further investigations revealed hyperlipidemia with
sustained increase in blood pressure 155/100 mmHg. An MRI showed significant atherosclerotic plaques
at the carotid sinus with severe renal artery stenosis.
questions.sourceExplanation: Essential (primary) hypertension is the most prevalent form overall; renal artery stenosis may indicate secondary hypertension in this patient.

questions.question: 5. Name TWO types of hypertension (other than essential hypertension)?
questions.caseText:

examination, his blood pressure was 150/95 mmHg. Further investigations revealed hyperlipidemia with
sustained increase in blood pressure 155/100 mmHg. An MRI showed significant atherosclerotic plaques
at the carotid sinus with severe renal artery stenosis.
questions.sourceExplanation: “Secondary” describes cause while “malignant” describes severe/accelerated disease, so these are not parallel categories.

questions.sourceExplanation: Vasodilators and diuretics are antihypertensive medication families; treatment choice depends on the patient.

Afterload :

abdominal mass revealed a bruit. A Doppler ultrasound confirmed an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)

Q1: suggest a reason for the bruit in the auscultation?
questions.sourceExplanation: Turbulent flow through an aneurysmal segment can produce a bruit, though it is not inevitable.

was rushed to KFSH, where a doppler ultrasound confirmed that the aneurysm had increased in size (7
cm diameter).The surgeon ordered the patient to be moved to the operating room and the blood

4- Why did the surgeon want to keep the blood pressure below 90 mmHg?
questions.printedAnswer:
Because beyond 90 mm Hg, the pressure will cause an aneurysm rupture of aneurysm (the tension in
the wall is increased).
questions.sourceExplanation: Permissive hypotension can limit bleeding and wall stress before hemorrhage control in selected ruptured AAA; 90 mmHg is not a universal rupture threshold.

questions.printedAnswer: Mitral valve stenosis caused by narrowing of mitral orifice.

questions.question: 2. Give the surface marking of the mitral valve.
