questions.question:
SAQ26)
1. How is the pulmonary function test conducted?
questions.printedAnswer:
To measure the pulmonary function test, a spirometer is used. The patient is asked to inhale deeply,
hold it for a second, and then exhale as fast and hard as he can.
questions.sourceExplanation: Spirometry measures forced expiration after maximal inspiration; repeated acceptable maneuvers are standard, and a one-second hold is not essential.

questions.question: 2. What are the parameters measured during pulmonary function tests?
questions.caseText: SAQ26)
questions.sourceExplanation: FEV₁, FVC and their ratio are core spirometric measures; full pulmonary function testing may also include lung volumes and diffusion.

questions.question: 3. How do the parameters change in the obstructive pulmonary disease?
questions.printedAnswer: In obstructive disease, FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC all decrease.
questions.caseText: SAQ26)
questions.sourceExplanation: Obstruction lowers FEV₁ disproportionately, reducing FEV₁/FVC; FVC may be normal or reduced, not invariably low.

questions.question:
SAQ27) A man presents with severe vomiting, a BP of 90/40, and a heart rate of 140 BPM. What is the
effect of giving him IV fluids?
questions.sourceExplanation: IV fluid can restore circulating volume and preload after vomiting if the patient is fluid responsive and has no contraindication.

questions.question: SAQ28)How can the compliances be related to each other?
questions.sourceExplanation: Lung and chest-wall compliances combine in series: 1/CRS = 1/CW + 1/CL.

questions.question: SAQ29) Patient has bilateral pneumothorax the amount of air enter can be measured?
questions.printedAnswer: by the difference between Resting volume of CW and lung.
questions.sourceExplanation: At FRC, inward lung recoil balances outward chest-wall recoil. Their separate resting volumes explain the direction of recoil, but do not alone measure clinical pneumothorax air volume.

questions.question: SAQ30) Compliance of lungs is equal to?
questions.printedAnswer: change in volume divided by transmural pressure
questions.sourceExplanation: Lung compliance is change in volume divided by change in transpulmonary (transmural) pressure.

questions.question:
SAQ31) What is the diagnosis of the hypoxia using the parameters:
Low PaO2
High PaCO2
No arterial alveolar difference for PO2 or PCO2
questions.sourceExplanation: Low PaO₂, high PaCO₂ and a normal A–a gradient indicate hypoventilation, which lowers alveolar oxygen while retaining CO₂.

questions.question: 31. Give 2 body circulatory responses during exercise.
questions.printedAnswer:
1) Vasodilation of the active muscles to supply them with enough blood flow for exercise
2) Central command from the motor cortex triggers mass sympathetic discharge, which increases heart rate, contractility and cardiac output.
questions.sourceExplanation: Exercise increases blood flow to active muscle through local vasodilation and raises heart rate, contractility and output through central command/sympathetic drive.

questions.question: 32. Give 2 acute responses to compensated heart failure
questions.printedAnswer:
1) Activation of sympathetic reflexes cause constriction of veins which causes increase in venous return
2) Sympathetic activation also increases heart rate and contractility, increasing cardiac output.
questions.sourceExplanation: Acute sympathetic activation constricts veins and increases heart rate and contractility, temporarily supporting venous return and output; chronic activation can be harmful.

questions.question: 33. 2 ways to treat decompensated heart failure
questions.sourceExplanation: Diuretics relieve congestion; digoxin is appropriate only in selected cases and is not general first-line heart-failure therapy. The listed pair is not a complete current treatment plan.

examination reveals bilateral pitting ankle edema, and auscultation reveals crackles (rales) at the lung
bases.
Vital signs:
● Blood Pressure: 105/70 mmHg
● Heart Rate: 102 beats per minute
● Respiratory Rate: 24 breaths per minute.
The figure attached shows changes in his cardiac function curves. Black Is normal, and Red represents
changes in the patient before and after compensation.
questions.sourceExplanation: Veins have a thinner media, thicker adventitia, irregular/collapsible lumen and often valves; muscular arteries have a thicker smooth-muscle media, rounder lumen and elastic laminae. Muscle-layer counts vary by vessel.

questions.question:
SAQ 35) A 72-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a two-week history of
progressive fatigue, severe dizziness, and two recent episodes of near fainting (presyncope).
On examinations, his blood pressure is 138/82 mmHg, and his pulse is regular at 36 beats per
minute. A 12-lead ECG shows complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes,
with an atrial rate of 80 bpm and a ventricular escape rate of 36 bpm. He is diagnosed with
third-degree (complete) atrioventricular (AV) block and admitted to the cardiac care unit for
urgent temporary pacing.
Q1: Explain the concept of an "escape rhythm" in the context of a complete AV block and
describe how the intrinsic firing rates change as you move down the cardiac conduction
system.
questions.printedAnswer:
Escape rhythm acts like a backup in case of pacemaker (SA node) failure,
SA node: 60–100 beats/min
AV node: 40–60 beats/min
Bundle of His/Purkinje fibers: 20–40 beats/min
questions.sourceExplanation: An escape rhythm is a slower subsidiary pacemaker that prevents ventricular standstill when upstream impulses fail. Intrinsic rates slow down the system: SA node ~60–100, junctional ~40–60, ventricular/Purkinje ~20–40 bpm.

questions.question: Q2: Describe the difference between the two types of second-degree AV block.
questions.printedAnswer:
Mobitz I: PR interval gets longer, longer, longer then QRS drops & Mobitz II:
PR interval stays the same then QRS suddenly drops
questions.caseText:
SAQ 35) A 72-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a two-week history of
progressive fatigue, severe dizziness, and two recent episodes of near fainting (presyncope).
On examinations, his blood pressure is 138/82 mmHg, and his pulse is regular at 36 beats per
minute. A 12-lead ECG shows complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes,
with an atrial rate of 80 bpm and a ventricular escape rate of 36 bpm. He is diagnosed with
third-degree (complete) atrioventricular (AV) block and admitted to the cardiac care unit for
urgent temporary pacing.
questions.sourceExplanation: Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation before a dropped QRS; Mobitz II has unchanged PR intervals with intermittent dropped QRS complexes.

questions.question:
Q3: Compare the microscopic structural features of both Purkinje fibers of the conduction
system and working ventricular cardiomyocytes, focusing on:
● a) Cell size and color
● b) Number of desmosomes
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Purkinje are larger and paler due to glycogen when cardiomyocytes are smaller and
darker
B) purkinje has less intercalated discs while cardiomyocytes have well developed ID
with many desmosomes
questions.caseText:
SAQ 35) A 72-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a two-week history of
progressive fatigue, severe dizziness, and two recent episodes of near fainting (presyncope).
On examinations, his blood pressure is 138/82 mmHg, and his pulse is regular at 36 beats per
minute. A 12-lead ECG shows complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes,
with an atrial rate of 80 bpm and a ventricular escape rate of 36 bpm. He is diagnosed with

questions.sourceExplanation: Purkinje fibers are larger and paler because of abundant glycogen. They have fewer/smaller desmosomal junctions than working ventricular myocytes; both remain connected by intercalated discs.

questions.question:
Q4: In this patient with complete AV block, which structure normally provides the electrical
connection between the atria and ventricles? Describe its course.
questions.printedAnswer:
Its bundle of His, it originates near the AV node near the coronary sinus
opening then it goes through the fibrous skeleton, then it runs along the membranous
interventricular septum and divides into right and left bundle branches
questions.caseText:
SAQ 35) A 72-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a two-week history of
progressive fatigue, severe dizziness, and two recent episodes of near fainting (presyncope).
On examinations, his blood pressure is 138/82 mmHg, and his pulse is regular at 36 beats per
minute. A 12-lead ECG shows complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes,
with an atrial rate of 80 bpm and a ventricular escape rate of 36 bpm. He is diagnosed with
third-degree (complete) atrioventricular (AV) block and admitted to the cardiac care unit for
urgent temporary pacing.
questions.sourceExplanation: The AV bundle (His) is the normal electrical bridge through the fibrous skeleton. It runs from the AV node through the central fibrous body/membranous septum, then divides into right and left bundle branches; its origin is not specifically at the coronary sinus opening.

questions.question:
SAQ 36) A 62-year-old male with a long-standing history of untreated essential hypertension
presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden-onset, worsening
shortness of breath and a persistent cough producing pink, frothy sputum.
On physical examination, his blood pressure is 210/120 mmHg, his heart rate is 105
bpm, and bilateral pulmonary rates are heard halfway up both lung fields (indicating
pulmonary edema). An echocardiogram reveals signs of severely elevated ventricular
filling pressures with an overall reduced ejection fraction, but notable stiffening of the
left ventricular wall without any documented signs of permanent tissue remodeling.
Shortly after admission, he develops crushing retrosternal pain radiating to the inner
(medial) left arm. ECG and coronary angiography show ischemia of the anterior wall of
the left ventricle and the apex.
Q1. Describe how the patient's acute hypertensive crisis alters the appearance of his PV
loop (red dashed lines) compared to a healthy individual (green continuous line). Which
change (increased, decreased & no change) will be expected in the following
parameters?
A. End-Systolic Volume (ESV)
B. Stroke Volume (SV)
C. Peak Systolic Pressure
questions.printedAnswer:
ESV is increased, Stroke volume is decreased, and Peak systolic Pressure is
increased
questions.sourceExplanation: With acute afterload elevation, the ventricle ejects less at a higher pressure: ESV rises, SV falls, and peak systolic pressure rises. The marked dashed loop is higher and narrower than the control loop.

questions.printedAnswer:
A) Because they have narrow lumens and smooth muscle walls, producing high
resistance to blood flow.
B) Their smooth muscles adjust to lumen through active vasoconstriction and
vasodilation
questions.caseText:
SAQ 36) A 62-year-old male with a long-standing history of untreated essential hypertension
presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden-onset, worsening
shortness of breath and a persistent cough producing pink, frothy sputum.
On physical examination, his blood pressure is 210/120 mmHg, his heart rate is 105
bpm, and bilateral pulmonary rates are heard halfway up both lung fields (indicating
pulmonary edema). An echocardiogram reveals signs of severely elevated ventricular
filling pressures with an overall reduced ejection fraction, but notable stiffening of the
left ventricular wall without any documented signs of permanent tissue remodeling.
Shortly after admission, he develops crushing retrosternal pain radiating to the inner
(medial) left arm. ECG and coronary angiography show ischemia of the anterior wall of
the left ventricle and the apex.
questions.sourceExplanation: Arterioles have small lumens and substantial smooth muscle, creating high adjustable resistance. Changing their radius by vasoconstriction or dilation changes TPR and arterial pressure.

questions.question:
Q5. Trace, in order, the valve, chamber and vessels through which the raised left
ventricular filling pressure is transmitted back to the pulmonary capillaries.
questions.printedAnswer:
Left Ventricle>>Mitral Valve>>Left Atrium>>Pulmonary veins/venules

On physical examination, his blood pressure is 210/120 mmHg, his heart rate is 105
bpm, and bilateral pulmonary rates are heard halfway up both lung fields (indicating

Shortly after admission, he develops crushing retrosternal pain radiating to the inner

questions.sourceExplanation: Raised LV filling pressure transmits backward through the open mitral valve to the left atrium, pulmonary veins, and pulmonary capillaries.

questions.question:
Q6. The heart rate is 105 bpm.
a. Name the pacemaker
b. Give its location
c. Name the blood supply
d. State where the sympathetic preganglionic fibers arise from
questions.printedAnswer:
A) SA node
B) Subepicardial at the junction of the Superior Vena Cava and the Right Atrium
C) 60% from the Right coronary artery, 40% from the left circumflex artery
D) They arise from the lateral horns of the upper thoracic spinal cord segments
(T1-T4/T5)
questions.caseText:
SAQ 36) A 62-year-old male with a long-standing history of untreated essential hypertension
presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden-onset, worsening
shortness of breath and a persistent cough producing pink, frothy sputum.
On physical examination, his blood pressure is 210/120 mmHg, his heart rate is 105
bpm, and bilateral pulmonary rates are heard halfway up both lung fields (indicating
pulmonary edema). An echocardiogram reveals signs of severely elevated ventricular
filling pressures with an overall reduced ejection fraction, but notable stiffening of the
left ventricular wall without any documented signs of permanent tissue remodeling.
Shortly after admission, he develops crushing retrosternal pain radiating to the inner
(medial) left arm. ECG and coronary angiography show ischemia of the anterior wall of
the left ventricle and the apex.
questions.sourceExplanation: The SA node lies subepicardially near the SVC–right atrium junction. Its arterial supply varies (usually RCA, sometimes LCx); a fixed 60/40 split is not universal. Cardiac sympathetic preganglionic neurons arise around T1–T5.

questions.question: Q7. Name the artery most likely occluded.
questions.printedAnswer:
Left anterior descending artery/ LAD
Anatomy

questions.question:
SAQ 1) A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department after experiencing chest pain and
difficulty breathing while playing golf. He reported a tingling sensation on the medial side of his left arm.
Upon evaluation at the hospital, he was diagnosed with a myocardial infarction and advised to undergo
coronary artery bypass surgery
1. Identify the artery that is obstructed in the provided angiographic image.
questions.sourceExplanation: The angiographic target is the LAD. Its anterior interventricular course and territory make it a common culprit in anterior-wall infarction.

questions.question: 2. Specify the two regions that are affected by the arterial blockage.
questions.printedAnswer: Anterior two thirds of interventricular septum, Anterior wall of Left ventricles
questions.caseText:
SAQ 1) A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department after experiencing chest pain and
difficulty breathing while playing golf. He reported a tingling sensation on the medial side of his left arm.
Upon evaluation at the hospital, he was diagnosed with a myocardial infarction and advised to undergo
coronary artery bypass surgery
questions.sourceExplanation: LAD branches supply the anterior LV and anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum.

questions.question: 3. Explain the reasons behind the patient’s difficulty in breathing and dizziness.
questions.printedAnswer:
Difficulty in breathing is due to reduced cardiac output to supply bronchial circulation in lungs.
Dizziness is caused by decreased perfusion to the brain due to inadequate cardiac output during the
myocardial infarction.
questions.caseText:
SAQ 1) A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department after experiencing chest pain and
difficulty breathing while playing golf. He reported a tingling sensation on the medial side of his left arm.
Upon evaluation at the hospital, he was diagnosed with a myocardial infarction and advised to undergo
coronary artery bypass surgery
questions.sourceExplanation: LV ischemia can reduce forward output and raise pulmonary venous pressure, causing dyspnea; reduced cerebral perfusion can cause dizziness. Reduced bronchial blood supply is not the usual explanation for breathlessness.

questions.question:
4. Based on the anatomical basis, describe how a myocardial infarction can result in symptoms on the
medial side of the arm.
questions.printedAnswer:
The referred pain to the medial side of the arm occurs due to the shared nerve pathways
between the heart and the arm.
The heart and the medial side of the arm are both innervated by spinal segments T1-T4, leading to
referred pain during myocardial infarction.
questions.caseText:
SAQ 1) A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department after experiencing chest pain and
difficulty breathing while playing golf. He reported a tingling sensation on the medial side of his left arm.
Upon evaluation at the hospital, he was diagnosed with a myocardial infarction and advised to undergo
coronary artery bypass surgery
questions.sourceExplanation: Visceral cardiac pain afferents travel with sympathetics to upper thoracic spinal segments (about T1–T5). Convergence with somatic input from the medial arm causes referred pain.

questions.question: 5. List the pathophysiological factors contributing to myocardial infarction.
questions.printedAnswer:
Reduced oxygen supply due to anemia or hypoxia, Increased oxygen demand due to
physical exertion or stress.
questions.caseText:
SAQ 1) A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department after experiencing chest pain and
difficulty breathing while playing golf. He reported a tingling sensation on the medial side of his left arm.
Upon evaluation at the hospital, he was diagnosed with a myocardial infarction and advised to undergo
coronary artery bypass surgery
questions.sourceExplanation: MI occurs when myocardial oxygen supply falls below demand. Coronary atherothrombosis is common; anemia/hypoxemia reduce supply, while exertion or stress raises demand.

questions.question: 6. Name one vessel that can be utilized for coronary artery bypass surgery.
questions.printedAnswer: The great saphenous vein/ internal thoracic artery
questions.caseText:
SAQ 1) A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department after experiencing chest pain and
difficulty breathing while playing golf. He reported a tingling sensation on the medial side of his left arm.
Upon evaluation at the hospital, he was diagnosed with a myocardial infarction and advised to undergo
coronary artery bypass surgery
questions.sourceExplanation: The great saphenous vein or internal thoracic artery can be used as a coronary bypass conduit.

questions.question: 7. Explain the reason behind the irregular rhythm that may be observed on an ECG.
questions.printedAnswer:
Since LAD is obstructed, no supply to the anterior IVS which houses the right and left bundle branches.
If those branches are blocked, ventricular function is deteriorated thus resulting in an abnormal rhythm
on ECG.
questions.caseText:
SAQ 1) A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department after experiencing chest pain and
difficulty breathing while playing golf. He reported a tingling sensation on the medial side of his left arm.
Upon evaluation at the hospital, he was diagnosed with a myocardial infarction and advised to undergo
coronary artery bypass surgery
questions.sourceExplanation: LAD septal branches supply parts of the conduction system, so ischemia may cause conduction disturbance or arrhythmia. It does not necessarily deprive both bundle branches completely.

questions.question:
SAQ 2) During a cardiac surgery procedure, a surgeon must identify and avoid damaging the
structure that carries the right branch of the atrioventricular bundle within the right
ventricle.
1. Name the structure that contains the right bundle branch in the right ventricle.
questions.sourceExplanation: The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) carries the right bundle branch across the right ventricle toward the anterior papillary muscle.

questions.question: 2. Name the artery that supplies the right bundle branch.
questions.caseText:
SAQ 2) During a cardiac surgery procedure, a surgeon must identify and avoid damaging the
structure that carries the right branch of the atrioventricular bundle within the right
ventricle.
questions.sourceExplanation: The LAD and its septal perforators are a major blood supply to the bundle branches, though contributions vary.

questions.question: 3. Which condition do you expect if this artery is blocked?
questions.caseText:
SAQ 2) During a cardiac surgery procedure, a surgeon must identify and avoid damaging the
structure that carries the right branch of the atrioventricular bundle within the right
ventricle.
questions.sourceExplanation: Occlusion can cause myocardial ischemia or infarction in the supplied territory and may impair conduction; infarction is a possible consequence, not inevitable from every isolated occlusion.

questions.question:
SAQ 3) During a coronary artery bypass graft surgery, the internal thoracic arteries are harvested. After
their removal, which arteries primarily supply the anterior thoracic wall and intercostal spaces?
questions.sourceExplanation: Posterior intercostal arteries supply much of the thoracic wall, but anterior intercostal supply normally comes from internal thoracic branches (or their musculophrenic/superior epigastric continuations). The printed answer is incomplete after bilateral internal thoracic harvest.

questions.question: SAQ 4) PIA runs with which vein:
questions.sourceExplanation: If PIA means posterior interventricular artery, it typically accompanies the middle cardiac vein. If it means posterior intercostal artery, it accompanies posterior intercostal veins; the abbreviation is ambiguous.

questions.question: SAQ 5) What is the arrow pointing towards?
questions.sourceExplanation: The arrowed vessel is the LAD in the anterior interventricular sulcus.

questions.question: SAQ 6) In case of Myocardial ischemia, trace the path of the catheter dye inserted for angiography:
questions.sourceExplanation: Selective left coronary angiography opacifies the left main coronary artery and its branches, including LAD and circumflex; the printed route naming only LAD is incomplete.

questions.question: SAQ 7) During surgery, the student cut the vein that’s close to LAD. What is it?
questions.sourceExplanation: The great cardiac vein runs beside the LAD in the anterior interventricular sulcus.

questions.question: SAQ 8) Right coronary artery dominant means that:
questions.printedAnswer: PIA originates from the right coronary artery
questions.sourceExplanation: Right coronary dominance means the posterior interventricular artery (PDA/PIA) arises from the RCA.

questions.question: SAQ 9) Innervation of the external cricothyroid is by the
questions.sourceExplanation: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid. The printed answer “inferior laryngeal nerve” is incorrect.

questions.question: SAQ 10) the external laryngeal nerve is damaged. Which structure is first affected?
questions.sourceExplanation: The external laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid; injury first weakens vocal-fold tension and high-pitch phonation.

questions.question:
SAQ 11) Answer the following questions:
1. What branches does this artery give?
questions.printedAnswer: Anterior Interventricular Artery (LAD) and Circumflex Artery
questions.sourceExplanation: The left main coronary artery divides into the LAD (anterior interventricular) and circumflex arteries.

questions.question: 2. What damage to the heart results from the occluded Artery?
questions.printedAnswer: Left atrium, Left ventricle, Anterior 2/3rd of the interventricular septum and moderator band
questions.caseText: SAQ 11) Answer the following questions:
questions.sourceExplanation: Left-main occlusion can affect the LV, parts of the LA, and anterior two-thirds of the septum; exact territory depends on lesion level and collateral flow. Moderator-band involvement is not guaranteed.

questions.question:
3. Define coronary dominance and relate the clinical importance of this concept in relation to the
occlusion shown in the Angiogram.
questions.printedAnswer:
In 80% of cases the PIA comes from the right coronary artery (Right Dominance) and this helps by
compensating and supplying the heart in case the LAD or the Left coronary artery is blocked.
-This patient most probably has a left dominance (PIA comes from Left Coronary Artery) so that when
his left coronary artery was blocked, he lost both branches the LAD and PIA and therefore he died.
questions.caseText: SAQ 11) Answer the following questions:
questions.sourceExplanation: Dominance is defined by which coronary system gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery. Left dominance means it arises from circumflex. This does not reliably compensate for LAD/left-main occlusion or predict death; the printed rationale is wrong.

questions.question: 4. Explain the mechanism of the cough.
questions.printedAnswer:
1) Air rapidly inspired
2) Epiglottis closes and vocal cords shut tightly
3) Abdominal Muscles contract pushing against diaphragm and Intercostal Muscles Contract.
4) Epiglottis and Vocal Cords Suddenly Open Exploding the air.
questions.caseText: SAQ 11) Answer the following questions:
questions.sourceExplanation: Cough involves inspiration, glottic closure and pressure buildup by expiratory muscles, then glottic opening with forceful expiration. Epiglottic closure is not required.

questions.question: 5. Which of the following is located at the 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line?
questions.caseText: SAQ 11) Answer the following questions:
questions.sourceExplanation: The cardiac apex normally lies at the left fifth intercostal space near the midclavicular line.

questions.question: Q3. What are the muscles that cover the intercostal nerves?
questions.printedAnswer: the internal intercostal muscle and innermost intercostal muscles

questions.question: Q4. What is the term used for the condition in which multiple ribs are fractured?
questions.caseText:
SAQ 12) A 65-year-old female patient presents to the emergency department after falling from her chair
at home. She reports a sudden onset of sharp chest pain on the left side, especially when breathing deeply
or coughing. The patient has difficulty taking deep breaths and exhibits shortness of breath.
questions.sourceExplanation: Flail chest requires a free, unstable segment, typically from multiple adjacent ribs fractured in multiple places; fractures alone do not define it.

questions.question:
SAQ 13) 25-year-old male who was stabbed in the chest during a mugging is brought to the emergency
room in a semiconscious state, gasping for air (Dyspnea). On examination, a knife was seen penetrating
the anterior thoracic wall at the level of the fourth intercostal space along the left sternal border. His
blood pressure was 90/40 mm/Hg, heart sounds seemed distant, and he appeared cyanotic. A working
diagnosis of cardiac tamponade was made, and the patient was sent for treatment.
Q1. Name the layers of the pericardium in between which this fluid was trapped.
questions.sourceExplanation: Tamponade fluid collects in the pericardial cavity between parietal serous pericardium and visceral serous pericardium (epicardium).

questions.question: Q2. Mention the nerves supplying the different layers of pericardium.
questions.printedAnswer:
The phrenic nerve innervates the fibrous pericardium. The autonomic nervous system
innervates the visceral pericardial layer.
questions.caseText:
SAQ 13) 25-year-old male who was stabbed in the chest during a mugging is brought to the emergency
room in a semiconscious state, gasping for air (Dyspnea). On examination, a knife was seen penetrating
the anterior thoracic wall at the level of the fourth intercostal space along the left sternal border. His
blood pressure was 90/40 mm/Hg, heart sounds seemed distant, and he appeared cyanotic. A working
diagnosis of cardiac tamponade was made, and the patient was sent for treatment.
questions.sourceExplanation: The phrenic nerves provide sensory supply to fibrous and parietal serous pericardium. Visceral pericardium receives autonomic innervation.

questions.question: Q3. Give the blood supply of pericardium.
questions.printedAnswer: Internal thoracic vessels and descending aorta
questions.caseText:
SAQ 13) 25-year-old male who was stabbed in the chest during a mugging is brought to the emergency

Q1. What is meant by a “murmur”?
questions.printedAnswer:
An abnormal sound heard ,caused by turbulent blood flow
within the heart or major blood vessels
questions.sourceExplanation: A murmur is an audible sound produced by turbulent blood flow across the heart or great vessels.

questions.question:

questions.question: C. Suggest a reason for your choice.

The second right interspace (orange circle) is where you hear the aortic valve. The intern placed it on the

questions.caseText:

dizziness (syncope) and ‘bluish fingers’ (cyanosis) when he attempts to start an exercise program for the

sample of pleural fluid. The resident inserts the needle near the lower border of the 8th rib at the right
anterior axillary line and withdraws small quantity of pleural fluid. The next day, during your rounds,
the patient complains of tingling and numbness of the skin of his chest at the level of the 8th rib down
toward the midline above the umbilicus on the right side.

questions.sourceExplanation: The needle crossed the intercostal neurovascular bundle near the inferior border of the rib, injuring the intercostal nerve.

and a 100-pack-year tobacco history. On ultrasound, an aneurysm at the early part of the thoracic aorta

Fragmentation of elastic lamellae, loss of smooth muscle, and accumulation of amorphous extracellular
matrix in media
questions.sourceExplanation: Thoracic aortic media contains elastic lamellae, smooth muscle and matrix; aneurysmal degeneration may show elastic fragmentation, smooth-muscle loss and matrix accumulation.

questions.question: Q3) Describe what is a bronchopulmonary segment.
questions.printedAnswer:
It is a structurally separate and functionally independent unit of the lung tissue. Each lung contains
about 8-10 bronchopulmonary segments, each containing: its own segmental bronchus and a branch of
the pulmonary artery, and share the lymphatics and pulmonary veins
questions.caseText:

questions.sourceExplanation: A bronchopulmonary segment is a surgically separable lung unit supplied by a segmental bronchus and pulmonary arterial branch; pulmonary veins run between segments. Segment count is usually 10 right and 8–10 left.

questions.question: Q1. A problem in the endocardial cushion material, which of the following will be affected?

SAQ 1)
1) What is cell 3?
questions.sourceExplanation: Endocardial cushion defects classically cause an atrioventricular septal/canal defect; mitral abnormalities can accompany it, but “mitral valve” alone is incomplete.

questions.question:
Q2. End of canalicular stage and start of terminal sac stage is important for viability of a premature
born. At which week does this lung development occurs?
questions.sourceExplanation: The terminal sac stage begins at about 26 weeks in standard timelines, with overlap and course-specific rounding to 28 weeks; the printed value is a convention, not a sharp boundary.

questions.question: Q3. Reason for Respiratory Distress Syndrome.:
questions.printedAnswer: Problem in surfactant production from Type II pneumocytes
questions.sourceExplanation: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is caused by inadequate surfactant from immature type II pneumocytes, increasing alveolar surface tension.

questions.question: Q4. Most common embryological defect:
questions.sourceExplanation: Ventricular septal defect is the conventional answer for the most common congenital heart defect, though prevalence depends on cohort and definition.

questions.question: Q5. Origin of smooth part of right atrium:
questions.sourceExplanation: The smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum) derives from the right horn of the sinus venosus.

questions.question: Q6. What is the origin of the heart?
questions.sourceExplanation: The heart develops from splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm in the cardiogenic region.

questions.question: Q7. When does the embryo’s heart start beating?
questions.sourceExplanation: The embryonic heart begins beating around day 22, near the end of week 3.

questions.question: Q8. Reason for the foramen ovale to close?
questions.printedAnswer: Increased pressure in the left atrium
questions.sourceExplanation: After birth, increased pulmonary flow raises left atrial pressure above right atrial pressure, functionally apposing septum primum against septum secundum.

questions.question: Q9. What is the cause of ventricular septum defect in tetralogy of fallot?
questions.sourceExplanation: Tetralogy of Fallot results from anterosuperior malalignment of the conotruncal septum, producing a VSD and associated outflow changes; neural crest abnormalities can contribute but are not the sole explanation in every case.

questions.question:
Q10. A baby is born with the left ventricle facing the right side. He is said to have dextrocardia. Why
does this happen?
questions.printedAnswer: Bulbus cordis loops on the left side
questions.sourceExplanation: Dextrocardia results when the heart tube loops abnormally leftward instead of the normal rightward loop, placing the apex on the right; “bulbus cordis loops” is shorthand.

questions.question:
A) What part of the conducting system is shown in the image?
B) Give one identification point
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Bronchiole
B) Lack of hyaline cartilage/ lack of seromucous acini/ lack of submucosa
questions.sourceExplanation: A, bronchiole of the respiratory conducting system. B, its folded wall has smooth muscle and lacks cartilage and submucosal glands, which distinguish it from a bronchus.

questions.question:
A) What cells are visible in the microscope?
B) Give two histological characteristics
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Cardiac Muscle Cell Tissue
B) Intercalated discs and branching of the cells
questions.sourceExplanation: A, cardiomyocytes. B, branching striated cells and dark transverse intercalated discs distinguish cardiac muscle.

questions.question:
A) Identify the artery indicated in the picture
B) Give one identification point
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Small muscular artery
B) Internal Elastic Lamina (IEL)
questions.sourceExplanation: A, small muscular artery. B, a distinct wavy internal elastic lamina and concentric smooth-muscle layers distinguish it from the thinner-walled accompanying vein.

questions.question:
A) Name the layer indicated by X
B) Give the function of Y
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Respiratory mucosa layer
B) Goblet cells: secrete mucus
questions.sourceExplanation: X is the respiratory mucosa lining the airway. Y is a goblet cell, which secretes mucins that form particle-trapping mucus.

questions.question:
A) Identify the capillary shown in this image.
B) Give one identifying feature of this capillary
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Continuous capillary
B) Pericyte ‘hugging’ it/continuous endothelium
questions.sourceExplanation: Continuous capillary. The endothelial layer and basal lamina are uninterrupted, without fenestrae. A pericyte supports the outside wall, but pericytes alone do not define this type.

questions.question:
A) Identify structure A.
B) State its function.
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Purkinje fibers.
B) Conducts action potential under endocardium.
questions.sourceExplanation: Purkinje fibres are the pale, large subendocardial cells. They rapidly distribute impulses through the ventricular myocardium.

questions.question:
A) Identify the type of blood vessel shown.
B) Give one identification point.

A) Large Elastic artery
B) Many fenestrated elastic laminae
questions.sourceExplanation: Elastic artery. Numerous wavy fenestrated elastic lamellae in its media stretch during systole and recoil in diastole.

questions.question:
A) Name the layer indicated by X.
B) Give the function of Y
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Respiratory mucosa
B) Secrete mucus
questions.sourceExplanation: X brackets respiratory mucosa, with epithelium and underlying connective tissue. Y indicates submucosal seromucous gland tissue. Mucous cells supply mucins and serous cells add a watery secretion.

questions.question:
A) What type of cell is indicated by X?
B) What is its function?
Answers
A) Type II pneumocyte
B) Produces surfactant for alveoli to prevent them from collapsing.
A) Name the structure shown in the slide.
B) Give one identification point.
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Bronchiole
B) Lack of hyaline cartilage, thick layer of smooth muscle.
questions.sourceExplanation: First image (p. 274): Type II pneumocyte, a plump cell at a septal junction. It releases surfactant, reducing surface tension and the tendency of alveoli to collapse. Second image (p. 275): Bronchiole. The folded lining and surrounding smooth muscle are visible, with no supporting cartilage plates.

questions.question:
A) What cells are visible in the microscope?
B) Give two histological characteristics
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Cardiac Muscle Cell Histology
B) Intercalated disks & branching of the cells
questions.sourceExplanation: Cardiac myocytes. Branching fibres and intercalated discs are the two requested features.

questions.question:
A) Name the cells pointed at with number 2
B) What’s the function of these cells?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Type 2 alveolar cell / type 2 pneumocytes
B) Surfactant secretion
questions.sourceExplanation: Type II pneumocytes. Their plump profiles stand out from the attenuated type I lining. They secrete surfactant.

questions.question:
A) What is the function of the structure pointed by black arrow
B) What is structure X
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Production of pericardial fluid, phagocytosis, and acts as an antigen presenting cell
B) Coronary artery
questions.sourceExplanation: The arrow identifies epicardial mesothelium, which contributes lubricating serous fluid. X is a coronary artery in subepicardial connective tissue. The key’s extra immune functions are secondary to the requested surface function.

questions.question:
A) Identify and name both A and B
B) Give one identification point for A
questions.printedAnswer:
A) A- Capillary, B- Small muscular artery
B) Capillaries have a single layer of endothelial cells
questions.sourceExplanation: A is keyed as a capillary, identified by a thin endothelial wall without a smooth-muscle media. The image alone gives limited evidence to separate it from a small venule. B has the muscular wall of a small artery.

questions.question:
A) identify the structure pointed at and name its function
B) name the organ shown in this slide
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Hyaline cartilage. It functions to keep the airway open and prevent collapse
B) Trachea
questions.sourceExplanation: The arrow points to hyaline cartilage, which holds the lumen open. A broad cartilage ring and respiratory mucosa fit trachea.

questions.question:
A) Identify the structure pointed by the arrow.
B) Name two identification points.
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Respiratory bronchiole (you can see the wall made up of cuboidal epithelium and some alveoli)
B) presence of smooth muscle / cuboidal cells / lack of cartilage
questions.sourceExplanation: Respiratory bronchiole. Alveoli interrupt segments of cuboidal bronchiolar lining and smooth muscle. This distinguishes it from a terminal bronchiole and an alveolar duct, whose wall consists almost entirely of alveolar openings.

questions.question:
A) identify the structure highlighted by the letter C and give two identification points
B) identify the structure highlighted by the letter D and name its function
questions.printedAnswer:
A) purkinje fibers, identification includes pale cytoplasm, large size, and striations at the periphery
B) cardiac muscle cells, function is contraction to push blood
questions.sourceExplanation: C marks Purkinje fibres, larger and paler from glycogen, with peripheral myofibrils. D is working myocardium, which generates force to eject blood.

questions.question: Name this type of epithelium
questions.sourceExplanation: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar respiratory epithelium. Nuclei at different heights create the stratified appearance.

questions.question:
A) what is the arrow pointing at
B) In which layer can this structure be found
questions.sourceExplanation: Seromucous glands lie in the airway submucosa, deep to the lining, and deliver secretion to the lumen.

questions.question:
A) Identify structure 22 and its function
B) Identify structure 23 and its function
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Pneumocyte (alveolar) type I, gas diffusion
B) Pneumocyte (alveolar) type II, producing surfactant and regeneration
A) Is the given image a bronchiole or bronchus?
questions.sourceExplanation: The key assigns 22 to type I pneumocyte (thin gas-exchange lining) and 23 to type II (surfactant and epithelial repair). The thin processes and plump profiles are the distinguishing clues. Individual nuclear profiles in this low-resolution figure are hard to verify independently.

questions.question:
A) Is the given image a bronchiole or bronchus?
B) What are differentiating features between a bronchiole or bronchus?
C) Identify structures 1 through 4
D) What type of epithelium is present at E?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Bronchus
B) Bronchioles lack cartilage and glands
C) 1- cartilage, 2- vessels, 3- glands, 4- smooth muscle
D) Ciliated pseudostratified epithelium, goblet cells present as well
questions.sourceExplanation: Bronchus, because it has cartilage plates and submucosal glands, both absent from bronchioles. 1 supports the wall (cartilage), 2 are vessels, 3 are seromucous glands, and 4 is smooth muscle. E is ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells.

questions.question:
A) Identify the region marked X
B) Identify the region marked Y
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Alveolar duct
B) Alveolar Sacs
questions.sourceExplanation: X is an alveolar duct, an elongated passage opening into alveoli along its length. Y marks terminal alveolar sacs, common chambers into which clusters of alveoli open.

questions.question:
A) Name the cells marked with the red arrow
B) Name the function of these cells
C) How abundant are they?
D) Name the congenital condition where these cells are absent
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Pneumocyte type II
B) Secrete surfactants
C) 60% of the alveolar cells
D) Respiratory distress syndrome
questions.sourceExplanation: Type II pneumocytes, cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant. They account for roughly 60% of alveolar epithelial cells by count, using the booklet’s rounded split. Incorrect premise: neonatal respiratory distress syndrome typically reflects insufficient surfactant production from immature type II cells. The cells need not be absent. NHLBI (https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/respiratory-distress-syndrome)

questions.question:
A) Name the cells marked with the blue arrows
B) State the function of these cells
C) How abundant are they?
D) What is the type of these cells?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Pneumocyte type I
B) Gas exchange
C) 40% of alveolar cells
D) Squamous Epithelum
questions.sourceExplanation: Type I pneumocytes, thin simple squamous alveolar epithelial cells adapted for diffusion. About 40% of the epithelial cells by the booklet’s approximation, they cover about 95% of the surface. LungMAP cell atlas (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9202574/)

questions.question:
A) Identify the cells marked with the green arrows
B) What is the function of these cells?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Alveolar macrophages
B) Clean inspired air
questions.sourceExplanation: Alveolar macrophages phagocytose deposited particles, microbes and cell debris in the alveoli.

questions.question:
A) Identify the cells marked with the red arrow
B) Name the location of these cells
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Mesothelial cells
B) Visceral pleura
questions.sourceExplanation: Mesothelial cells form the simple squamous surface of the visceral pleura covering the lung.

questions.question:
A) Identify the structure shown
B) Arrow is pointing at the cilia and asking about its function
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Trachea
B) Sweep fluids and foreign particles out of the airway so that they stay out of the lungs
questions.sourceExplanation: Hyaline cartilage and respiratory mucosa identify the trachea. Ciliary beating moves mucus and trapped particles toward the pharynx.

questions.question:
A) Name the structures X and Y indicated by the arrows
B) What is the function of Y
questions.printedAnswer:
A) X: Type 1 pneumocyte; Y: Type 2 pneumocyte
B) Synthesize surfactant
questions.sourceExplanation: X is the thin type I lining suited for diffusion. Y is the plumper type II pneumocyte that synthesizes surfactant.

questions.question:
A) What is this structure?
B) Mention its function
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Arteriole
B) Controls blood flow to organs
questions.sourceExplanation: Arteriole. Its small lumen with a thin circumferential smooth-muscle coat lets it vary resistance and local blood flow.

questions.question:
A) Name the artery
B) Give the main identification of this artery
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Aorta
B) 30-40 circular smooth muscle + fenestrated elastic lamellae
questions.sourceExplanation: Aorta, an elastic artery. Its media has numerous fenestrated elastic lamellae alternating with smooth muscle. The lamellae are a stronger clue than a fixed count of muscle layers.

questions.question:
A) Name the structure shown
B) Give 2 features of this epithelium
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Bronchiole
B) Bronchioles lack cartilage and glands compared to bronchus
questions.sourceExplanation: Bronchiole. Incomplete key: absent cartilage and glands describe the wall. For the requested epithelium, name its ciliated lining and relatively low columnar-to-cuboidal cells, with club cells increasingly prominent distally.

questions.question:
A) What is the name of structure no. 2?
B) What is the function of structure no. 3?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Endocardium
B) Conduct action potentials to the ventricles
questions.sourceExplanation: 2 is endocardium. 3 contains subendocardial Purkinje fibres that rapidly transmit impulses to working ventricular muscle.

questions.question: What is this vessel and state its function?
questions.printedAnswer: Arteriole- resistance vessel- controls the flow of blood to the capillary
questions.sourceExplanation: Arteriole. A small round lumen and muscular wall allow contraction to regulate flow into capillary beds.

questions.question: Which one has keratin filaments (A, B, and D) name it and where is it found in C
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Desmosome
C) intercalated discs in cardiac myocytes
questions.sourceExplanation: A shows a desmosome with dense plaques, a junction occurring at cardiac intercalated discs in C. B and D do not show that paired-plaque arrangement. Wording correction: epithelial desmosomes anchor cytokeratin. Cardiac desmosomes anchor desmin. Cardiac desmosome microscopy study (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6416832/)

questions.question: What is the name slide B of this and where is it found (on the model)?
questions.sourceExplanation: Olfactory mucosa, at model site 3 in the superior nasal cavity. This specialized epithelium contains olfactory receptor neurons.

questions.question: Which epithelium is found in the frontal sinus? Mention the name
questions.sourceExplanation: Respiratory epithelium, generally pseudostratified ciliated columnar. Cilia move mucus toward the ostium.

questions.question: What drains into the middle meatus?
questions.printedAnswer: Frontal, maxillary, middle and anterior ethmoidal
questions.sourceExplanation: Frontal, maxillary, anterior ethmoidal and middle ethmoidal drainage reaches the middle meatus. Posterior ethmoidal drainage reaches the superior meatus and the sphenoid drains to the sphenoethmoidal recess.

questions.question:
What is the function of the structure in black (arrow was towards trachealis)?
A) Decrease diameter of trachea
B) Decrease diameter of esophagus
C) Decrease diameter of secondary bronchus
questions.sourceExplanation: A — Trachea narrows. The trachealis bridges the posterior ends of the tracheal cartilage and reduces tracheal diameter when it contracts. B names the adjacent oesophagus and C a different airway level.

questions.question: Identify Structure marked by arrow:
questions.sourceExplanation: Purkinje fibres. The cells are pale and lie near the ventricular lining.

questions.question: Name the first layer involved in the passage of Oxygen during inspiration:
questions.sourceExplanation: O₂ first encounters the surfactant-bearing alveolar liquid film before traversing type I epithelium, basement membrane and capillary endothelium.

questions.question: Name the structure below:
questions.sourceExplanation: Bronchiole. Its low lining and wall without cartilage plates help distinguish it from bronchus.

questions.question: Name the following layer:
questions.sourceExplanation: The vessel type is small muscular artery. If “layer” is literal, the conspicuous circumferential smooth muscle is tunica media immediately outside the internal elastic lamina.

questions.question:
Which of the following is found in the aorta:
A) A
B) B
questions.sourceExplanation: A — Aortic pattern. A shows layered elastic tissue typical of the aortic media. B shows rounded cells in lacunae, a cartilage pattern.

questions.question: Which one is a resistance vessel?
questions.sourceExplanation: A has the relatively thick smooth muscle and small round lumen of an arteriole. B has the thinner wall and less round lumen of a venule.

questions.question:
A) What is the function of this layer at arrow A?
B) Identify the layer at B
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Vasoconstriction
B) Internal elastic lamellae
questions.sourceExplanation: A is the muscular layer, which constricts the lumen. B is the internal elastic lamina at the intima–media boundary.

questions.question:
A) what is the process marked by the blue arrow?
B) What is the histological name of the cell marked by A?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Expiration (getting rid of CO2)
B) Capillary endothelium
questions.sourceExplanation: CO₂ diffuses from blood to alveolar air and is then exhaled. Precision: the arrow depicts diffusion across the barrier. Expiration is the subsequent movement of gas out of the lungs. A is capillary endothelium, the thin blood-facing lining.

questions.question:
A) Identify the tissue ?
B) Where can we find it ( layer and organ)
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Cardiac muscle
B) Myocardium of the heart
questions.sourceExplanation: Myocardial cardiac muscle, identified by branching striated fibres and intercalated discs.

questions.question:
A) Identify the structure shown by arrow A
B) Where is this type of blood vessel located
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Elastic fiber
B) Large arteries such as the Aorta
questions.sourceExplanation: Elastic fibre/lamella. Such abundant elastic material is typical of the media of large elastic arteries such as the aorta.

questions.question: Identify one cell and its function and where is this found?
questions.printedAnswer: Type one pneumocyte , gas exchange located in the lung
questions.sourceExplanation: A type I pneumocyte lines lung alveoli. Its flattened processes minimize the diffusion distance for gas exchange.

questions.question:
Identify the epithelium indicated by the Blue arrow and mention 1 type of cell found in
this region
questions.sourceExplanation: Olfactory epithelium. An acceptable cell is the bipolar olfactory receptor neuron, whose cilia sample odorants.

questions.question: Identify where this tissue is found and give the clinical significance of the layer marked as 1
questions.sourceExplanation: Intrapulmonary bronchus, identified by cartilage and glands. Smooth muscle in layer 1 constricts the airway in asthma. The slide supports bronchus, with precise branch order harder to infer from histology alone.

questions.question:
A) Which lobe is the tumor located in?
B) The patient presented with ptosis, anhidrosis, miosis. Name the structure compressed by this.
questions.printedAnswer:
A) superior lobe of the right lung
B) sympathetic trunk/sympathetic chain
questions.sourceExplanation: A, right upper lobe. The arrow is on the patient’s right, opposite the L marker. B, the ipsilateral sympathetic chain is affected, explaining Horner syndrome through loss of sympathetic supply to the pupil, eyelids and facial sweat glands. The separate face photo illustrates the signs.

questions.question:
A) Name structure X
B) Name structure Y
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Mitral valve
B) Right ventricle
questions.sourceExplanation: X is the mitral valve between LA and the thick-walled LV. Y is the right ventricle on the other side of the septum, with a thinner wall and more trabeculated contour.

questions.question: Name structure 13, 26, 18, 7c, and 7a
questions.printedAnswer:
13: Right pulmonary artery
26: Right main bronchus
18: Superior vena cava
7c: Descending (thoracic) Aorta
7a: Ascending Aorta
questions.sourceExplanation: 13 is the right pulmonary artery crossing toward the right hilum, 26 the air-filled right main bronchus, 18 the SVC anterior/rightward, 7c descending thoracic aorta near the spine, and 7a ascending aorta anteriorly.

questions.question:
A) A patient presents with dysphagia, which structure is affected (A or B)
B) Name the structure
questions.sourceExplanation: A is the left atrium, directly anterior to the oesophagus. Enlargement can compress it. B is more anterior/rightward and lacks that close oesophageal relation.

questions.question: A) What is indicated by A, D, E, and X?
questions.printedAnswer:
A: Trachea
D: Aortic knuckle (arch)
E: Apex of the heart
X: Costodiaphragmatic angle/recess
questions.sourceExplanation: A is the tracheal air column, D the aortic knuckle on the upper left mediastinal contour, E the lower left cardiac/apical contour, and X the lateral costophrenic angle, the radiographic correlate of the costodiaphragmatic recess.

questions.question:
A) Which is the typical rib, and which is the atypical rib
B) What structure is marked with the arrow in A, and what structures run through this
questions.printedAnswer:
A) A = atypical, B = typical
B) Groove; subclavian artery
A) If you got stabbed at the 4th intercostal space, what chamber of the heart will be affected?
questions.sourceExplanation: A is an atypical first rib, broad and flattened. B is a typical curved rib. The indicated groove is for the subclavian artery posterior to the scalene tubercle. The subclavian vein lies in the anterior groove.

questions.question:
A) If you got stabbed at the 4th intercostal space, what chamber of the heart will be affected?
B) What’s the structure that is marked in green?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Right ventricle
B) Descending aorta
questions.sourceExplanation: With the intended anterior parasternal track, the right ventricle is the most exposed chamber. The green mark points to the descending thoracic aorta near the vertebral body. The exact injured structure depends on the entry point and trajectory.

questions.question:
A) Name X and Y
B) Name 2 structure that the artery labeled Y supplies
questions.printedAnswer:
A) X: Right coronary artery, Y: Posterior interventricular artery (PIA)
B) Supplies the posterior ⅓ of the interventricular septum and right ventricle
questions.sourceExplanation: X is the RCA in the right AV groove. Y is the posterior interventricular artery, which supplies the inferior/posterior third of the septum and adjacent inferior ventricular myocardium, including part of the right ventricle in the depicted pattern.

questions.question:
A) Identify what is indicated by 1 and 3
B) Which point 1, 2, 3, or 4 is the most common region for rib fracture.
questions.printedAnswer:
A) 1: neck, 3: anterior surface of the rib
B) 2
questions.sourceExplanation: 1 is the neck near the vertebral end and 3 the anterior shaft. The expected fracture site is 2, near the rib angle. 1 and 3 are away from the angle and 4 is costal cartilage.

questions.question:
Which of the labeled structures in the given PA radiograph of the chest indicates the aortic arch? (Batch?)
A) A B) B
C) C
D) D
E) E
questions.sourceExplanation: D — Aortic arch. The aortic knuckle projects to the patient’s left above the heart. A is near the trachea, B the right heart border, C the right cardiophrenic angle, and E the left ventricular contour.

questions.question:
Identify the cardiac chamber with the filling defect marked by the red arrow in the cardiac CT? (Batch?)
A) Left Ventricle
B) Right Atrium
C) Left Atrium
D) Right Ventricle
E) Ascending Aorta
questions.sourceExplanation: C — Left atrium. The filling defect is in the posterior left-sided chamber just anterior to the oesophagus. A is thicker-walled and more anterior/lateral, B is right-sided, D is anterior, and E is an arterial lumen.

questions.question:
A) Name the vessel indicated by X.
B) What is the name of the vessel running with it?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Anterior interventricular artery (LAD)
B) Great cardiac vein
questions.sourceExplanation: X is the LAD and the accompanying vein is the great cardiac vein. Both run in the anterior interventricular sulcus.

questions.question:
A) Name structure X.
B) What is the sound made by closure of this valve
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Mitral valve
B) S1 sound
questions.sourceExplanation: X is the mitral valve between LA and LV. Its closure contributes the mitral component of S1 at the start of ventricular systole.

questions.question:
A) Identify structures 1 and 7.
B) This cross section is in which section of the mediastinum?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) 1: brachiocephalic vein, 7: trachea
B) Superior mediastinum
A) A patient was stabbed at the 4th right intercostal space. Which heart chamber was most likely damaged?
questions.sourceExplanation: 1 is the left brachiocephalic vein, crossing anterior to the arterial branches. 7 is the central air-filled trachea. The veins, upper trachea and arch branches place this slice in the superior mediastinum.

questions.question:
A) A patient was stabbed at the 4th right intercostal space. Which heart chamber was most likely damaged?
B) Identify structure 7.
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Right ventricle
B) Descending aorta
questions.sourceExplanation: The intended anterior parasternal track threatens the right ventricle because it lies directly behind the sternum. 7 is the descending thoracic aorta, posterior to the heart beside the spine. A right-sided wound can reach another structure depending on the track.

questions.question:
A) What is indicated by 4 and 8?
B) What is the clinical significance of structure C?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) 4: aortic knuckle, 8: apex of the heart
B) Structure C can be used for a patient undergoing a thoracentesis procedure.
questions.sourceExplanation: 4 is the aortic knuckle and 8 the cardiac apex. C marks the costophrenic recess region where dependent pleural fluid collects. It can be accessed for thoracentesis with site selection by ultrasound.

questions.question:
A) Which lobe is the tumor located in?
B) Name 2 structure compressed by this.
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Right superior lobe
B) Right subclavian vein, brachial plexus, sympathetic trunk
questions.sourceExplanation: It is in the right upper lobe. Two neighboring structures at risk are the inferior brachial plexus and sympathetic chain. Subclavian vessels are also nearby.

questions.question:
A) Name structures 7 and 1
B) Which part of the mediastinum is this?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) 1 is left brachiocephalic vein and 7 is the trachea
B) The superior mediastinum section
questions.sourceExplanation: 7 is the trachea and 1 the left brachiocephalic vein. The trachea and brachiocephalic vein above the roots of the great vessels identify superior mediastinum.

questions.question:
A) Identify the structure where the red arrow is pointing
B) Which nerve would be endangered if the area pointed at with a yellow arrow is dilated?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Internal Thoracic Artery
B) Left Recurrent Laryngeal (arch or aorta dilation compresses it)
Typical rib, question asked to identify head and body, and where the easiest place to
fracture would be.
questions.sourceExplanation: Red marks the internal thoracic artery, which descends from the subclavian artery. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is vulnerable to dilation at the arch indicated in yellow because it loops under the arch near the ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.question:
A) Identify A and B
B) Name two things A supplies
questions.printedAnswer:
A) A- Left anterior descending artery (LAD); B- Circumflex artery
B) LAD supplies 2/3 of the anterior interventicular septum and the anterior wall of the left ventricle
questions.sourceExplanation: A is LAD, which runs toward the apex and supplies the anterior two-thirds of the septum and anterior LV wall. B is circumflex, which follows the left AV groove.

questions.question: Identify which auscultation point you would use in order to listen to a left ventricular hypertrophy
questions.printedAnswer: Red point (refers to the aortic valve)
questions.sourceExplanation: Auscultation. Incorrect premise/key. LV hypertrophy itself has no valve-specific auscultation point. The apical site is where an associated S4 can be assessed. If the intended question was an aortic stenosis murmur as a cause of LV hypertrophy, the aortic area is the right second intercostal space by the sternum. The red arrow in the figure points toward the apical area. European Society of Cardiology examination of aortic valve disease (https://www.escardio.org/communities/councils/cardiology-practice/scientific-documents-and-publications/ejournal/volume-18/physical-examination-in-aortic-valve-disease-do-we-still-need-it-in-the-modern/)

questions.question:
A) Identify this artery shown in the angiogram
B) name a branch that can be given by this artery
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Left coronary artery
B) Answers may vary. Correct answers include left circumflex, left anterior descending
questions.sourceExplanation: The left main divides into LAD and circumflex. Either branch is acceptable.

questions.question:
A) Identify which vertebra is a thoracic vertebra
B) Give two identification points
questions.printedAnswer:
A) The middle one
B) Answers may vary. Possible answers include demifacts, transverse facets, elongated spinous process going
inferiorly
questions.sourceExplanation: The middle specimen is thoracic. Rib facets on the body and transverse processes, together with a long inferiorly sloping spinous process, identify a typical example.

questions.question:
A) Name the artery shown in this angiogram
B) Name the artery which most likely gives rise to the arteries which supply the SA and A V nodes
C) Name a vessel that can be used for a coronary bypass
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Right coronary artery
B) Right coronary artery
C) Answers may vary. Correct answers include great saphenous vein and internal thoracic artery
Note: focus on if the question asks about a vein or artery.
questions.sourceExplanation: The vessel courses in the right AV groove. RCA is the most frequent source of both nodal arteries, with individual variation. Bypass examples are internal thoracic artery and great saphenous vein.

questions.question:
A) Name the part of the vein bisected by the black line
B) Into which structure does this vein drain
C) Into which portion of the mediastinum does this portion fall into
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Arch of azygous vein
B) Superior vena cava
C) Middle mediastinum
Note: Azygous vein is in posterior mediastinum but arch of azygous vein, like all other vessels draining into the
heart, is in the middle mediastinum.
questions.sourceExplanation: It passes over the right lung root and drains to the SVC. Classification varies: the key labels the terminal arch middle mediastinum. Some standard four-compartment descriptions list the arch with the superior mediastinum near the T4–T5 plane. The descending azygos trunk is posterior, and the final junction’s relation to the plane matters. Mediastinal compartment anatomy (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK539819/)

questions.question:
A) Identify structures 1 and 2
B) Identify structure 3
questions.printedAnswer:
A) 1 is right ventricle 2 is right atrium
B) tricuspid valve
questions.sourceExplanation: 1 is anterior right ventricle, 2 right atrium on the patient’s right, and 3 the tricuspid valve between them.

questions.question:
A) Identify the structure pointed at in the arrow
B) Identify which structure it arises from
C) Identify its venous drainage
D) Identify the arteries which supply the anterior part of the ribs
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Posterior intercostal artery
B) Thoracic aorta (descending aorta)
C) Azygous veins
D) Anterior intercostal arteries
questions.sourceExplanation: The arrow identifies a posterior intercostal artery, supplied by thoracic aorta at spaces 3–11. Spaces 1–2 usually come from the supreme intercostal artery. Veins drain via the azygos system. Anterior intercostals arise from internal thoracic and musculophrenic arteries.

questions.question:
A) Name the muscle shown
B) Name the complete motor nervous supply of this muscle
questions.sourceExplanation: Its dome separates thorax from abdomen. Motor supply is via the right and left phrenic nerves (C3–C5).

questions.question:
A) Identify the green structure superiorly and name its drainage
B) Identify where the structure drains
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Thoracic duct, 3/4ths of the body (lower limbs, pelvic cavity, abdominal cavity, left arm, left sides of thorax
and head OR another answer may be left jugular lymph trunk, left subclavian, lymph trunk, left
bronchomediastinal lymph trunk)
B) Drains into the junction of the left jugular vein and left subclavian vein
questions.sourceExplanation: The superior green channel is the thoracic duct. It drains both sides below the diaphragm plus the left upper quadrant above it, and normally ends at the left internal jugular–subclavian junction.

questions.question:
A) Label blood vessels 112, 113, and 117.
B) Which labelled artery supplies the AV bundle branches?
C) In a left-dominant circulation, which blood vessel gives off the posterior interventricular artery?
D) In case of damage to blood vessel 117, which parts of the heart might become necrotic?
E) Which blood vessel anastomoses with blood vessel 117
F) Name one vein that parallels blood vessel 113.
questions.printedAnswer:
A) 112 — left coronary artery
113 — Anterior interventricular artery (LAD)
117 — circumflex branch of the left coronary artery
B) Blood vessel 113 — anterior interventricular artery
C) The circumflex branch of the left coronary artery supplies part of the posterior
interventricular septum in left-dominant circulation by giving the posterior interventricular
artery.
D) Left atrium and left ventricle
E) The circumflex branch of the left coronary artery anastomoses with the terminal branches of the right
coronary artery.
F) Great cardiac vein
questions.sourceExplanation: A, 112 = left main, 113 = LAD in the anterior interventricular groove, 117 = circumflex in the left AV groove. B, LAD septal branches supply much of the bundle-branch system, with some shared supply. C, circumflex gives the PIA in left dominance. D, a circumflex lesion can affect LA and lateral/posterolateral LV, with wider inferior territory in left dominance. E, distal RCA and circumflex can anastomose in the AV groove. F, the great cardiac vein parallels LAD anteriorly.

questions.question:
A) Label blood vessels A, B, and C.
B) a. Name one branch given by blood vessel A; b. Name one vein that parallels this branch
C) Which conducting tissues will be affected in case of damage to blood vessel A?
D) In a right-dominant circulation, which artery is given by blood vessel A?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) A — right coronary artery; B — Anterior interventricular artery (LAD); C — circumflex branch of the left
coronary artery
B) a) Right marginal artery b) Small cardiac vein
C) AV and SA nodal tissue
D) In right-dominant circulation, the right coronary artery gives the posterior interventricular artery which
supplies the posterior one third of the interventricular septum.
questions.sourceExplanation: A is RCA, B LAD and C circumflex, distinguished by their right AV, anterior interventricular and left AV courses. Right marginal is an RCA branch and can run with the small cardiac vein. The SA and AV nodes are at risk where their branches arise from RCA. A right-dominant RCA gives the posterior interventricular artery.

questions.question:
A) What is the name of the main artery shown in this angiogram
B) Name 2 of the branches given off by this artery
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Right coronary artery
B) 1-Right circumflex; 2-Posterior Interventricular artery (PIA)
questions.sourceExplanation: RCA angiogram. Terminology correction. This shows RCA in the right AV groove. Examples of two branches are right (acute) marginal and posterior interventricular in a right-dominant heart. The printed “right circumflex” is not a standard name for a separate RCA branch in this setting. ACC/AHA coronary segment nomenclature (https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2014.12.018)

questions.question:
A) What is the name of the main artery shown in this angiogram
B) Name the branch (indicated by the red arrow)
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Left coronary artery
B) Left marginal artery
questions.sourceExplanation: Left coronary system, with a left marginal (obtuse marginal) branch tracking along the lateral LV wall.

questions.question:
A) Name the branch (indicated by the red arrow)
B) Mention the part of the heart that is supplied.
questions.printedAnswer:
A)Left circumflex
B)The left circumflex along with all the branches of the left coronary artery will all continue the blood supply
to the left ventricle, except for the area parallel to the posterior interventricular sulcus (supplied by PIA)
questions.sourceExplanation: Left circumflex rounds the left AV groove. Its main territory includes lateral/posterolateral LV and part of LA. Incomplete key: in left dominance it can also supply inferior myocardium and posterior septum through its PIA.

questions.question:
A) 19 year old medical student was confused as to the labels shown in the echocardiogram. He visits your
office, requesting help on the ultrasound image of the heart. Using your knowledge, Identify :-
a) X
b) Y
c) Z
d) T
e) M
f) O
B) Out of curiosity, the medical student questions about the approaches done to achieve the ultrasound imaging
of the heart. Using your knowledge, what are the approaches needed to achieve the echocardiogram?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) a) X = Left ventricle
b) Y = Mitral valve
c) Z = Tricuspid valve
d) T = Right atrium
e) M = Right ventricle
f) O = Left atrium
B) 1. Transesophageal and 2. Transthoracic (Different views-Apical/Parasternal and sub-xiphoid)
questions.sourceExplanation: X = LV (thick wall), Y = mitral valve, Z = tricuspid valve, T = RA, M = RV and O = LA. The valves divide their respective atria and ventricles. TTE uses chest windows such as apical, parasternal and subcostal. TEE images from the oesophagus.

questions.question:
A) Label structure 15 and 16
B) What is the function of 15
C) Which number is showing the aorta
D) Which number is showing the pulmonary trunk
questions.printedAnswer:
A) 15: chorda tendinae; 16: papillary muscle
B) prevents the cusps of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves from everting into the atria when the ventricles
contract
C) (5)
D) (6)
questions.sourceExplanation: 15 is chordae tendineae and 16 papillary muscle. Tension on the chordae stops AV leaflets prolapsing during systole. 5 is aorta and 6 pulmonary trunk.

questions.question:
A) Label structure 8 and 12
B) Which number is showing the tricuspid valve
questions.printedAnswer:
A) 8: right ventricle/ trabeculae carneae ; 12: mitral valve
B) 10
questions.sourceExplanation: 8 marks trabeculae carneae in the right ventricle, 12 is mitral valve, and 10 is tricuspid valve. Trabeculae are the irregular ventricular wall ridges. The tricuspid and mitral valves separate right and left atria from their respective ventricles.

questions.question:
A) Label structure X
B) Label structure Y
C) What is the function of X
questions.printedAnswer:
A) SA node
B) AV node
C) Pacemaker of heart
questions.sourceExplanation: X is the SA node at the SVC–RA junction and initiates normal sinus rhythm. Y is the AV node near the inferior interatrial septum.

questions.question:
A)What is this case called?
B)What structure will it compress?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) anneyuresm of arch of aorta
B)Compresses left recurrent laryngeal nerve
questions.sourceExplanation: The intended diagnosis is an aortic arch aneurysm. It can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and cause hoarseness because the nerve hooks under the arch. A radiograph suggests the lesion and cross-sectional imaging defines it.

questions.question:
A)What is the name of this structure during embryonic life?
B)What would happen if this structure failed to constrict and close after birth and what structure can it put in
danger?
questions.printedAnswer:
A)Ductus arteriosus
B)Patent ductus arteriosus , left recurrent nerve
questions.sourceExplanation: Ductus arteriosus connects pulmonary outflow to the aorta. Failure to close gives PDA, generally with a postnatal left-to-right shunt. The nearby left recurrent laryngeal nerve can be affected by dilation or intervention.

questions.question: Name the structures 2,4, and 6.
questions.printedAnswer:
1. Left brachiocephalic
2. right brachiocephalic
3. Brachiocephalic artery
4. left common carotid artery
5. Left subclavian artery
6. esophagus
7. trachea
questions.sourceExplanation: 2 = right brachiocephalic vein, 4 = left common carotid artery among the arch branches, 6 = oesophagus just posterior to the trachea.

questions.question:
A) Which of X or Y represents the area of the apex of the heart?
B) Where is the auscultation point of the aortic valve?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Y (at the left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line)
B) 2nd right intercostal space (near the body of the sternum)
questions.sourceExplanation: Y is the apex point at the left fifth intercostal space on or just medial to the midclavicular line. X is on the opposite side. Listen to the aortic valve at the right second intercostal space along the sternal border.

questions.question:
A) Which sulcus/ groove of the heart do the arrows point at?
B) Name another sulcus/ groove of the heart.
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Anterior interventricular sulcus (this is anterior view of heart from CAT)
B) Coronary/ atrioventricular sulcus
questions.sourceExplanation: The arrows track the anterior interventricular sulcus, between ventricles on the anterior surface. The coronary (AV) sulcus is another example and separates atria from ventricles.

questions.question:
A) Which of X or Y make up the sternocostal surface of the heart?
B) What makes up the superior border of the heart?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) X (the right ventricle makes up the sternocostal/ anterior surface)
B) Right and left atrium, and root of the great vessels
questions.sourceExplanation: X is the right ventricle, forming most of the sternocostal surface. The atria form the superior border in the standard anterior description, with great-vessel roots emerging there.

questions.question: Label the following
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Jugular Notch
B) Sternal Angle
C) Midsternal Line
D) Midclavicular Line
questions.sourceExplanation: A jugular notch is the superior depression in the manubrium. B sternal angle is the manubriosternal ridge. C midsternal line runs down the sternum’s centre. D midclavicular line runs vertically through the clavicle’s midpoint.

questions.question: Label the following
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Axillary fossa
B) Anterior Axillary Line
C) Midaxillary Line
D) Posterior Axillary Line
questions.sourceExplanation: A is the axillary fossa. B anterior axillary line descends from the anterior fold, C midaxillary line from the apex of the axilla, and D posterior axillary line from the posterior fold.

questions.question: Label the following
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Scapular Line
B) Midvertebral Line
questions.sourceExplanation: A is the scapular line through the inferior scapular angle. B is the midvertebral line over spinous processes.

questions.question: Label the following
questions.printedAnswer:
A) Sternal Angle
B) Transverse Ridges
C) Body of Sternum
D) Xiphoid Process
E) Articular Facets for rib VII
F ) Articular Facets for rib III - VI
G) Articular Demi facets for rib II
H) Rib I attachment site
I) Articular site for clavicle
questions.sourceExplanation: A = sternal angle, B = transverse fusion ridges, C = body, D = xiphoid process, E = facet for seventh costal cartilage, F = facets for cartilages 3–6, G = demifacets for second cartilage, H = first cartilage attachment, I = clavicular notch. The second cartilage straddles the manubriosternal junction, whereas the clavicle articulates superolaterally with the manubrium.

questions.question:
A) Mention the site where the arrow is pointing
B) What lies behind this? (mention 3 important points)
questions.printedAnswer:
a) Sternal angle (or Angle of Louis)
b) 2nd rib, T4/T5 IV disc, and is where the Level of Bifurcation of Trachea
occurs
questions.sourceExplanation: The arrow indicates the manubriosternal junction. It identifies the second costal cartilage, the plane of the T4–T5 disc, and the approximate level of tracheal bifurcation.

questions.question:
A) Identify and name A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I , J, K
B) What type of rib is shown in the figure?
C) What ribs have this type of rib?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) A- Neck
B- Tubercle
C- Head
D- Internal Surface
E- Costal Groove
F- Tubercle
G- Neck
H- Crest
I- Articulate Facets
J- Articulate Facet
K- Non articulate surface
B) Typical Ribs
C) Ribs 3-9
questions.sourceExplanation: A/G = neck, B/F = tubercle, C = head, D = internal surface, E = costal groove, H = crest of head, I = facets of head, J = articular facet of tubercle, K = nonarticular area of tubercle. Ribs 3–9 are typically grouped as typical, with a two-faceted head, a neck and tubercle, and a costal groove along the inferior internal shaft.

questions.question:
A) Identify and name A, B, C, D, E, F
B) What type of rib is shown in the figure?
C) What ribs have this type of rib?
D)Why are there 2 grooves present?
questions.printedAnswer:
A) A- Head
B- Neck
C- Tubercle
D- Scalene Tubercle
E- Grooves
F- Costal Cartilage
B)Atypical Rib
C) Ribs 1,2,10-12
D) Subclavian Artery and vein
